#6780. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley Wears the Backless Dress to End All Backless Dresses

Every so often, a moment in the middle of the fashion month marathon makes even the weariest editors sit up a little straighter in their seats. This season, it came courtesy of Demna, whose spring 2027 show featured a formidable cast of characters, from sultry sirens in sequins to coiffured OAPs to rich-bitch equestrians. Joining this crew was Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, in an enormous faux-fur coat and sunglasses, looking like the kind of woman who knows her way around a prenup.

Catching up ahead of the LACMA gala this weekend, the star confirmed that our new favorite leading lady is still very much in the room. “She’s back,” Huntington-Whiteley tells me, albeit wearing slightly less clothing this time around. She swapped the enrobing coat for an ostensibly demure high-necked black dress that’s more of a barely-there number at the back. “It’s very Demna-coded, and I think there’s definitely something very similar in spirit to the character,” she says.

The characters, Rosie explains, were divided into three archetypes: “The rebellious aristocrat, the snob and the eccentric. I actually felt like my character embodied a little of all three. There was something obviously very commanding and unapologetic about her, with a certain sort of eccentricity and attitude. I also love that she didn’t take herself too seriously.” It seems the transformation was convincing enough for Derek Blasberg to tell her, “I can see you dug really deep for this character.”

Rosie’s trip into the Demna-verse served as a reminder that a little theatrics can go a long way. “My job as a model is basically being able to step into different characters and explore a designer’s vision. It’s about really understanding their world and finding a way to bring that character to life that feels authentic and natural to me,” she says, adding: “It’s always a reminder, when you do projects like this, of how important attitude is with the clothes we embody. Ultimately, clothes are clothes, but the way you wear them, the attitude and the way you embody them are what really make something memorable, what makes something iconic.”

Rosie’s earliest memories of Gucci are firmly rooted in the Tom Ford era. “Of course, back then I could never afford Gucci, but what’s always struck me is that the brand has this glamour to it. It’s unapologetic,” she says. Those campaigns, she remembers, were everywhere when she was starting out, “at a time when fashion imagery felt like something you really studied and committed to memory. They become part of your reference bank, so to speak. I loved that era and always will. I’ve really worn and loved Gucci on the red carpet ever since, and certainly in my real life too.”

Wearing Gucci at the LACMA Art+Film Gala in 2012.

As for her favourite Gucci looks over the years, a few spring to mind. Currently taking the crown (aside from this weekend’s LACMA look, of course) was her 2012 LACMA appearance, for which she wore another open back number, this time in green. “It was sharp and clean, but really sexy.” Clearly, Rosie and Gucci have had a few good outings together, and if Demna has anything to do with it, there are probably a few more characters still to come.

#6779. 22 Killer Watches I Saw at One of New York’s Most Exclusive Collector Hangs

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

I knew the watch collector meetup I was going to was legit when its organizer sent this text to the group: “We’ve engaged an off-duty NYPD detective to work security for our dinner. So, now really no reason not to bring your best!”

Last Wednesday night, at a fancy steakhouse in Midtown Manhattan, I was reminded why I love these enthusiast-organized events. This one was relatively small in comparison to blowouts like Rolliefest, but the idea was the same: A dozen or so collectors brought along their most prized timepieces and plunked them down on the table unattended (besides the off-duty NYPD detective, of course). When I asked one attendee if I could take his Breguet—similar to one heading to auction this weekend with a $73,000 estimate—across the room to take a photograph, he reacted like I’d asked if I could breathe oxygen: Of course! What a silly question. Events like these genuinely reflect the best of the hobby: deeply passionate collectors who really just want to share their watches with like-minded obsessives.

Between bites of miniature beef wellingtons and medium-rare steak, the guests passed around and ogled the dozens of grails on display. There were new classics on the table—including Vacheron Constantin’s Ultra-Thin, a leading contender for watch of the year—alongside plenty of old ones, including every flavor of vintage Rolex, from GMT-Masters to Daytonas to Explorer IIs. I was standing with one collector as he examined a pretty vintage Rolex GMT-Master. He stopped and looked around. So-and-so must be here, he muttered aloud. How did he know? Because he recognized the shade of the patina on the dial.

This particular group started getting together a couple of years ago, after the collectors @HorologicallyMinded, @s_h_lemon, @null_islands, and @jmsfisk (everyone at the event asked to remain anonymous) met at another watch-related retreat. @HorologicallyMinded, or HM, says that collecting was at one point something he did in solitude. “People generally judge when they learn how much watches cost,” HM tells me. “You paid how much for that!?” But he and the other three founders began meeting up for monthly dinners before eventually taking turns to organize these larger events. “This group has been the most rewarding part of this hobby,” HM says. “It’s been so great to have a group of people that have a common interest, but it’s not work-related and no one judges.”

Although the group has grown, the core four are still instrumental in making sure the functions go off without a hitch, with just the right spread of watches on the tables. “It is very deliberate and the four of us generally coordinate on it,” HM says. “We specifically make sure there is something for everyone.” That means ensuring there are at least a handful of watches worth less than $10,000—this time, that included several Rolex Datejusts, a Vulcain Cricket, and a gold Breitling from the 1940s. “We knew we were having some relative newbies and different people have different budgets, and we want everyone to be comfortable.” On the other end of the spectrum, some grail-level pieces were special requests from other members of the group.

All the watches wound up getting plenty of TLC. “I love the fact that we’re a group that can, and did, totally geek out about a vintage Longines Legend Diver, while a Doré dial Patek is on the same table,” HM says.

Below are some of the very best pieces I saw that night.

A Patek Philippe ref. 3970, part of the house’s historic lineage of pieces that combine a perpetual calendar with a chronograph. The dial on this one is so tasty.

A skeletonized Breguet Ref. 3355PT00PA0—maybe the watch of the night for me—on a show-stopping platinum bracelet.

A few years ago, MB&F started making more approachable versions of its sci-fi-ready watches and allocating them through a lottery system. This is the M.A.D2, with an outer ring on the dial that spins around very quickly. It’s really fun.

The aforementioned Rolex GMT-Master is a ref. 16760, a model produced during the ’80s that’s nicknamed the “Sophia Loren” thanks to its curvaceous profile.

Omega has incredible stuff in its archives. This is a chronograph from the ’30s that’s controlled entirely through that single button at 2 o’clock.

A couple of real bangers here. The Vacheron on the left is known as the “Cioccolatone,” because it resembles a square of chocolate. At the center is the Patek Philippe ref. 3417, an antimagnetic watch with just about the prettiest typography you’ll ever see on a watch. Zohran Mamdani should adopt that cursive for signs in the city, because it can make just about anything look nice: Warning: Rats. Or maybe, No Dumping Here.

A cloisonné dial from—of all brands—IWC! I am such a sucker for a cloisonné, which refers to the intricate images carefully fashioned from wire and colorful baked enamel.

A beautiful example of one of the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch from the ’50s through the ’70s, back when the latter was still a rugged outdoor outfitter. The shades of orange, yellow, and blue are dreamy.

A monochromatic take on the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar, which was produced in the ’80s and ’90s but looks incredibly modern.

Universal Genève finally relaunched last year after decades on the shelf, but it’s hard to beat the originals. This Polerouter comes on an extremely cool “wave” bracelet, which basically uses a repeating chevron pattern to make the slinky bit of metal appear to be in motion.

During World War II, a dozen watch manufacturers came together to make models following a strict set of specifications for the British Ministry of Defence. One of those brands was Longines, which produced this strapping piece.

You didn’t think we’d wrap this list up without a gorgeous yellow-gold Daytona, did you?

The ultimate fusion of sport and luxury watches. Heuer supplied this ’70s-era Carrera to Ferrari’s racing team, including legendary drivers like Jacky Ickx, Niki Lauda, and Clay Regazzoni.

This Patek is cool, but the bracelet is insane.

This isn’t your average Patek Philippe Nautilus. PP began producing this reference 3800 in 1981 as a smaller counterpart to the original. The few times I’ve gotten to try one on, I’m always struck by how perfect the proportions are. It’s nice and thin and looks just right on the wrist.

The United States Merchant Marines’ logo really punches up this Day-Date.

The ref. 6541 is the most beloved version of the Rolex Milgauss. It was produced in the ’50s and features a signature honeycomb dial. One sold for $2.5 million at auction in 2023.

Is there a better way to time your yacht race than with this Heuer Skipper? Probably not.

It’s good to have doubles, especially when it comes to vintage Rolex Explorer IIs.

#6778. ‘Love Is Blind’ Star Rob Feeley Releases Lengthy Statement, Claims Fans Saw “a Small Part of a Much Bigger Experience”

Love Is Blind Season 11 star Rob Feeley is breaking his silence after a truly messy season. Quick recap: Rob got engaged to Michaella Giorgio in the Pods, but things went south during a cast-wide bar hang, where Rob told everyone he didn’t care about their relationship. Obviously, Michaella ended things, and Rob has some things to say now that he’s watched the season.

“Now that the reunion has aired and this chapter comes to a close, I’ve been reflecting on everything this experience has taught me,” Rob wrote on Instagram. “I’m truly grateful for the people I’ve met, the memories made, and the personal growth that came with both the incredible moments and the challenges. Looking back, there are moments I wish I had handled differently. There were times when I felt overwhelmed and let my emotions get the best of me. While those moments don’t reflect the person I strive to be, I recognize that they happened, and I take responsibility for how I reacted and where I could have communicated better.”

Rob went on to “acknowledge the hurt I caused Michaella,” saying “she deserved to feel heard, respected, and understood. I’m genuinely sorry for the times I fell short and for how I reacted in certain situations. My intentions don’t change the fact that my actions affected her, and I take responsibility for that.”

Rob also confirmed that he and Michaella have been in touch since the show filmed two (two!) years ago, and that they have moved on with “mutual respect.” He then reminded fans that they only saw “a small part of a much bigger experience, and not every conversation or situation can be fully understood from what makes it onto the screen.”

The burgeoning reality star ended his musings by teasing some “projects and opportunities” he’s been working on, and noted that “There’s a lot to look forward to in the coming weeks, and I’m excited to share what’s next.”

So...guess we’ll see what happens (next season of Perfect Match, perhaps?).

#6775. Studio Visit: The Unassuming Chinatown Space Where Zane Li Has Built an Award-Winning Brand

Behind designer Zane Li’s desk is an oversized whiteboard with every look from his spring 2027 collection neatly pinned up in orderly rows. “Every time I start a new collection, I always put the past collection behind me because I want to have an extension of ideas from the past season, and then see what we can do new,” he says. “Especially right now, we’re at the kind of inspiration-gathering and silhouette-designing phase.”

We’re at the Chinatown office and studio for his label Lii, located along a particularly trendy stretch of dingy Canal Street. It’s a surprisingly small, modest space considering how much the 26-year-old Li has captured the attention of the fashion industry in the three short years he’s been running his business. Just this year, he has taken home both the LVMH Karl Lagerfeld Prize for Innovation and the top honor at the CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund, and was also nominated for the CFDA Award for Emerging Designer of the Year.

Across from Li’s desk, industrial racks filled with past seasons’ designs.

The third-floor space is essentially a small white-walled square with high ceilings and three windows looking onto a balcony that faces an interior airshaft. On one wall is a vintage-style sink, and at the center of the room is a Donald Judd-ish birch table from the popular furniture shop Lichen in Ridgewood, Brooklyn. Directly across is a floor-to-ceiling industrial rod set-up stuffed with brightly-colored samples, some in plastic coverings.

Li’s desk is spare and tidy—an orange stapler and tape dispenser, a blue square of Post-Its, a paper cup of coffee, and a rectangular box of Chinese cigarettes. In some ways, it evokes his own work—familiar American sportswear shapes distilled into geometric forms and rendered in cheery Crayola hues of pink, red, powder blue, and kelly green. “Lii is about making familiar things unfamiliar, in a certain way—through fabrics, through colors,” Li says. “We want to take certain shapes into people’s real life and keep the volume, keep the look, but make the garment practical and make it accessible for the wearer.”

Art and photography are frequent starting points, and next to his desk is a baker’s rack stuffed with thick picture books. Not far from his laptop are photo printouts and a binder filled with fabrics. “We’re trying to see what kind of combo or what kind of formula looks good visually,” he says. “And from there I’ll start patterning, I’ll start designing, which is a personal and abstract process, I will say, because it’s not really ... I try not to start a collection from a garment. I kind of always try to start collections from either a piece of Ellsworth Kelly work, a piece of installation art, a Balenciaga gown.”

Li’s CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund and LVMH Karl Lagerfeld prize on a shelf.

Art and design books near Li’s desk are sources of inspiration.

Li lives just a few blocks away—he measures the time it takes for him to get from the studio to his home not in distance or in traditional markers of time, but in “half-ciggies.” “I can’t even finish a cigarette walking from here to my apartment,” he says. He splits his time between here, where the clothes are designed; China, where they are manufactured; and Paris, where his press and sales teams are located. He starts his days around 9 or 10 am, grabbing orange juice at the deli downstairs to drink while checking emails and dealing with urgent press or sales matters. Then he’ll go out and get lunch from a local spot, grab a coffee, and start the design part of his day, which often can stretch to 2 am, to stay in touch with his partners in China.

Li pulls a Rineke Dijkstra book of photography from his crowded shelf as an example of a source of inspiration he returns to. “Her narrative about people, about what you can see from an image, and what their moods and emotions are, is really strong,” he says. “And I tend to want my garment, my design or idea, to evoke the same feeling. So, sometimes if I feel bored or if I don’t feel like what I want to do, then I’ll look at this book, and it gives me an instant hit—and then we’ll start from there.”

Printouts or art and archival fashion serve as inspiration.

Zane has a board from the previous season set up behind his desk to help him work on the season ahead.

Li pulls off a three-tiered, asymmetrical skirt made from a spongy scuba fabric as an example of a recent design he’s particularly proud of. “It’s quite comfortable to wear, but, also, has this supportive shape thanks to the fabric. And we just decided to make a paneled skirt with darts that’s feminine, but I think the material made it look sporty as well.” He also pulls out an oversized, color-blocked polo shirt with hanging fabric off the sleeves. “We always try to explore ideas of a T-shirt because we feel like this is something so practical and so easy, but there’s a lot of possibilities in it,” he says. “I like the shape and having a graphic-ness on the body. We tested 10 different prototypes—about what kind of proportion, how long the strings should be to make the garment look balanced, and so on. It’s kind of fun. It’s kind of like you’re drawing squares or drawing just circles on the paper, and you’re trying to find the perfect, the most balanced circle on the paper.”

“It’s kind of like the practice of that,” he continued. “Which is really flat, and I really enjoy the transformation from that flat pattern into something that people wear on the body, and feels quite three-dimensional.”

It’s a marvel to think that Li has built so much from such a small space in such a short time. Currently, he is the only full-time employee—his husband, the stylist Jason Rider, is heavily involved but has his own career, while his studio and production managers are still freelance. Li says he plans to use the winnings from his recent prizes to help build out a more robust team. There is one silent team member keeping watch in the corner: a dummy mannequin, usually used for draping. Li mostly designs on his computer, so she’s more of a mascot. “She’s my good luck charm,” Li says, giving her a hug. “She brings me comfort.”

#6774. Martine Rose Is Balenciaga’s New Creative Director

Martine Rose is Balenciaga's new creative director. The London-based designer will start on November 16, taking over the French-Spanish label from Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose departure was announced yesterday after three seasons at the house.

It's the first time Martine Rose has taken charge of a major fashion house, but it isn't her first Balenciaga gig. She worked as a menswear consultant under Demna from 2015 to 2018, helping shape the oversized proportions and left-field clothes that defined his early years at the brand. Now she's returning with control of the whole enterprise.

“It is a true privilege to be appointed creative director of Balenciaga, a house with an extraordinary heritage and a fearless creative spirit,” Rose said in a statement. “Balenciaga has been shaped by remarkable creative talents before me. I am committed to honoring this legacy and look forward to creating the next chapter in this rich and beautiful story.”

Rose founded her eponymous label in 2007 and has built it into one of the most influential brands in British fashion. Her collections pull from soccer and nightlife club culture, music, and the everyday wardrobes of London dwellers: suits get stretched out or squeezed in, tracksuits become tailoring, loafers turn into mules. It's menswear, on her terms.

Through her career, Rose has collaborated with Nike, Clarks, Supreme, Stüssy, and Tommy Hilfiger, and her clothes have been worn by everyone from Kendrick Lamar to Lewis Hamilton to Timothée Chalamet. But despite her idiosyncratic influence over what menswear looks like now, Rose has yet to have worked the top job at a house of Balenciaga's size. Her appointment makes her the first woman to lead the brand in its 109-year history. Her appointment makes her the first woman to lead the brand in its 109-year history.

“Martine Rose embodies this spirit with a fresh, fearless and deeply contemporary vision,” said Kering CEO Luca de Meo. “Her connection to the new generation and her instinctive understanding of culture bring a new dimension to the house.”

It's a big appointment, and one fashion people have wanted for a long time. Rumors that Rose had signed with Balenciaga have been swirling for weeks, but now it's official. The house hasn't yet said when her first collection will arrive, but whenever it does, we'll all be watching.

#6772. Rihanna Completes Her Sporty Shopping Look With a Pair of Suede Sneaker Mules

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Rihanna is simply not on the same fashion playing field as the rest of us. Sure, she’s besties with some of the world’s biggest designers, and she has access to many of the latest collections before they even hit the stores, but she also just has an utterly sui generis approach to styling. In her universe, a burger run calls for a tiered, tiramisu-colored maxi dress and clerical errands are done in oversize, avant-garde suits. When it comes to tricks, like wearing a foulard as a skirt or treating an exposed-bra as a statement piece, she’s always at the head of the pack. Then, of course, there’s her maternity wear, which speaks quite loudly for itself.

So, it should come as no surprise that, even when she’s keeping things casual, Rihanna still manages to slip in a fabulous surprise or two. And on Sunday, that intriguing touch came courtesy of some hybrid footwear, which RiRi casually incorporated into her sporty off-duty look.

As she enjoyed a bit of nighttime shopping at the Grove in Los Angeles, the “Diamonds” singer bundled up in a baby-pink button-up and cocoa-colored slacks, which she layered underneath an ecru trench with a shiny golden lining.

Rihanna tied the coat loosely around her waist so as not to conceal the Neapolitan-colored outfit underneath, and she complemented her trench’s interior with a thick gold collar necklace. In her hand, she carried a monogrammed Speedy from Louis Vuitton, and she popped on a pair of chunky creamsicle-colored sunglasses from Saint Laurent.

But it was the most nondescript element that turned out to be the most striking. To match her coat, the singer and business mogul slipped into a pair of buff-colored suede sneakers from the New Balance x Miu Miu collaboration, which were first unveiled back in 2024. However, these hybrid shoes weren’t actually sneakers at all, but rather mules, giving new shape to the classic New Balance 530 SL silhouette that they were inspired by.

And this is just the latest evidence of the ongoing designer deconstruction of the shoe. At Chanel, Matthieu Blazy is offering up sandals that only cover the wearer’s heels. At Saint Laurent, Anthony Vaccarello presented Oxfords made out of see-through PVC.

Now, leave it to Rihanna to pull out the perfect transitional footwear for fall.

#6770. Here’s Your First Look at the Broadway Cast of ‘Paddington: The Musical’

Hold on to your hats (and your little blue toggle coats): Paddington is New York City-bound.

Next year, the multiple-Olivier Award-winning theatrical sensation that is Paddington: The Musical opens at the Al Hirschfeld Theatre on Broadway—bringing with it, yes, the four-foot-tall puppet that is Paddington Bear himself, but also a wonderfully star-studded cast.

Performers in the New York production will include Kelvin Dukes as Tony, Drew Gehling (Waitress) as Mr. Brown, Allison Guinn (Operation Mincemeat) as Lady Sloane, Tony Hale (Veep, Arrested Development) as Mr. Curry, J. Quinton Johnson (Hamilton) as Grant, Leslie Rodriguez Kritzer (The Fantasticks) as Millicent Clyde, Zonya Love (The Color Purple) as Tanya, Serena Parrish (Don’t Say Good Luck) as Judy Brown, Karen Ziemba (Contact) as Mrs. Bird, Chip Zien (Into the Woods) as Mr. Gruber, and, as Mrs. Brown, one Jessie Mueller (Waitress, Carousel), making her first appearance on Broadway since starring in Tracy Letts’s The Minutes in 2022.

Additionally, Arti Shah and James Hameed, who brought Paddington Bear to life onstage in the West End, will reprise their joint role at the Hirschfeld.

“This just felt like the right show, with the right message,” Mueller tells Vogue of her grand return to the Main Stem. “Paddington is a character I’ve known and loved all my life! And I’m so excited to be back on Broadway to share this story of love, family, kindness and inclusion.”

“I really hope the Broadway audience can find a place in their hearts to look after this bear,” says the show’s composer, Tom Fletcher. (Paddington’s book has been adapted by Jessica Swale, and Luke Sheppard directs.) “Writing the songs for Paddington: The Musical has been the greatest honor of my life, and it goes without saying that getting to bring our show to New York is an actual dream come true.”

He goes on: “The importance of kindness is at the heart of our story in London, and I hope we can bring that message to New York and spread kindness like marmalade.”

New Yorkers should be on the lookout for a polite little bear from Peru in the spring: Previews of Paddington: The Musical begin on Tuesday, March 30, with an opening night set for Sunday, April 18.

#6769. Can Rian Johnson’s New Camera App Make Your iPhone Photos Look Like His Movies?

Shooting beautiful photos with an iPhone isn’t always the simplest task. Though the cameras are serviceable for a phone, Apple’s complex, built-in processing usually spits out vibrant but flatly lit images. Enter Knives Out and Star Wars director Rian Johnson and his longtime cinematographer Steve Yedlin. With the help of programmer Eric Johnson, the filmmakers recently introduced Chromagraph, a new camera app for iOS built on the same color science Yedlin developed over many years for their movies.

Open up the app, and you’re met with a relatively simple interface—in some ways, even simpler than Apple’s stock camera app—that serves an even simpler purpose: taking great pictures. Snap a photo, and the app captures an image in RAW format, containing the unprocessed data directly from the camera’s sensor. Then it applies Yedlin’s color science, creating a very “filmic” look with more contrast, grain, halation, and an overall color curve resembling classic film stocks. The user can then adjust the look of their pictures any which way they want using the provided sliders.

Chromagraph is hardly the first replacement camera app for the iPhone—and yes, it’s iPhone-only for now. Apps like Halide and Adobe’s Project Indigo offer a lot more options and might be more fit for professional use. But to Johnson and Yedlin, Chromagraph is built to reflect the more point-and-shoot quality of a smartphone camera, keeping its UI simple and its feature set relatively small, giving the average user an easy new tool for taking beautiful photos with the device they carry around every day.

A week after it went live, Johnson and Yedlin sat down to talk about what inspired them to build Chromagraph, reverse-engineering Apple’s own processing techniques, the often misguided debate between film and digital, and the magic of taking a beautiful picture.

Rian Johnson: With love. [Laughs]. I take a lot of pictures with my phone. I'm an amateur photographer, and I have a film camera that I use. I have a few other cameras, but the reality is, this is what I walk around with all day long. I had gone through different versions of taking regular pictures and pulling them into photo editors and trying to get them to look the way I wanted them. And then I started messing around with third-party apps to take RAW photos and then taking those into editors, and that gave me a little more control. But I realized what I really wanted was to be able to take a picture with my iPhone and have it, at least to start, look the way that our movies look, which are done by taking digital cinema files and Steve applying color science to them. I asked Steve, "Could we do this on an iPhone?" And I think Steve was a little hesitant, just because the iPhone sensor, while it's very good for a phone sensor, it's still a phone-sized sensor. It's still pretty noisy. There's a lot of limitations. But come on, let's just try.

Steve Yedlin: The reason that you can get better quality images out of the phone—even though, as Rian said, the sensor is great for a phone—is this burst-merge methodology, where you're actually taking several shots at different exposures and merging them to reduce noise in the shadows and extend latitude in the highlights. And while it's computational, it's real photographic data. It's not generated or artificial. It's photo data. Since Rian wanted to make it into a camera app instead of just processing. As Eric, my coding partner, and I dug into it, we realized on the Pro iPhones, as a developer with the API, you can request Apple's ProRAW that's already done that burst-merge thing. So with the Pro phones, it was a little bit easier, but with the non-Pro phones you can’t, as a developer, request that from the camera. It just won't do it. So we made our own burst-merge for non-Pro phones. We knew that if we were actually gonna give this to other people, and it's not just for us, we know more people have non-Pro than Pro. It would be too bad if every non-Pro phone has reduced latitude and higher noise.

Yedlin: That was about nine or 10 weeks. We got 20 years of color science and then nine or 10 weeks to bundle it for iOS.

Johnson: Well, I guess we use the word "look" kind of liberally. One of the fun things about the app, I think, is that it starts out just looking good. It does have a perspective on what looking good means, and starts out like that. What I love is you're starting out with an image that doesn't look like an iPhone picture. It doesn't have the flattened HDR dynamics. If there's some kind of garish light source in the frame, it handles that the way, to my eye, a film camera would. It doesn't do any kind of digital freaking out with it. It just looks like a beautiful, mellow, very filmic image. And then, it's not even necessarily that it looks like our movies. What I've been enjoying recently is seeing how far I can push it using the different controls in the app and how many different quote-unquote looks I can actually achieve starting from the base.

Johnson: Well, I mean, again, there's a little bit of a thing right now in movies and in visual culture where “filmic look” has come to mean a very specific thing.

Johnson: The thing is, when we say “filmic look,” the reality is, movies that for nearly a century existed on film had so many different looks to them. I guess just the notion that film looks a certain way is part of a bigger thing right now that I enjoy pushing back against. But I'll say, with the app, it looks like you started with a medium like film, not an iPhone sensor.

Yedlin: If you think about the pre-digital days where there were only a couple of film stocks that were barely different from each other, and maybe one or two print stocks that were also barely different from each other, but you got all these movies look totally different ways. You're never going to say that a Gordon Willis movie looks like a Vittorio Storaro movie. There's so much craftsmanship that goes into it. And this thing isn't the photographer; it's just the photo processing.

It’s just like, we’re not going to use a different recipe if Wake Up Dead Man is more dark and gothic with horror movie elements, and Glass Onion is more sun-drenched Greece. That's in the content. That's the artist, the craftsmanship of shooting it, so they look totally different. The whole thing about a processing system is that it looks artful no matter what that content is. It's not making the “look,” or the craftsmanship, or the content, but it's always going to look artful. The app does very much use the model of how film dyes work.

Johnson: And the reality is we both grew up watching movies shot on film. We came up together shooting stuff on film. We love that look. So that's a personal subjective thing.

Johnson: On the most zoomed-out level, what you just described, “you shoot it and it looks good,” it describes when I just shoot with my Leica M6, when I shoot with a film camera. If you get the exposure right then it's kind of dialed in. It also, though, describes how I've gotten used to shooting our movies when we shoot them digitally. We don't have a digital technician on set tweaking all the stuff. What Steve does is, he's created his color science and a LUT that basically interprets what you shoot, that's preloaded on the camera. So we can really just shoot with the Alexa [digital camera] as if we're shooting with a film camera. We can just meter it, and we can go, and we'll know that what comes out is gonna be in the pocket of what we want.

The other thing about shooting with your phone: very often, you just see something, you pull your phone out of your pocket, you want to be snapping as soon as you can. So the simplicity is really reflective of what you use it for. Honestly, one of the things that we kept coming back to was how smart Apple's UI design was in their camera app, which makes sense. They're great designers. We would try to do something clever, and then it would be funky, and then we’d go back to the camera app and say, "Well, how did Apple do it?" We're also not UI designers. We're still tweaking this. We're still taking any suggestions anyone out there has. This is very much still a first pass at it.

Johnson: For me, I open it up and it works just fine. For me, it's literally just my thumb naturally tends to be here when I do this, so I want it to be there when I press this. It's things like that, until you really start spending hours using the app, or put it out there and have people using it, that you know what you need to fix.

Johnson: First of all, it's been extraordinary and really emotional for both of us to see the beautiful photos that people are taking with the app. We really made this just so we would have it. It was almost an afterthought, putting it out there. What I love, day to day, is I'm taking more photos with my phone and it makes me think about light differently.

Johnson: It's not just capturing everything. Suddenly, when I see a scene and I'm taking out my phone to shoot it, I'm thinking about the contrast of the sunlight versus the dark areas of the frame because I know there's going to be more disparity between them in this finished image. I'm thinking more filmically and photographically, which is fun.

Johnson: It’s a point-and-shoot camera. The thing is, even though we want it to look good, there's a very specific use for your phone in taking pictures, which is exactly what you describe. You don't want to be sitting there fiddling with a bunch of settings. You want to pull your phone out and snap what's right in front of your face. We weren't aiming to make a tool on the level of a SLR camera, a DSLR, or even a good mirrorless full-frame camera.

Yedlin: I think that simplicity—we don't have a million looks, the simple UI, the point-and-shoot—it's all part of the same thing, which is the joy of photography. It’s what's so fun about seeing everybody enjoying it and snapping these pictures. It's not a professional camera, and it also admits what the iPhone can and can't do. We've had some people ask for more professional, manual controls over exposure and stuff like that, but the bottom line is that at the core of it, there's only certain things that camera can do. There's both the physical restrictions, but also the restrictions of what Apple even allows you, as a third party, to request from the camera. So part of it is just stripping all that out and not pretending that it's this pro camera.

Johnson: No, we haven't really considered that. But I'm all for anything that's fun. Somebody else asked me a question, phrased in a different way: could you have a “Wes Anderson” look? Or noir, black-and-white film, or this or that? You can achieve any of those looks with just a little bit of messing the sliders around. The idea of thinking of it as this kind of magic filter you put on that instantly makes it look like that is… I don't know, that seems less fun to me.

Yedlin: Also, I think it's a misattribution. I mean, Wes Anderson shoots on the same film stocks that everybody else shoots on. It's not like when you snap the camera, it's going to make everybody stand square to the wall and make Luke Wilson be in your shot.

Johnson: That's one of the things I enjoy about it. And actually the same way that I do with film, I love the little gap between [looking through] the viewfinder and then opening up the photo. I develop my own film, and it’s a little bit like that magic moment when you pull it out of the final rinse and go, “What did we get here?” That's a kind of a feature, not a bug.

Johnson: Yeah, but also I would say there's a difference between how I think about it when we're shooting our films professionally—we want the entire film to have a consistent look, and we talk about what that look is—and as an amateur, just shooting pictures for my own pleasure, where I much more enjoy the thing I just described. I don't want to sit there in a DI suite and tune it. The notion of having it be kind of, snap it, and then, “Ooh, what did I get?” And then, “Ooh, what can I do with it?” It’s a bit more like opening a Christmas present as opposed to engineering a toy from the ground up.

Yedlin: And the other thing is, the fact that it's possible doesn't mean that you know how to do it. The reason we have all of our own complicated math is because we can't do this with any of the available sliders that would be in a color corrector or a photo editing app, or anything like that. When we shoot our films, we're seeing it live. We don't have to wait for the process. To me that's really satisfying. There's a lot of movies where the color grade is such a heavy lift, where they're inventing every shot from scratch. We save a lot of time because the overall look starts with what we want, and then we can use that limited time to really finesse it and for the colorist to do his magic.

Johnson: Yeah, it's not a moral stance. The first Knives Out was the movie where we really switched over to shooting full digital, and it was a long, long, long discussion to the point where Steve and I only made the decision because our line producer came into the office and was like, "You have to make this this decision because we have to order a camera package."

Johnson: That's a big part of it. Steve said during that discussion, "It's honestly easier for me to make digital look like film than to make film look like film.” Because it has to go through a digital backend process regardless, and all you're doing is adding steps in terms of the scan and the limitations of all that. With The Last Jedi, where we shot a combo of film and digital, we had some frustrations with both the physical film stocks and also the cameras themselves. Work was being put in jeopardy because this is literally antiquated pieces of equipment that you're working with.

I don't want to just shit-talk film or the process. It would be fun to accept some limitations and say, “No, for this one we're going to shoot on film again.” But I guess the other thing that I really fundamentally agree with Steve about, an argument that he made that really landed with me, is just to let go of the notion of giving up your control and your artistry, in terms of what you want it to look like, to a brand name. “It’ll look that way because I'm shooting on X or Y or Z.” To kind of take control back. “I want it to feel like this, I want it to look like this. How do we achieve that?” People who shot on film for years and years and years, for decades, for the past century, did that. They would bend it to their will. And I think today there's a little bit of a magic thinking that started to permeate visual culture, which is you shoot on film to get the “film look.”

Johnson: I’ve taken beautiful shots with the stock app, absolutely. As somebody who loves cameras, who loves tech, who loves amateur photography, that just goes with the territory. There's a thousand different ways to do it. There are people taking vibrant, large format digital shots that I think are astounding, and there are people taking glass plate, eight-by-ten photos with a camera from the 1800s that I think look absolutely amazing. It’s just enjoying the process and getting something you think is beautiful.

#6766. Sabrina Carpenter Would Love to Star in a 9 to 5 Movie Musical

The star talks Dolly Parton, the French New Wave, and her Johnnie Walker short with Damien Chazelle.

For Sabrina Carpenter, a song and a role each offer a different way into a story. “Acting and music have always gone hand in hand for me,” she tells ELLE exclusively. “With music, I get to tell stories through my own perspective, and with acting I get to step into someone else’s world and bring their story to life, and that is always an exhilarating feeling for me.”

Carpenter gets to move between those perspectives in a new Johnnie Walker film directed by Damien Chazelle, the Oscar-winning visionary behind Whiplash and La La Land. With the Short n’ Sweet star at its center, the clip nods to French New Wave cinema through the director’s signature motion-driven style.

The short begins with Carpenter, in a mod embellished minidress, stepping into an unusually quiet party. As someone pours her a Go Go Highball, her signature Johnnie Walker cocktail, the scene comes to life: the guests spring into motion, and Carpenter gets swept up in the revelry while a meta quartet of directors looks on. Here, she opens up to ELLE about working with Chazelle, her favorite New Wave films, and the movie musical she’d most want to star in (hint: it’s a certain blonde’s workplace comedy).

This past year has been pretty surreal. Coachella will always be a standout for me, probably for the rest of my life. I had so much fun creating that show. Also getting to perform onstage this year with Madonna and Stevie Nicks. [I’m] still processing that.

Sometimes the best moments are just spending time with the people you love, and this summer spending some downtime with my close friends and my sister, we loved our Go Go Highballs for sure.

Getting ready for my Met Gala after-party comes to mind. But I can’t always reveal all the details to you guys; there’s no fun in that.

Working with Damien was a dream! I’ve admired his work for so long, and he has a brilliant way of making even the smallest moments feel larger than life. I love how he was able to capture the humor and playfulness that come with life’s unexpected moments.

I love La La Land! I think there’s something really special about creating a short moment or scene that feels almost like a whole movie, so I’m always trying to approach these projects from a cinematic viewpoint.

Two of my favorites are The Umbrellas of Cherbourg and Cleo from 5 to 7.

Well, I just rewatched 9 to 5 and you know I’m the biggest Dolly [Parton] fan. So that would be a fun one.

#6765. After a Devastating Fire, This South Australia Lodge Has Returned as One of the World’s Wildest, Most Wonderful Stays

The first thing you’ll notice while driving across Kangaroo Island is the trees. More specifically, their strange, topsy-turvy appearance: blackened, skeletal eucalyptus trunks that sprout lime-green foliage from about halfway up. As you get closer to the southern edge of the island, where the land falls away into the roiling waters—the final frontier of the inhabited world before Antarctica—the foliage becomes increasingly flattened and twisted, whipped by the unrelenting Southern Ocean winds. Pulling into a set of pale, discreet limestone gates and up a series of long, winding roads that serve as a driveway, you might even spot the charred branches’ fresh leaves glowing almost neon in the afternoon light.

And then, it appears: a sinuous, low-slung ribbon of limestone and glass hugging the clifftop, an architectural marvel that shines like a beacon above the scrubby, sun-bleached coast. At last, you’ve made it all the way to Southern Ocean Lodge.

No matter where you’re traveling from, it’s an undertaking to get here (though it will become a little easier once Qantas launches its direct New York to Sydney flights in 2028). But from the very first glimpse, you’ll sense it was all worth it—not only is Southern Ocean Lodge one of the world’s most epic and spectacularly situated hotels, but it’s also a symbol of extraordinary resilience. When the catastrophic Black Summer bushfires tore across Kangaroo Island in January 2020, the original lodge—first built in 2008, and widely considered the crown jewel of Australian luxury tourism—was reduced to ash in a matter of hours. For founders James and Hayley Baillie, the husband-and-wife duo behind the property, walking among the ruins was understandably devastating. But they quickly decided the hotel must have a second act. The original architect, Max Pritchard, went back to the drawing board to reimagine the property from the ground up, refining its footprint to embed it even more deeply into its surroundings, and in late 2023, it finally reopened—sleeker, tougher, and somehow even more breathtaking than before.

What changed? The angles, for one. Pritchard reoriented the entire 25-suite building slightly to the southwest, ensuring every curved glass pavilion now frames the uninterrupted drama of Hanson Bay’s rugged headlands. A subtle tweak on paper, but in practice, it’s a revelation: morning light now falls even deeper into the living spaces, and the vast blue skies and white surf crashing against the bluffs are a permanent, constantly shifting wallpaper. The spa was moved into its own pavilion, and a four-bedroom compound with its own infinity pool was added just above the hotel’s central hub. Perhaps most importantly, the retreat is now an off-grid fortress and engineered to the highest-tier bushfire standards, ensuring it’s ready to endure whatever Mother Nature throws at it next.

On the balmy day I arrived in late spring, the scene was altogether more calm: a light sea breeze barely ruffled the coastal mallee. Stepping into the Great Room, the lodge’s communal heart, the ceiling seems to hover weightlessly, and the panoramic, floor-to-ceiling glass walls curve around like the cockpit of a spaceship. There, my travel companion (in fact, my mom) and I were handed welcome glasses of Adelaide Hills sparkling and canapés—crisp seed crackers topped with crushed avocado and golden arancini crowned with a cloud of shaved cheese—then ushered directly toward the view of rolling green and gold headlands drifting down into a crescent of pristine white sand stretching as far as the eye can see. There was no formal check-in process, as all of that had been done even before arrival, and nearly everything here—the food, the experiences, and even the cellar full of curated South Australian wines—is included in the nightly rate. Sitting beside the suspended, Jetsons-esque fireplace with a cocktail in hand as sea eagles circle outside, the already whisper-thin threshold between the serene, glass-walled sanctuary of the resort and the untamed wilderness beyond seemed to dissipate entirely.

The effect in the rooms was similar: we were guided down the curved, light-dappled corridor to a Flinders Suite—after the intrepid British navigator Matthew Flinders, who charted (and named) Kangaroo Island in 1802—where the floor plan steps down into a glass-wrapped sunken lounge designed to feel as if it’s floating above the coastline. At three in the afternoon, the space was still lit with honeyed sunshine, picking out the crisp oatmeal and fresh ocean blues of the interiors, while a small fireplace crackled away on the far wall. And as the afternoon melted into evening, the mood had mellowed even further. The stark white clifftops in the distance warmed to a shade of amber, casting long shadows across the dunes. By the time we were getting dressed for dinner, the horizon was deep, bruised pink, and, stepping outside, you could just about see the Southern Cross constellation sparkling in the twilight sky.

As for that dinner? Every meal here a masterclass in hyper-local dining. (Anyone who’s been to Australia already knows how universally excellent the food is across the board—so for something to dazzle at this level takes serious culinary chops.) Meals revolve around whatever has arrived from island producers that morning—when I was there, that included sweet Kangaroo Island marron from local purveyor Scott Wilson, silky confit king salmon, and handmade orecchiette tossed with fennel-spiked pork and garden peas. (Naturally, I felt it was my journalistic duty to try both mains.) Sitting in the candlelit dining room as the dark fully swallowed the headlands—and even with guests seated at different tables—the room had the warm, convivial feeling of a private dinner party. Then again, that was probably also helped by the fact that, should you so wish, every dish can arrive accompanied by unpretentious pairings from that encyclopedic wine list, which runs the gamut from crisp coastal whites to velvety reds from vineyards on the island itself.

Somehow, I’ve got this far without even mentioning the wildlife—that’s primarily why people come to Kangaroo Island, after all. (Clue’s in the name, I suppose.) Even on the drive over, after our up-and-down 30-minute prop flight from Adelaide, we spotted wallabies hopping through the scrub and clusters of Kangaroo Island kangaroos through the ramshackle roadside fences; simply lazing around the lodge itself presents plenty of opportunities to watch ospreys soar past the windows, or to use the provided binoculars in your room to keep watch for pods of dolphins carving through the breaks below.

The real highlights, though, are the daily excursions led by the lodge’s team of in-house naturalists. They rotate shifts between guiding drives and sharing local lore at dinner, and many are in their 20s and 30s, here on three- to six-month seasonal residencies, ensuring they’re still as excited by it all as you are. Don’t let those fresh faces fool you, however: almost all of them are either studying for (or already hold) degrees in environmental science, marine biology, or conservation, and they carry that formidable academic depth with classic Aussie irreverence. Our guide on two afternoons, Angela, could break down the exact timeline of the post-bushfire regenerative cycle, yet introduced a sprawling colony of Australian sea lions by noting that their daily routine of sleeping 20 hours and sunning themselves on the sand was “basically me on my days off.”

On the subject of those sea lions: The following morning, Angela took us and a few fellow guests 40 minutes or so away in a minivan and down onto the wide, windswept beaches of Seal Bay, where we were able to walk (albeit slowly and quietly) just yards from dozens of wild sea lions. Some were dozing in tangled pairs right in the dune grass, while another sat upright like a whiskered Buddha, tilting its snout toward the salty surf spray. Upon walking to the water’s edge, one curious pup swam right over to me and surfaced just a few feet away, before somersaulting back beneath the waves—pure magic.

Later, venturing inland into the gums to the Hanson Bay Wildlife Sanctuary, the wildlife safari continued with a stroll through the eucalyptus forests, where we spotted a solitary koala wedged asleep in the crook of a high fork in the branches; upon stepping out into the wide-open pastures, we wandered through packs of kangaroos bounding solo across open ground, nibbling at tall she-oak branches, and heading to the shaded undergrowth to nurse their little joeys.

The most breathtaking visit of all, however, was the afternoon out that came billed as Wonders of Kangaroo Island. Wondrous, indeed: Over three and a half hours traversing Flinders Chase National Park on the island’s rugged western tip, the weather took on a moody, cinematic flavor as the skies turned steel gray and the Southern Ocean grew especially tempestuous. First up was a visit to Admirals Arch, where a timber boardwalk snakes down through the coastal heath toward the sea. Descending into the enormous limestone grotto, where jagged stalactites hung like giant teeth, we could hear a mysterious chorus of asthmatic grunts and wheezes; peering through veils of salty sea-mist, we discovered it was the barking of half a dozen raucous long-nosed fur seals, slipping and sliding around the slick rock ledges and tidepools.

Then, we paid a visit to the delightfully named Remarkable Rocks: a group of colossal smooth granite boulders, appearing from the far distance like a mythical sea monster that’s washed ashore. Up close, it’s more like a surrealist sculpture park, 500 million years in the making. Hollowed out by centuries of wind and sea into fantastical, wave-like shapes, the rocks perch precariously on the edge of the abyss, their weathered gray surfaces splashed with rust-like orange lichen. As the gale-force winds whipped so hard you could lean forward into the gusts and still remain upright, with nothing between us and the endless emptiness of the Antarctic on the other side, it was impossible not to feel small, even insignificant. It was strangely comforting.

Back at the lodge that evening, after a long, luxurious bath, it was time for another slap-up meal—seared beef carpaccio with pickled shallots, followed by pan-roasted barramundi over braised Asian greens, crowned with a nest of crispy enoki. (All washed down with a yuzu mocktail for me and a velvety local Shiraz for my mom.) On the way back to the room, I paused before a delicate, quiet installation along the hallway wall. Mounted against the smooth plaster were fragments of melted glass, charred stone, and shattered pottery gathered directly from the ashes of the original property after the catastrophic 2020 fires. The work is titled Relics, and was created by local Kangaroo Island artist Janine Mackintosh; as the placard accompanying it noted, Mackintosh didn’t want the piece to feel grim, but rather a joyful tribute to the lodge that stood here first.

There was plenty of heartache and hand-wringing after the devastation wrought by the fires, to be sure—and one imagines there were several moments when the Baillies doubted it would even be possible to recreate the singular alchemy of this place. Thank goodness they did. Really, there could be no greater testament to the indomitable spirit and grit of this island community than bringing its crown jewel, Southern Ocean Lodge, back—perhaps not bigger, but undoubtedly better than ever before.

#6764. Bob Dylan Just Dropped a 39-Disc Box Set. I Listened to Every Single One

It showed up in my inbox on a Tuesday afternoon without any particular fanfare, just an email from Legacy Recordings with a link to a stream. Artist: Bob Dylan. Title: Rolling Thunder Revue — The 1976 Live Recordings. Total Tracks: 381.

The link brought me to a bare-bones Sony Music web page, a couple light grey boxes arranged against a dark grey background. A small window in the middle of the page occupied maybe 10% of the available space. Inside the window were lines of text with lengthy, baroque file names, one on top of another. You could see about five at a time, starting with the first:

Bob Dylan_The Rolling Thunder Revue The 1976 Live Recordings_G0100060414779_01_01_Visions of Johanna_USSM12603067_CT122.

Bob Dylan_The Rolling Thunder Revue The 1976 Live Recordings_G0100060414779_01_02_If You See Her, Say Hello_USSM12603068_CT122.

This, it hardly needs to be said, is not the ideal way to familiarize yourself with the 31 hours and 18 minutes of new music included in the latest box set from Bob Dylan Industries. Like previous installments of the Live Recordings series, 1976 is an exhaustive accounting of (nearly) every second of (nearly) every show and concert given by Bob Dylan on a legendary tour. If a document of a performance from this tour exists, it is here, whether you want it or not.

There’s a certain thrill to a release like this, especially for the Dylan mujahideen, those of us willing to engage in the struggle. The 1976 Live Recordings is best thought of as a choose-your-own-adventure set, allowing you the opportunity to ramble along with the Rolling Thunder Revue at whatever pace you find comfortable. You can dip in on St. Petersburg (4/23/76) for the first recorded edition of “Idiot Wind,” then mosey on to Gainesville (4/25/76) for the only-ever performance of “Dink’s Song,” then settle in for a long date with Oklahoma City (5/18/76), one of the strongest complete shows. And if you want to summit the whole mountain—well, hit “play” on Lakeland (4/18/76) and let it rip. Just remember to stay hydrated.

As exciting as the sheer volume of new Bob Dylan music is, these ultra-complete tour retrospectives can be an intimidating listening experience. This is especially true in the case of The 1976 Live Recordings, which captures not the crackerjack bonhomie of the inaugural Rolling Thunder Revue, but the second, flabbier incarnation—halitosis and head scarves rather than whiteface and roses.

Dylan caught lightning in a bottle with the first Rolling Thunder, trucking around northeastern college towns with his ramshackle rock carnival while simultaneously 1) shooting an autofictional art film, and 2) trying to piece his broken marriage back together (partially by forcing his wife to act in said art film). The looks were immaculate, the vibes heady, the performances electric. Just peep a few minutes of a 1975 “Isis”—talk about the ghost of electricity howling in the bones of a face. The music press tailed the show from town to town throughout, breathlessly reporting on the latest feats of derring-do from Bob and co-conspirators. Rolling Thunder became a viral sensation, a meme, an object of FOMO decades before the term was invented.

For Dylan, it was the culmination of a thrilling 24-month period in which he’d returned to touring, recorded three brilliant albums, and reclaimed his reputation as the most vital force in rock songs. Taken together, Planet Waves, Blood On The Tracks, and Desire, along with the Before The Flood tour in ‘74 and Rolling Thunder in ‘75, seemed a clear statement of intent. You can’t repeat the past? Whaddya mean you can’t, of course you can.

Riding high on good will and good press, Bob got the band back together the following year. It was only natural. The first Rolling Thunder had been an experiment of sorts, a burst of creativity fueled in large part by spontaneity and esprit de corps. There was a real “let’s put on a show!” energy to the proceedings. Tour dates were announced only a few days in advance, the itinerary unfolding according to the whims of the man in the wide-brimmed hat, and concerts were given not in theaters, but in New England’s stuffiest gymnasia and rotary halls.

The mercurial, DIY approach was a big part of the magic, but it also limited the tour’s reach. The sequel would be a professional operation: fully produced, well-rehearsed, hosted in cavernous coliseums across the American South. Better, boozier, browner.

Those latter two descriptors certainly applied to Rolling Thunder ‘76. As for the former, it depends on who you ask. The energy of the ‘75 shows was dialed back considerably, the wiry charge dissipating somewhere between the action on stage and the tens of thousands in the stands. It would have been impossible to reproduce the energy of a room like Plymouth’s War Memorial Auditorium (capacity 1,500) in a place like Fort Collins’ Hughes Stadium (capacity 30,000), and Bob didn’t even try. Instead, he and the band dialed up the cream quotient, turning the sound into something thicker, a little less wild. If Rolling Thunder ‘75 was a bantamweight, dodging and dancing around the ring, ‘76 was a heavyweight—slower, steadier, with a brutal left hook.

Some of the best Desire cuts (“Hurricane,” “Sara”) were stripped from the ‘76 setlists, replaced with Blood On The Tracks material that neatly mapped the emotional geography of Dylan’s crumbling marriage. Most shows included some, if not all, of the following: “Tangled Up In Blue,” a tale of missed connections and cruel fate; “You’re A Big Girl Now,” a bitter, disillusioned sequel to “Positively 4th Street;” “Idiot Wind,” the breakup song to end all breakup songs, a kiss-off to both a former lover and a former self; and “You’re Gonna Make Me Lonesome When You Go,” a sweet little number written, not coincidentally, about the young A&R rep Bob had been seeing on the side. To the surprise of no one, Sara Dylan would file for divorce early the following year.

Listening now, it’s clear that the live Blood material is the lifeblood of Rolling Thunder ‘76. Bob is invested in these songs like they’re written in his soul: performances of “Idiot Wind” and “Shelter From The Storm” highlight every show in which they appear, and “Tangled” is always interesting, even if it’s occasionally more tuneless than it ought to be. The other stuff is more hit-and-miss.

Take the 4/22/76 taping for the Midnight Special television program, which notably lacks any Tracks tracks. Instead, Bob and company meander through an abbreviated selection of greatest hits in a vain attempt at pleasing the crowd (and, presumably, network execs hoping to sell ad spots against the programming). It’s the Dylan pupu platter: a few “protest” songs, a few mid-Sixties rockers, and a couple contemporary cuts as a sop to the actual fans present. Several Rolling Thunder cast members make appearances—Joan Baez, Bobby Neuwirth, Roger McGuinn—but no one’s heart seems to be in it. Dylan was dissatisfied with the results at the time, and he refused to allow the performance to air. Now here it is a half-century later, available for all of us to judge ourselves. Turns out Bob made the right call.

I can’t help but compare The 1976 Live Recordings to last year’s salvo from BD Industries, Through The Open Window: The Bootleg Series Vol. 18 1956-1963. That volume covered plenty of well-trod ground, tracing Bob’s earliest days in the Greenwich Village folk scene. Still, producers Sean Wilentz and Steve Berkowitz managed to string the collection’s hundred-odd tracks into something coherent and compelling. The result is a release that is intentional, engaging, and, despite its marathon length, essential.

The same cannot be said about this latest set. On a personal level, I find 1976 Bob much more compelling than I do 1962 Bob—I like my Dylan aged, like a fine Cabernet. But the experience of listening to The 1976 Live Recordings is somewhat less satisfying than that of Through The Open Window. Any time I return to Sony Music’s cursed promo portal, I feel like I’m pulling the lever of a slot machine. Sometimes I hit a jackpot like “Going Going Gone,” with its revised lyrics about “diamonds and rust,” a nod—or a shot?—at Baez. Other times I get bupkis—yet another by-the-numbers edition of “Oh Sister.”

It’s worth noting that The 1976 Live Recordings, like previous releases of the 1966, 1974, and 1975 tours, isn’t being marketed as part of the Bootleg Series. The first Bootleg volume—released all the way back in 1991, now closer to the beginning of Bob’s career than it is to the present—set a high standard for classic rock box sets. Deep, voluminous, and impeccably sequenced, the inaugural release presented an extraordinary alternate history of The Great American Artist, one nearly as strong as the actual history. Even if selections were weighted toward Dylan’s first decade, a number of brilliant recordings from Bob’s wilderness years were also included. See “Lord Protect My Child,” a powerfully vulnerable ballad from the Infidels sessions. See also the alternate take of “When The Night Comes Falling From The Sky,” featuring the hot-rod stylings of Roy Bittan and Little Steven Van Zandt. “Blind Willie McTell,” “Foot of Pride,” “Series of Dreams”—the list goes on and on. My favorite Bob record shifts with the seasons; there are simply too many colors in the man’s mind to settle on one. Sometimes, however, the answer to that question is the last disc of the first volume of the Bootleg Series. It is that good.

Whatever its merits, I won’t ever say the same about The 1976 Live Recordings. Rather than present a considered set of highlights from the ‘76 run, Bob Dylan Industries has simply thrown open the gates of the vault. The words of William Mulholland upon the opening of the Los Angeles Aqueduct come to mind: “There it is, take it.” Those of us familiar with the Expecting Rain message boards have had it for years—most of it, anyway. I had my fingers crossed that someone would have rustled up a tape of Salt Lake City (5/25/76), which featured the only-ever performance of “Lily, Rosemary, and the Jack of Hearts,” but no such luck. If a tape of that show does exist, it’s still sitting in a tomb somewhere, waiting for someone to ride through the devilish cold and find it.

That, more than anything, is the central disappointment of The 1976 Live Recordings: there’s very little here that hasn’t already been in circulation for some time. Of course, bringing new and heretofore unknown delights to light was never the primary purpose. Neither was telling a story in the manner of Open Window. A release like this will surely boost the cultural footprint of Rolling Thunder ‘76, particularly amongst lower echelons of Dylan fans—those who do most of their listening through YouTube and have no idea what a FLAC is—but that’s more a happy byproduct than a raison d’etre.

The real aim here is purely legal: the maintenance and extension of copyright. EU law dictates that recordings published within 50 years of their creation are protected for 70 years following their publication. Miss that deadline and the recording enters public domain, allowing any interested parties to do with it what they will. This simple fact explains the last decade-plus of releases from Bob’s archives: The 1966 Live Recordings in 2016, The 1974 Live Recordings in 2024, and now The 1976 Live Recordings in 2026. There’s a lot of juice left to squeeze in these lemons, and Sony Music is intent on squeezing them.

The general attitude of Bob Dylan Industries seems to be that any scrap of music ever made by Dylan is worth preserving and exercising ownership over. There is a cold, calculating logic behind these box sets, one which prioritizes financial motives over the music itself. The 1976 material would benefit greatly from the deft hand of a curator, someone who had dedicated the time to separate the wheat from the chaff (releasing the complete Fort Worth show on streaming services is a poor substitute). This careful editorial approach is what makes the inaugural Bootleg Series release or Through The Open Window such powerful collections. In this case, however, it would yield an incomplete copyright arrangement. So here we are instead.

Fine by me. Even if The 1976 Live Recordings ends up being too much of a good thing—seriously, if I ever hear another “Vincent Van Gogh,” it’ll be too soon—I can’t say I’m dissatisfied with the finished product. If anything, it makes me excited for the years to come, as later Dylan tours approach their semicentennial.

I’ve long been obsessed with the 1978 shows, for instance. That year’s incarnation of Dylan featured radically glitzy rearrangements, powerhouse Street-Legal cuts, and a plethora of ruffled shirts. The At Budokan live album documented a specimen from the early days of the tour, but the best performances came at the end, as Bob refined the schmaltzy big band sound into something soulful and desperate. I’ll be first in line for a hypothetical 50-disc The 1978 Live Recordings set. Then there’s the gospel tours of ‘79 and ‘80, and the “Bob Is Back” run from ‘81, and the butt rock and eyeliner era from ‘84… It goes on and on.

The important thing is that this music was made, and now it is being made available. Copyright holders and Dylan obsessives can agree on that much, even if we’re getting different things out of a release like The 1976 Live Recordings. We always did feel the same, we just saw it from a different point of view.

#6761. Few Bags Have Had the Staying Power of Balenciaga’s Le City—Now It’s Turning 25

It’s hard to believe that 25 years have passed since Balenciaga’s Le City bag arrived on the scene—the design riffing on a motorcycle jacket, the sans-logo attitude unapologetically cool. A quarter-century is long enough that some see the bag mostly with nostalgia while others are discovering its It-status for the first time.

Certainly, in the midst of the mythic maison’s creative director shakeup—the departure of Pierpaolo Piccioli, the appointment of Martine Rose—Le City remains an enduring constant, riding out every era from its creation by Nicolas Ghesquière through Alexander Wang and Demna, who proposed his own version, the Neo City, in 2020.

Starting tomorrow, Balenciaga is kicking off Le City’s anniversary with celebratory activations in several cities around the world. Le City House will bow in its Paris hometown for nine days, with New York, Tokyo, Shanghai, Beijing, and Seoul staggered through the end of the year. The spaces also exist to launch a major collaboration involving the artist provocateur Damien Hirst. Folks, get ready for DAMIENCIAGA, a limited edition Le City capsule that transposes some of his famous works to the characteristic Arena leather.

A few days prior to the reveal, I made a site visit to the historic address of 10, Avenue George V, where Cristobal established his atelier and where customers more recently could purchase Demna’s Couture. Le City House is altogether different: a multi-modal, Y2K-coded experience that is sleek yet visitor-friendly and daresay playful.

Upon entering, a prototype of Le City from 2001—compact and in brown cotton canvas—sits in a see-through cube atop a Parisian bench painted glossy blue. There’s a floor-to-ceiling display of Le City as eye candy: bags in vivid shades of Maldives Green and Ultra Violet; in surface treatments such as tweed panels and brogue trims; and in novelty one-offs (including Ghesquière’s Multicolor City Mondriaan in red, yellow, and blue). Nearby are the “closets” that boast bags belonging to celebrity collectors such as Nicole Ritchie, the French footballer Hugo Ekitike, Clémence Poésy and Isabelle Huppert (each Le City House will feature different boldface names) propped with daily items and old Blackberry devices that double as labels (Ritchie’s, for instance, is from 2005). Small screens flash Parisian landmarks while a full-length panel rotates editorial, street style, and paparazzi photos. For all the glimpses of Kate Moss, Chloe Sevigny, Mary-Kate Olsen, and Sienna Miller, Le City is clearly the star.

Further back, past a metal railing bedecked with padlocks is the room with Hirst’s creations. The most rarefied, done by hand, is doused in splashes of pigment like his Spin Paintings and exists as an edition of 25. The others—his multicolored spots arranged like a butterfly; his mandala of wings; his uniform grid of dots; and a compilation of his ideas as embroidered patches—will be more widely available.

The second space, dubbed “Le Salon,” functions like a leather workshop-turned-bag spa. Artisans stationed on Platner stools will be personalizing bags: replacing the lacing along the top handle, offering custom charms, and hand-painting or etching initials on the rectangular pocket mirror that has remained one of Le City’s defining details. People can also make an appointment to have their old bags assessed for extra refresh services.

Finally, there is a photo kiosk programmed as though straight out of a teen magazine quiz circa the 1990s, only that the theme is not crushes or careers, but which Le City is right for you. One result might yield Le City Moto (“Bold, confident and a little rebellious”); another Le City Mini Backpack (“Your match understands that you have your hands full”). Alas, you do not actually receive a free bag.

If Le City House represents a fun, public-facing commemoration of Balenciaga’s best-selling bag, the maison’s vast archive on the outskirts of Paris offers the contextual perspective. This is where, thanks to a tour provided by Heritage and Cultural Director, Gaspard de Massé, I found myself learning about how the Le City—eschewing conspicuous branding but rather adorned with a sexy mix of laces, buckles, and studs—almost never came to be.

Nicolas Ghesquière with the Balenciaga city bag in 2004. Photographed by Robert Fairer, Vogue, September 2004

As the lore goes and he recounts, Ghesquière was working on a motorcycle-inspired bag in 2000 when Moss saw a version and showed interest in it. He gave her one and offered others to his inner circle—women like Marie-Amélie Sauvé, Carine Roitfeld, and Emmanuelle Alt—initially calling it Le Lariat, then Le Motorcycle. Le First and Le City followed based on their sizes, until eventually, the latter stuck for the entire family.

The 3,000-square-meter temperature- and humidity-controlled space is filled not only with the kind of heaving mobile shelving units found in institutional archives, but also the storage of patrimonial furniture, Cristobal’s actual library, and two stunning paintings positioned upright (one is by Bernard Buffet of his wife, Annabel, wearing a pink Balenciaga gown; the other, surprisingly, is of Gabrielle Chanel in a soigné white ensemble by A.M. Cassandre).

Of course, we end up over at the units stacked with Le City models, never carried and originating from the workshops. You need not be prone to It-bag lust to marvel over the sheer number and variety—some 879 at last count. Dream of a shade and it’s probably in the mix. There are evolutions and iterations: the burnished studs that morphed to resemble thimbles; the brogue trims that evoked Derby shoes; the metal hardware; the Part Time with its seam down the middle or the square Velo format (presumably to fit inside a bicycle basket).

So how, in De Massé’s mind, has Le City remained such a hero piece? “I think it’s extremely identifiable, and because of that, it doesn’t really feel like taking a risk,” he says. “You know that you’re buying this particular bag for a specific reason; and undoubtedly, part of that reason is that you’re joining all those other people who already own one. There’s something of a community spirit around it; it’s not an exclusively ultra-luxury community, nor is it mass market. It occupies this interesting space somewhere in between.”

He goes on: “For today’s generations, it can also function as a kind of madeleine de Proust, something that evokes a particular moment or memory. I remember Britney Spears in the 2000s, for example. Even if I didn’t personally experience that period in the same way, those images are part of my imagination, and the bag allows me to reconnect with an aesthetic or a moment that I liked. There’s something reassuring about that. Of course, it’s different for everyone; but I think that recognizability, combined with the fact that the bag feels approachable and accessible, is fundamental to its success.”

Indeed, few bags have had such staying power independent of the promotion machine, off-duty model shot, or hype cycle. But Le City is a bag that also happens to wear well. The non-boxy shape proved easy to carry and the Arena leather already appeared lived-in, becoming more cherished as it was subjected to life’s vicissitudes. Remember Mary-Kate’s endless attachment to her mint green bag—not despite, but possibly because of, its glaring red wine stain?

Although Le City has never needed reinvention, it was updated in 2024 when various vintage styles were studied together, so that the new construction—hand-assembled from 25 panels—signified a faithful “amalgamation.” The launch was announced with a campaign of portraits by Mario Sorrenti starring Moss as well as Mona Tougaard, Juyeon, and Yang Chaoyue. Last year, an “ultra-luxe” version marked the first runway appearance of Le City, coinciding with Piccioli’s debut. Another campaign followed, this time by David Sims—Le City’s original fashion photographer—marking a reunion and full-circle moment.

The campaign for the Hirst series features Ritchie dressed in a draped yellow top over jeans, her gaze smoldering as the mandala butterfly bag hangs from her forearm. Ekitike cradles one of the patchwork styles alongside the Seine.

For Hirst, Le City was imprinted on his mind even before the collaboration opportunity arose. “I think everyone knows it, don’t they? It’s one of the most iconic bags of the last 25 years,” he tells Vogue via email. “You associate it with the noughties, with Kate Moss, yet it’s still remained so relevant.”

This is a whole other Hirst than when he was preserving sharks in tanks or encrusting skulls with diamonds, yet the bags are not without a hint of subversion seeing as the original Spot Paintings were named after pharmaceutical drugs or chemical compounds and the Butterfly mandalas alluded to mortality, spirituality, and the passage of time.

Hugo Ekitike with the Balenciaga “DAMIENCIAGA” bag.

It’s likely his 25 hand-painted Le Cities (or is it Les Citys?) will have collector value. They look like they were a thrill to make, the layers of vivid paint leaving barely a trace of original surface. The artist suggests the best part will be when people make the bags their own. “It’s not just a ‘Balenciaga’ or a ‘Hirst’… they’re adding their personality to it. And I think that’s what fashion is all about.”

They are also a reminder that fashion loves a revival. Each Le City House will be reintroducing people to a cultural moment well before quiet luxury, and whatever we are shifting into now. Thanks to the anniversary, the bag is definitely back; the bolder, the better. To wit, Le City x Hirst even boasts a logo of sorts: ‘Damienciaga’ appears in a fine silver script along one side.
