#6760. The Real-Life Wardrobe of Jamie Campbell Bower, Who Only Wears Suits If They’re McQueen

“I don’t know, I suppose I’m an artist,” Jamie Campbell Bower says with a laugh, after I ask him to describe himself. He’s correct, in more ways than one. If you’ve been consuming pop culture for the last decade and change, it’s less a matter of if you’ve seen the 37-year-old Londoner before, but where. He’s acted in some of the biggest franchises in Hollywood—including Twilight, Harry Potter, The Mortal Instruments, and Stranger Things—while also nurturing a multifaceted music career. As of this month, he’ll be heading to Middle-earth as Celeborn in the third season of Amazon Prime’s epic Lord of the Rings series, The Rings of Power.

During a hectic week of Rings of Power in New York City, Bower and I spent a quiet early morning talking about the bands that helped him find his style as a teenager, the difference between performing as an actor and a musician, and why he loves playing the bad guy.

All clothing and accessories, subject’s own. Coat by MM6 Maison Margiela. Sweater by John Lawrence Sullivan. Vintage skirt. Shoes by John Lawrence Sullivan. Sunglasses by Persol (throughout). Necklace (bottom) by Kinraden. Other jewelry by Pianegonda.

Jamie Campbell Bower: It’s complexity. With any character, there has to be a level of complexity. Playing in the shadow self is really illuminating, to be Jungian. You have to know it in order for it to not take over. I found it particularly interesting to rationale and reason, even though this character was doing terrible things. I have always found it really interesting to dig away and find the why. So much of that character was really about isolation and pain and not feeling like they had a sense of belonging in the space for them. Obviously, they find this power that gives them this sense of safety. It becomes the wall, and it gives them purpose, and it hides them from the world and from being hurt. What draws me to any character is complexity and understanding the balance. It’s almost anthropological in a way.

It was amazing. I was so terrified on day one. I’m always nervous about joining any show, doing any gig. But I remember day one of actually shooting with other cast members, turning around to Nick Müller, our A-camera operator, and I just went, “Look, Nick, you’ve been here way longer than I have. If I’m in your way, just tell me to fucking move.”

I’d been a part of Twilight as well—joined that on the second movie after watching a cultural moment explode—and I was in that position again with Stranger Things. It was so big. I was joining this new world, but everyone was wicked and super kind. I made some amazing friends. I love Millie [Bobby Brown]. She’s just the best. She’s like my little sister, and also like my big sister at times as well. She’s got so much sage advice and is so brilliant at what she does and so driven. I am in awe of her, and I was from the moment I met her.

I’ve got the hand of Vecna. I took it out on Fallon [the other] night. I told this story, but I got my bag searched in Mexico City on the way in over the weekend. We pulled up and one of the people there looked at me—her eyes got big. She said, “Vecna.” I’ve got three massive fuck-off suitcases. They’re going through them and I’m like, “Look, I’ve got the hand of Vecna in here. Do you want to see it?” And then it ended up being the quickest bag search ever. I got some elf ears with me as well, both made by the same guy, Barrie Gower.

It was the summer when I was 15. I spent it wearing a visor with spiky hair, because I used to skate growing up in super baggy jeans. I remember turning up being like, “That’s not you.” Skating is a part of who I am, but I was looking to represent myself in some way, shape, or form.

Then we started this indie band when I was 16, 17. Devonté Hynes had this band called Test Icicles. I always used to look at those guys with their skinny jeans and their big hair, and I was just like, “That’s a bit of me, that.” How skinny can my jeans get? How drain pipe-y am I? That’s where I really started to find my own identity.

I’ve been fortunate enough throughout my career to meet and work with such beautiful creative people in fashion and find myself more within that, too. I was talking about it to somebody yesterday: When you try a fit on that is not you, it’s like having a bad haircut. You don’t want to do that. I’m even the same if I’m doing a photoshoot. I always go through the rail and I’ll say, “That’s not my vibe. I can’t say that I’m going to wear that.” Of course, I’m always willing to try, I’m always willing to push. But you know yourself better as you get older.

It was from Alexander McQueen. I loved the identity of that brand, but I couldn’t afford a jacket, or a suit, or even a scarf. But the smaller pieces, the rings and the wallets, were like 100 bucks. Those were the things that I would gravitate towards and buy.

More recently, within the last 10 years, I remember coming here to New York for a show that I did called Will, going to Bergdorf, and buying a couple of pairs of Comme des Garçons trousers. As they were being rung up, I was like, “All right.” It wasn’t loads—we’re not talking thousands—but it was still a lot of money. That was probably the first big clothing purchase that I ever made. And I’ve still got the trousers. I used to wear them on stage in the band as well, which is foolish.

Got a bunch of stuff from H. Lorenzo the other day—some great shirts, some great jackets. I really like how they curate the store. My most recent purchase is a lot of stuff from the new Ann Demeulemeester collection. I actually just bought a sick leather trench from it—brown leather, which is fire.

Jacket by Thom Browne. Shirt, jeans, shoes by Ann Demeulemeester.

Going back to when we were kids: Test Icicles, the Libertines, the Rakes, Franz Ferdinand, Editors. Got to meet a few of those guys throughout my travels, which was always pretty sick. Nick Cave. Warren Ellis. Nick has got such a sharp style, as does Warren. Warren’s a bit more unbuttoned. I met Warren in Venice five years ago. He was stood at the end of the pier and I was so excited to meet him, I just bounded up. I was like, “Hi, Mr. Ellis. My name’s Jamie.” And I just blurted out to him for ages, and then I was like, “Thank you so much.” He said, "Good to meet you, mate. Bye.”

I think fluidity and being myself is always the main thing. I’ve never felt wholly comfortable in a regular suit. I remember we were invited to do a show in Venice, and the band that we were in was pretty heavy. We wore suits in an environment that for us felt almost quite subversive. The music that we played didn’t really fit that. I quite enjoyed that.

But on the whole, I don’t love suits too much. I like to keep it more interesting and fluid. I’m not saying that they can’t be interesting for other people, but I’ve never been interested [in them myself]. Apart from McQueen, but that’s because something like the McQueen shoulder is so identifiable and creates such an incredible silhouette. That’s probably the only time I’ve ever really been like, “I can wear this suit for a long time.” But yeah, I avoid anything that doesn’t feel right for me.

It’s hard to say. I do feel like so often they can blend. I’ve been so fortunate in my career, being drawn to things that feel like me and getting to explore different parts of myself on film. That does have an effect on the music that I’m making at the time.

With a film or a television series, you’re saying someone else’s words and building a character, but also at times injecting your own personal experience into that. In music, they are your words. You can make a choice to be like, “I’m going to build a world in this song to express something.” Or I can just be like, “This is me.” So, they can scratch different itches, but I think that they work in symbiosis sometimes.

The original movies came out when I was 12, so they were pretty seminal. I remember being in Hong Kong on a trip when The Hobbit was coming out. I was on my own, and I went to a cinema in a place called Pacific Place to watch it. That made a really big impact on me—it felt like a fantastical world that I could see myself in.

I started auditioning for it in 2024. Walking into it, of course, I was elated. I felt so lucky and so happy, like I was a little kid again. Like, I was 11 or 12 on stage in some provincial town outside of London, and now I get to fuckin’ walk into this Lord of the Rings world and be an elf? Dude, that’s sick.

Three non-negotiable albums that everyone… Oh, bloody Nora!

I discovered Dylan when I was like 16, when we were reading [J. D.] Salinger and Allen Ginsberg and books like On the Road. Let’s go with a classic. Freewheelin’ is old-school enough. It’s cool, pre-him going electric, which I adore as well. Highway 61 Revisited is a great record too. Take your pick between those two. Chopin’s Nocturnes are amazing. That’s a beautiful, beautiful piece to get into. Then there’s Nick Cave. I did an interview before and I chose Murder Ballads, which is a great record. But I also love some of the more recent work, like Ghosteen or Skeleton Tree. Ghosteen is amazing.

Oh, Ghosteen’s wicked. Let’s go with that. I referenced the artwork for Ghosteen on my last release. My album cover was by an artist called Thomas Cole, who did a collection of paintings about the journey from birth to death. He also did paintings of the Garden of Eden. From what I have now seen, those paintings heavily inspired the artist that did the paintings for Ghosteen as well, which is kind of insane.

So, he’s from the East. It’s the swearing.

When I shop for eyeliner these days, I feel like I’m going into a restaurant with a list of dietary restrictions. I have always had hooded eyes, but at 46, the hooding is more pronounced. I have sensitive eyes, too, and fine lines starting to set in. In short, I’m looking for an eyeliner to play up my gaze while downplaying any discomfort or signs of aging. It’s a balancing act, to be sure, but it’s one that the best eyeliners for older women can accomplish with finesse—and if it becomes tempting to skip eyeliner altogether, consider this advice from a pro: “Eyeliner actually becomes more important as we age,” says makeup artist Stevi Christine. “Lashes tend to thin over time, and a liner at the roots helps bring back that youthful fullness.”

Since I’ve found a few formulas that I swear by—including the Laura Mercier pencil that’s on this list—I see what Christine means. On days when I do wear eyeliner, I look more awake, chipper, and polished than on days when I don’t. The trick? Finding formulas that are not only flattering, but gentle on the eyes. Formulas for older women should also be easy to apply and remove without tugging at the lids. Ahead, find the eyeliners that check every box.

What type of eyeliner is best for mature eyes?

“Because of its rich color payoff, a smooth gel or cream eyeliner pencil is a great choice for enhancing mature eyes,” says Wagener. “Eyeliner with a creamy texture glides on effortlessly, providing a defined line that won’t tug at delicate skin.” On the other hand, Wagener tells her mature clients to steer clear of most liquid felt-tip liners. “They can be less forgiving and very difficult to use,” she says.

What to Look for in an Eyeliner for Older Women

When it comes to choosing an eyeliner for women over 50, makeup artists keep a few key factors in mind.

How should you apply eyeliner to mature eyes?

“Depending on the eye shape, I often line only the outer third or outer half of the upper lash line and then tightline the whole length of the lash line from underneath,” says Patinkin. “This is a great technique for lots of reasons.” First, she says, it contributes to a lifted look at the outer corner of the eyes, where the shadow is thicker. The technique also helps define the shape of the eyes without “eating up lid space,” she says. Tightlining is another technique makeup artists favor for mature eyes. “It makes the lashes look thicker because you’re filling in gaps between the roots of the lashes,” Patinkin says.

#6753. 11 Best Cowboy Boots in 2026, According to GQ Editors

You might think that cowboy boots are a privilege reserved for ranch hands and folks who can actually ride a horse. But with a little chutzpah, the best cowboy boots are just as adept on a saddle as they are on the subway. Is that so surprising? Before they blossomed into their fashionable forms, much of menswear’s most riffed on garments were rooted in function: cargo pants, work jackets, even suits. With enough time, they were adopted by civilians and adapted to their second lives as symbols of self-expression and creativity, not just job uniforms. Cowboy boots are no different.

In terms of styling, the classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with some well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage boot cuts) and with a snap shirt. And that's still a great approach. But if you open up your mind and step outside of the saloon, the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a ‘70s-inspired suit screams filthy rich oil tycoon if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or, why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots. So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

And if you’re having trouble, well, that’s why you’re here. We’ve wrangled together the best cowboy boots west—and east—of the Mississippi, from the budget-friendly to the ostentatious and every vibe in-between.

The good folks at Tecovas are living, breathing proof that direct-to-consumer brands aren’t all operated by algorithms tasked with solving imaginary problems. The DTC upstart might be the youngest of the bootmakers on this list, but it's quickly endeared itself to budget-strapped swashbucklers with a hankering for democratically-priced kicks.

Take, for example, the Cartwright, a handsome riff on a classic western silhouette made in Leon, Mexico, a bona fide cobbling capital of the world with over a century of expertise to draw on. It boasts hand-laid cording at the shaft, a resoleable Goodyear-welt construction, and a slew of colors and leathers to choose from, including genuine cowhide and goat leather. They’re not the cheapest boots on this list, but the relatively approachable price belies the craftsmanship involved. For $375, they’re one small step up from our favorite budget cowboy boots—but one giant leap in overall quality.

You can think of roper boots as the chilled-out version of the average western boot. Originally designed for calf roping, roper boots feature a shorter shaft and a shorter, squared off heel. These details made it easier for cowboys to dismount their horse and run after the calves they roped. Coincidentally, they also make roper boots easier to walk in which is why some people prefer them over other cowboy boots for everyday wear.

Our pick for the best roper boots currently goes to Red Wing. (Perhaps no surprise, given the brand also makes our favorite trend-proof boots.) Part of Red Wing's Heritage line, they're crafted with premium S.B. Foot Tanning Company leather, and feature Goodyear welt construction so you can have them resoled and keep ‘em going for a long time. Plus, if you’re just dipping your toes into the cowboy boot world, the minimalist uppers forgo the decorative western stitching which makes them easier to style.

If you’re after that western look but need a pair of boots that can handle the demands of a jobsite, a lot of guys will tell you to look to Ariat. That’s because they manage to blend classic cowboy style with modern-day features, and a palatable price point in perfect proportion. While they do offer a range of work boots in lace-up styles, their Groundbreaker boots are a standout with classic cowboy boot looks.

They’re made of full-grain leather, include a supportive and comfortable insole, and meet ASTM standards for slip resistance and electrical safety. Because it’s among Ariat’s most popular styles, it’s also available in a wide range of colorways, toe shapes, and even steel toe versions. Some more traditional cowboys will poo-poo the fact that these aren’t made stateside, but if you’re on a budget, you’ll get more than what you pay for.

Cowboy boots aren’t all rough-and-tumble affairs. In fact, the right pair can easily strut the red carpet or waltz into a fancy restaurant with panache. You’ll want a pair with leather that shines up well and in a darker colorway. For date nights and more formal affairs, these Tony Lamas will impress thanks to the exotic lizard skin uppers and low-key embroidery. They’re the kind of boots that can play well for the in-laws with a tailored suit or play a rock-’n’-roll star with some vintage jeans and a tight white tee.

These days, most boot brands walk in the shadows of one brand: Lucchese. They’ve been outfitting American presidents, high-profile celebs, and the Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders for decades and it’s all thanks to their commitment to high-quality craftsmanship. Though any pair of Lucchese’s would earn you more than a few approving head nods, the most coveted are the boots that they make in their Texas workshop.

Using a range of full-grain leathers and exotic leathers like caiman alligator and pirarucu fish skin, each pair is crafted by master bootmakers using time-honored techniques. The Gavin, in their iconic Black Cherry, is a picture-perfect style featuring smooth Santini goat leather uppers with intricate embellishments, welted construction, and lemonwood pegs—made the old-fashioned way, basically. They’ll cost you a pretty penny, of course, but they'll last pretty much forever, and the drip you’ll get in return is priceless.

From Ralph Lauren’s western-inspired sub-label, these RRL boots meld high-end materials with old-world craftsmanship and feature American-tanned leather uppers, Goodyear-welted construction, and vintage-style rubber soles—all crafted in a multi-generational Texas bootmaking factory.

Frye is another American brand with proven boot quality chops. (In fact, it claims to be America's oldest continually-operating boot company.) Its Roper boot has all the same strengths as Red Wing's, and comes in a non-roughout leather.

We don't typically include the same designers twice on one list, but Tecovas are that good. The Johnny is for anyone who wants a softer, slightly more charming boot than the eternal Cartwright up top.

For fellas whose style skews a little more regular-guy than rodeo, these lower-profile, lower-priced Ropers have a Goodyear welt and Vibram outsole. Bang for your, ahem, buck.

Wythe's playing-card-inspired boots feature all the bells and whistles, including premium leather inside and out, hand-applied details, lemonwood pegs, and second-to-none construction all-around. While some brands tap the expert bootmakers in Léon, Mexico to pump out high-quality mass-appeal boots, Wythe tapped these artisans to really let them cook.

All of Yuketen's shoes are perfect, which is a big part of the reason Drake's now carries them. And while they're best known for their moccasin styles, the brand makes an exceptionally handsome cowboy boot too. Really, they're just showing off now.

The classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage bootcuts) and a snap-button shirt. But open up your mind and step outside of the saloon and the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a '70s-inspired suit screams filthy-rich oil tycoon—if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots (though you certainly can). So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

Peter Middleton knows a thing or two about the lifestyle having cut his teeth at Ralph Lauren and used it as a springboard for his own western-inspired brand, Wythe. “To me the beauty and shape of the Cowboy Boot (and a lot of the original design intent) lies in its curves and that’s what makes a great boot SEXY. There isn't a lot of men's footwear that has these dramatic curves, leather, and a high heel but the right cowboy boot has them all.”

He says that good cowboy boots should be made with natural leathers that age well with wear, mould to the wearer’s feet, and can be recrafted repeatedly. His non-negotiables include full leather construction from the insole to the outsole, linings, uppers, and heels. Look for Goodyear welted construction which will allow you to have the boots resoled and extend their life. The toe bug (the fancy stitching at the toe), should sit right where your foot flexes to help cover up the crease that comes with each step. Preferably, this would be corded by hand, of course.

Price points will vary, and you can get some well-made boots for around $300. The really great stuff will often be twice that much. Middleton says, “the best thing to do is wait and save up until you can buy the version you actually want because its impossible to cut corners and still deliver the product you want.” So if you can be patient, save up. If you can’t, try buying secondhand. But if you simply can’t wait, you’ll do well enough with plenty of the mid-tier brands until you’re ready to upgrade.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you.

#6749. Around the World in 80 Handbags—Inside a New Istanbul Exhibition Devoted to the Exceptional Accessory

A handbag is rarely just a handbag. It can be a keeper of secrets, a declaration of status, or a traveling companion—not to mention a rather expensive place to keep one’s keys. At Beymen Tersane, Istanbul’s newest shopping destination, it takes on another role: that of a vessel for cultural memory. This idea lies at the heart of “Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag,” an exhibition inaugurated to mark the cultural complex’s opening, bringing together 80 creations from 55 international brands in a dialogue between contemporary design and the layered heritage of Anatolia and the Ottoman Empire.

Curated by Laurence Benaïm, the presentation is less an exercise in historical illustration than an invitation to look at memory through a different perspective. The challenge, she explained, was not to reproduce traditional motifs or reduce Ottoman references to decorative shorthand, but to translate their spirit into a modern design language. Her vision was that of a “curiosity cabinet of dreams and craftsmanship,” where newly commissioned pieces sit alongside archival treasures from the likes of Dior, Louis Vuitton, and Schiaparelli.

The journey unfolds across seven chapters, each exploring a different facet of the relationship between bags and cultural memory. Precious Envelopes includes the pouches once used by ambassadors to carry letters, imperial decrees and secrets, a reminder that the art of keeping things under wraps has a long history. Heavenly Gardens draws on the flora and fauna of İznik ceramics and Ottoman palace gardens, while Golden Jewels explores the allure of gold. Magical Boxes considers the bag as guardian of private possessions and hidden treasures, a function that has hardly lost its appeal. Nomad Memories traces the weaving, leatherwork, and saddlebag traditions that traveled from Central Asia to Anatolia. A final glance towards the future brings in three designs by young Turkish talents, selected through a competition supported by Beymen in collaboration with local universities. Among the historical highlights is a piece of luxurious archaeology: a massive Louis Vuitton wardrobe trunk, made in 1886 at the Maison’s Asnières atelier for Sultan Abdülhamid II.

A massive Louis Vuitton wardrobe trunk, made in 1886 at the Maison’s Asnières atelier for Sultan Abdülhamid II.

For Benaïm, the point is that heritage should not be treated as a fixed inheritance or an exercise in nostalgia. “Heritage isn’t about looking backwards. It’s about carrying the beauty of the past into the future,” she remarked. The exhibition, more than two years in the making, is a “love letter to Turkish culture” and an exploration of the ways in which fashion can preserve cultural memory while giving it new meaning. “There is no luxury without soul, without heart and without love, and without a sense of time,” Benaïm added.

The choice of venue is not incidental. Beymen Tersane occupies part of the historic shipyard on the Golden Horn, a site stretching back some 600 years, reimagined by Rem Koolhaas’s OMA as a 12,000-square-meter destination for fashion, art, and lifestyle. Rather than imposing another conventional department-store interior on the monumental structure, the architects conceived a horizontal sequence of eight galleries.

“Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag,” features bags by 55 international brands including newly commissioned pieces and archival treasures from the likes of Dior, Louis Vuitton, and Schiaparelli.

For Beymen Group CEO Elif Çapçı, the project continues the conversation started in 2023 with “Golden Opulence,” a 50th anniversary exhibition in which 50 international brands were commissioned for a unique piece. This time, the bag became the focus, “an object whose changing form and function offers a revealing record of shifting lifestyles, tastes and social codes,” Çapçı noted.

Rachid Mohamed Rachid, CEO of Mayhoola and chairman of Beymen, sees Beymen Tersane as part of a broader ambition to bring the cultural complexities of Turkey to the attention of the international luxury world. But there is something deeper at stake here than a showcase of commercial partnerships. “As Istanbul has always understood, the most interesting exchanges happen when different worlds meet without either having to surrender its identity,” he said.

And perhaps this is the point: The handbag, after all, is a meeting place of its own, a repository of craftsmanship, memory, and imagination. There is clearly more to it than what fits inside. Though isn’t it nice that it also accommodates a phone, a lipstick and a pair of sunglasses?

“Timeless Treasures—The Eternal Journey of the Bag” is on view at Istanbul’s Beymen Tersane through February 8, 2027.

#6746. Should You Put Your Stem Cells in the Bank?

High-yield savings vs. a bad beauty and wellness investment.

As part of the Future of Beauty Awards, the ELLE beauty team looked ahead at what will be next in beauty and wellness.

Recently, I was at a dinner with fellow journalists where the small talk turned from the mysteriously pierced earlobes in The Odyssey and the best facialists in New York to banking. Seoul, one person chirped, is where all the innovation happens. A woman said that she had banked hers years ago in Texas. Then another person said he had heard that Japan was the country with some of the best facilities. A personal finance TikToker, who had written several books about saving money, leaned over and curiously asked, “Why are you guys banking in other countries instead of the US or Switzerland?” “Not money,” I clarified. “Stem cells.”

Humans have long squirreled away things of value, but it’s only recently that hoarding your stem cells—the building blocks of tissues and organs that have the ability to renew and become other cells—has become dinner conversation. Stem cells diminish over time as we age, but much like with money, there are a few ways to save young cells for a rainy day. Parents can bank their baby’s cord blood, a bit like starting a 529 education plan for college tuition. (They can also donate cord blood to a public bank for free, to help anyone who might need a stem cell transplant.) For those interested in beauty, there’s hope that preserving young stem cells from fat might give you a nice supply of growth factors that could keep your skin bouncy later. And then for a cohort of celebrities like John Cleese, Chris Hemsworth, and biohacker Bryan Johnson, there’s the belief that stem cell banking could be a well from which youth, cryopreserved, springs eternal. It’s like heavily investing in a call option you hope will pan out later. After visiting a clinic in Panama, Hemsworth posted on Instagram: “With this kind of technology available, I plan to keep making films well into my 100s (or 1,500 in Asgard).”

The discourse around stem cells, according to several experts, ranges from “tremendous” and “promising” to “wildly outrageous,” “misleading,” “harmless nonsense,” and “potentially very dangerous.” “The phrase stem cells has almost become a health halo,” says Timothy Caulfield, professor at the Faculty of Law and the School of Public Health and research director of the Health Law Institute at the University of Alberta. To understand the buzz, you have to go back to 2012, when Shinya Yamanaka, MD, PhD, co-won a Nobel Prize with John B. Gurdon for discovering that you can take mature cells and turn them back into an embryonic state. They called these new, artificially created stem cells induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. Two decades later, Yamanaka’s findings are now being cautiously used on humans. In March 2026, iPS cell therapies were given conditional and time-limited marketing approval for seven years in Japan for heart failure and Parkinson’s disease, while studies continue to determine their efficacy and safety in clinical trials. In the U.S. in May, a patient received iPS cells in a clinical trial to study treatment of retinitis pigmentosa.

“Stem cells don’t do magic. They do biology,” cautions John O’Neill, PhD, cofounder of Sweet Chemistry and chief scientific officer of Xylyx Bio, Inc., a regenerative medicine company. “They may be capable of incredible, remarkable, and profound therapeutic benefits. But truly understanding, controlling, manufacturing, and scaling [stem cell usage] will take years and years and bazillions of dollars and an incredible amount of human power.” Aside from the conditional exceptions in Japan for treating heart failure and Parkinson’s disease, iPS cells are not available for medical use, clarifies Knut Woltjen, Dior Reverse Aging board member and associate professor at Kyoto University’s Center for iPS Cell Research and Application (the same center that Yamanaka helped create and direct in Japan). He says they “are primarily a research material.”

Nevertheless, do even a cursory Google search and you’ll find people proclaiming that some type of stem cell treatment “worked wonders.” In many cases, it’s uncertain where these stem cells are being sourced from. But some experts are skeptical that these treatments always involve the real thing. Caulfield calls it an “exploitative industry,” saying that “it’s gotten so bad that if you see the phrase ‘stem cells,’ I think that is a red flag for bunk.”

Even if people were receiving real stem cells, those cells can only do so much; many of the treatments marketed as such or as regenerative therapies have not undergone clinical testing to determine their safety and effectiveness, and it would likely take time before they become widely available for use in a nonmedical setting. “Today, the timing of marketing is quicker than scientific or research timing,” says Virginie Couturaud, Christian Dior Parfums scientific communication director.

The banks and places that collect, store, and process them are regulated by the FDA. Still, some states have their own specific licensing, inspection, and oversight requirements that prompt experts to ask, “If you bank your own stem cells, can they be used? Because it won’t necessarily fit into the regulatory environment,” says Robin Smith, MD, a partner at Exoceuticals, an exosome-based skin care brand. Federally, stem cell products that are used as medical treatments need the FDA’s approval and are regulated by the FDA, although Smith notes that several states have carved out exceptions for indications such as pain, wound healing, or orthopedics. In July, Wyoming enacted the Stem Cell Freedom Act, which allows physicians to administer certain non-FDA-approved therapies using a patient’s own stem cells and prohibits medical board sanctions. Wyoming State Senator Eric Barlow told local press: “We’ve got to press on the federal government because they’re not approving things fast enough.”

There is also the concern that because stem cells are so powerful, using your own could carry markers of the very same diseases or ailments that you are trying to treat. “They have so much potency and ability, they could become the wrong thing in the body and get the wrong signals,” O’Neill says. An investigative report by The New York Times in 2024 also found that some banked cord blood samples were contaminated, and that some parents were misled about their value. “We don’t know that the technology that was used X number of years prior will actually still be on par with the quality of the cells that we can generate at that time,” Woltjen says.

There are some proven, heavily researched stem cell therapies, including for certain types of cancer. But most experts don’t approve of using current therapies in a non-medical setting, pointing to the lack of scientific evidence, clinical testing, and regulations. “If you’ve paid $50,000 to go travel someplace to help your bad knee, there’s a placebo response. Unproven therapies have long been supported using testimonials and anecdotes. Good, independent clinical trials that show efficacy just don’t exist,” Caulfield says. He’d like to see more, not less, oversight. “People will say, ‘Your evil bureaucracy, the FDA, is keeping you from accessing these clearly efficacious therapies.’ But you’re not seeing as much regulation as is warranted. There have been situations where clinics have been held to task, but the FDA just doesn’t have the resources. If you layer RFK Jr. on top, the political will to take action has dissipated significantly over the last two years.”

This is not necessarily to discount stem cell–related beauty treatments or products. Exosomes, cell by-products that contain lipids and proteins and can be derived from stem cells, are now commonly seen in skin care formulations. “There are legitimate stem cell–derived factors,” O’Neill says, but “they are not the cells themselves,” using the cow and the milk as an analogy. In Seoul, a stem cell beauty treatment called stromal vascular fraction (SVF) extracts stem cells, growth factors, and other cells from fat tissue, and then reinjects them into the skin. Gabriel Chiu, DOM.D., founder and CEO of Beverly Hills Plastic Surgery, adds that there are strict guidelines for how this is performed. He has used banked and fresh stem cells from fat tissue for fat grafting, and says, “Patients have been very happy with the results.”

For people who have banked their stem cells, even if they aren’t sure how or if they will one day be used, the process offers mental reassurance. Cynthia Sakai, founder of the personal care and lifestyle brand Evolvetogether, banked her son’s stem cells and described it as safeguarding: “I remember thinking that this was something we could only do once, at the moment he was born. We could always decide later that we did not need it, but we could never go back and collect it again.” When Smith was later diagnosed with breast cancer, she felt reassured that her stem cells were there. But even she says, “If you bank your own stem cells, can they be used? Because it won’t necessarily fit into the regulatory environment.”

The experts generally agree that stem cell banking is not a must-do procedure. O’Neill doesn’t like to say “never.” But when I ask how he would advise a friend, he says, “I rarely make definitive statements like this, but in 2026, stem cell banking is not worth it. It doesn’t mean it won’t be worth it someday. But someday will not be next year or the year after.”

A version of this story appears in the November 2026 issue of ELLE.

#6745. The Vogue Business People Moves Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business People Moves Tracker, a running list highlighting the key executive appointments and exits across the fashion and beauty industries. From CEOs to creative directors to other key C-suite hires, we track the leadership shifts that are reshaping the industry.

Background: Caroline Deroche Pasquier joins Dior in a newly created role as director of press, VIP and cultural relations. She began her career at Saint Laurent before joining LVMH, where she worked at Louis Vuitton and Givenchy. During the last six years, Pasquier has led global communications for Bottega Veneta and then Versace. At Dior, she will work closely with the house’s creative director Jonathan Anderson, reporting to Olivier Bialobos, deputy managing director in charge of global communication and image.

Company comments: “[Deroche Pasquier’s] career spans communication, creative collaboration, international markets and cultural relationships, giving her a broad perspective on the development and expression of luxury brands,” the company said in a statement.

Background: Oliver Timm has voluntarily stepped down from Hugo Boss, where he’s been both chief sales officer and deputy CEO since 2024, as well as the company board. In the meantime, CEO Daniel Grieder, alongside CFO and COO Ivica Maric, will split Timm’s previous duties. Timm was initially appointed as chief sales officer in 2021, to oversee Hugo Boss’s two brands (Boss and Hugo), including wholesale, e-commerce, visual merchandizing, retail operations, and customer relations.

The announcement follows Hugo Boss’s 5% sales drop in Q3 — attributed to an ongoing turnaround at the company — and Frasers Group’s de-facto takeover of the company on October 23.

Company comments: “Oliver Timm and I have been working side by side throughout our careers for almost 30 years, and it is a great honor for me to look back on this time and the many moments we have shared. I will miss working alongside him,” said Grieder in a statement. “During his time at Hugo Boss, he has repositioned sales with a future-oriented omnichannel approach and a strong customer-centric mindset, making a significant contribution to our growth and digitalization. As I look back at these achievements, I wish him, also on behalf of the entire managing board, the very best for the future.”

Michael Murray, Hugo Boss chair and Frasers Group CEO, also shared his appreciation: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Oliver Timm for his contribution to Hugo Boss over the past years. We appreciate his commitment and wish him all the best for his professional and personal future.”

Background: Ben Hallam, most recently SVP of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, has been appointed as Lululemon’s chief brand officer. At the sportswear brand, Hallam will lead global brand marketing, brand creative, store experience, and community. He will join the company’s senior leadership team and report to CEO Heidi O’Neill who joined in April 2026.

The announcement comes after the appointments of Maggie Gauger as president and chief product officer and Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. On Friday, the company also announced the appointment of Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective November 23. Sunderland joins from Boston Consulting Group and will report to chief financial officer Meghan Frank. Searches remain underway for a chief technology officer and a chief communications officer.

Company comments: “Ben brings an exceptional combination of creative vision, commercial discipline, and experience transforming iconic, premium brands at scale,” O’Neill said in a statement. “His proven ability to translate brand strategy into distinctive and compelling guest experiences will be critical as we strengthen how our brand comes to life across every touchpoint. Ben will play a central role in building a stronger and more competitive Lululemon.”

Background: Daisy Shaw-Ellis has been appointed CMO of Malone Souliers, where she will oversee the brand’s global marketing and communications, with an emphasis on expansion in North America. Shaw-Ellis joins from Condé Nast, where she was most recently accessories and jewelry director for Vogue and Vanity Fair.

Company comments: “We are delighted to welcome Daisy to Malone Souliers as global chief marketing officer,” CEO Andrew Wright said in a statement. “Her experience in executive positions at some of the industry’s most established and influential titles, alongside her exceptional eye and proven track record in luxury brand-building, will both enhance and amplify our voice globally. This is a pivotal moment for Malone Souliers as we embark on a new and exciting trajectory, and we look forward to presenting the brand in new and exciting ways in the coming seasons.”

Background: Clarisse Godbillon, who was CFO and COO of Lemaire from 2020 to 2025, is returning to the brand as managing director. She left Lemaire in 2025 to become COO of Jacquemus, and made the move back to the French label after Laetitia Mergui stepped down from the head job earlier this year.

Company comments: “Clarisse possesses an in-depth understanding of the company’s various activities and a profound knowledge of its identity,” the house said in a statement. “As managing director, she will oversee the development of the brand and lead its strategic and operational direction, working closely with [the house’s artistic directors and majority shareholders] Christophe Lemaire and Sarah-linh Tran.”

Background: Lady Gaga has moved into the CEO role at Haus Labs, the clean beauty company she founded in 2019. This comes after co-founder and former CEO Ben Jones exited the brand in early October. Gaga will now lead all commercial aspects of Haus Labs, alongside her prior responsibilities of creative direction and product development.

Background: Ryan Lally has been promoted to chief brand communications officer at Ralph Lauren Corp. Formerly SVP of global public relations and brand communications, Lally will continue to build on the company’s global comms strategy in this newly created role, while overseeing talent partnerships, events and more. Lally has been with the company for more than two decades, and will continue to report to David Lauren, chief branding and innovation officer.

Background: Alexis Hoopes, formerly global fashion VP at Ebay, has joined The RealReal as chief merchandising officer. At Ebay, she led the company’s $10 billion global fashion business for two-plus years, including the expansion of its Authenticity Guarantee program to new categories, price points and markets, strengthening trust among buyers and sellers. Hoopes will now lead The RealReal’s merchandising strategy, focusing on its luxury assortment and personalized product discovery — as the platform further advances its AI capabilities and unlocks growth opportunities.

Company comments: “Alexis is a proven leader who brings a rare combination of luxury merchandising expertise, global marketplace experience and operational discipline,” Rati Sahi Levesque, president and CEO of The RealReal, said in a statement. “As we build on our leadership in luxury resale, her ability to connect exceptional merchandise with evolving consumer demand will be instrumental in accelerating growth.”

Background: Hector Muelas joined LVMH in 2015 as global VP of content and creative, after working for Apple. Between 2017 and 2019, he was chief brand officer of LVMH-owned luggage brand Rimowa under chief executive Alexandre Arnault. Muelas then returned to Apple as global group creative director in 2019, a role he held until 2021. He returned to LVMH in 2023 as Tiffany & Co.’s global chief brand and creative officer, reuniting with Alexandre Arnault.

He has now been named Louis Vuitton chief brand creative officer, a newly created position reporting to Louis Vuitton deputy CEO Damien Bertrand.

Company comments: “Hector will define and steer our creative storytelling across all touchpoints, thereby ensuring strong overall image consistency. Leading creative and content execution, he will oversee all brand campaigns, with the art buying team led by Magena Chansarel and the content factory team led by Carole Fuchs joining his organization. In close collaboration with our business units, regions, and creative talents, Hector will further elevate our brand desirability, ensuring the house continues to set the benchmark in cultural resonance, creative boldness, and emotional connection with our clients worldwide,” Bertrand said in an internal announcement.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky, who most recently exited the board at Chanel, but remains president of Chanel SAS and fashion, is now co-chair of The Fashion Pact. A non-profit organization, The Fashion Pact is a coalition of CEOs from more than 150 companies representing a third of the global fashion industry by volume. Pavlovsky will work alongside Inditex CEO Óscar García Maceiras and climate campaigner Paul Polman to build on the work of the pact in creating a net-zero fashion industry. (Chanel is among the coalition’s founding signatories back in 2019.)

Company comments: “As we look ahead to 2027, our focus is increasingly on translating collective ambition into implementation, and scaling solutions across the industry. Bruno’s appointment marks an important step in this journey, bringing valuable leadership and perspective as we work to strengthen collaboration across regions, business models and supply chains,” The Fashion Pact wrote on LinkedIn.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky joined Chanel in 1990 and became a board member in 2018, a duty he will now step down from. Since 2022, he has also been president of the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode. Pavlovsky remains president of Chanel SAS and of the house’s fashion activities.

Company comments: “This latest move marks the completion of the board’s evolution toward a composition of independent directors, bringing diverse external expertise and perspectives, while retaining executive representation through the global executive chair and global CEO. Bruno Pavlovsky remains fully committed to his role as president of Chanel’s fashion activities and president of Chanel SAS,” Chanel said in a statement.

Background: Zankov has appointed Jack Tobin, founder of luxury brand development consultancy Jack Tobin Agency, as CEO and business partner of Zankov, formalizing a partnership that has developed since Tobin began consulting for the brand two years ago. Since beginning its partnership with Jack Tobin Agency, Zankov has increased its international business more than tenfold and doubled its global stockist network.

Company comments: “Zankov is at an incredibly exciting stage in its growth. I have always envisioned having a partner who could join me in shaping the next chapter of the brand — someone who shares my ambition to build an enduring business while staying true to the creative vision that has always defined Zankov. Jack is the ideal partner to take this next step with, and I’m excited about what we can build together,” says Henry Zankov, founder and creative director.

Background: Net-a-Porter (NAP) has appointed Devina Foley as Americas president to oversee the retailer’s US and Canada strategy. With more than 20 years of experience across retail, merchandising and e-commerce, Foley will help strengthen NAP’s market positioning as it settles into a new era under LuxExperience Group. She has held senior leadership roles at Bandier, Rockets of Awesome and Gilt, following earlier positions at Loft and Gap Inc. Based in New York, Foley will report to NAP CEO Heather Kaminetsky.

Company comments: “Devina brings an impressive breadth of experience and a proven track record of driving growth and leading businesses through transformation,” Kaminetsky said in a statement. “Her leadership and expertise will be invaluable as we continue to grow Net-a-Porter’s US business.”

Background: LVMH has promoted Clara Boissonnas, formerly women’s leather goods product director at Louis Vuitton, to CEO of Pucci. Boissonnas joined Louis Vuitton in 2002 as a product manager, before exiting four years later. After a decade working across Lanvin and Byredo, she returned to LV where she helped shape the maison’s coveted leather goods business. At Pucci, Boissonnas will strengthen the brand’s distinctive creative identity, desirability, and international reach, while reporting to Pietro Beccari, chair and CEO of the LVMH Fashion Group. As for Saar Debrouwere, who has led Pucci since 2022, her future role will be announced in due course, according to the group.

Company comments: “Clara has made a significant contribution to Louis Vuitton through her deep product expertise, strong creative sensibility, and unwavering commitment to excellence. Her ability to combine creative ambition with a clear understanding of the business makes her ideally suited to lead Pucci into its next chapter,” Beccari said in a statement.

Background: Yanina Novitskaya, who has spent the last 19 years at Cartier, most recently as CEO of South East Asia and Oceania, is the next chief executive of Richemont-owned Delvaux. Delvaux, the world’s oldest fine leather goods house, was founded in Brussels in 1829. In its next chapter, Novitskaya succeeds Jean-Marc Loubier, who returned to lead the brand after its acquisition in 2021, and will report to Richemont fashion and accessories CEO Philippe Fortunado.

Company comments: “Yanina’s strong knowledge of the luxury industry will be instrumental in leading Delvaux into its next chapter, strengthening its distinctive positioning and continuing to drive product desirability and international growth,” Fortunato said in a statement.

Background: Marc Jacobs has appointed John Wattiker as CMO to lead the brand’s global marketing strategy. Wattiker joins the brand after almost 15 years at Hearst Magazines working in the company’s advertising business, where he most recently held the role of VP of fashion and luxury. Prior to Hearst, he worked in the banking sector. At Marc Jacobs, Wattiker will oversee efforts to strengthen brand positioning, deepen consumer engagement and further expand the recently acquired brand’s global reach and relevance under new owner WHP Global.

Company comments: “John brings deep experience across luxury, fashion and media, with a clear understanding of how to build brands and engage consumers,” Marc Jacobs CEO Eric Marechalle said in a statement. “He pairs creative instinct with strategic and commercial discipline and brings an extensive network of relationships built over the course of his career. I am confident he will be a great addition to our leadership team as we grow Marc Jacobs globally.”

Background: Chanel has appointed a creative makeup director, Lucia Pieroni. Previously, Pieroni was creative director of makeup at Shiseido-owned Clé de Peau Beauté (2006-2019), which led to a series of partnerships with photographers and designers where Pieroni helped shape beauty direction for fashion shows, editorials, and campaigns. At Chanel, she will work alongside the makeup creation studio reporting to Simona Cattaneo, president of fragrance and beauty.

Company comments: “Lucia possesses an extraordinary instinct for beauty. She perceives the individuality in every face and understands with precision how to reveal it, creating makeup that feels intuitive and expressive, while always celebrating singularity. Her artistic vision and unique savoir-faire will make this collaboration a decisive new chapter for Chanel Makeup,” Cattaneo said in a statement.

Background: Alistair McCallum, formerly global communications VP at Burberry, has been appointed chief marketing officer of Givenchy. McCallum arrives with international comms experience at fellow LVMH house Fendi, and before that, at Alexander McQueen, where he worked with now-Givenchy creative director Sarah Burton. He will report to brand CEO Amandine Ohayon.

Company comments: “The arrival of Alistair McCallum [...] on our executive committee brings recognized expertise in the luxury and fashion worlds to support our international ambition and teams worldwide,” Ohayon said in a statement.

Background: LVMH-owned jewelry brand Repossi has appointed Matthieu Soudan as managing director. The hire comes as the brand’s former CEO Anne de Vergeron returns to her management responsibilities at the LVMH group level. Soudan has been in the LVMH ecosystem for nine years, the majority of which were spent as general manager of Tag Heuer before moving to Bvlgari in 2025. At Repossi, he will lead the brand into its next phase within the world of contemporary high jewelry, while strengthening its positioning and global reach.

Company comments: “I am delighted to entrust the leadership of Repossi to Matthieu Soudan as we open a new chapter in the development of this distinctive maison. At Tag Heuer and more recently at Bvlgari, he has demonstrated a strong strategic vision, together with the ability to execute strategies that support operational excellence and the desirability of our maisons,” Stéphane Bianchi, group managing director and CEO of LVMH Watches & Jewelry, said in a statement.

Background: Capri has appointed Catherine So as the company’s chief legal and sustainability officer. So joins from Tiffany & Co., where she most recently served as senior vice president and general counsel, where she oversaw legal, compliance, intellectual property, litigation, governance and brand protection. She spent 15 years at Tiffany across various roles.

Company comments: “We are pleased to welcome Catherine to Capri Holdings. She is a highly respected legal leader with extensive experience with helping develop global luxury brands and executive teams through periods of transformation and growth,” CEO John D. Idol said in a statement. “Her expertise, leadership, and strategic perspective will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen our business and position our brands for long-term success.”

Background: Poshmark has made a string of executive hires. Creative consultant Jamie Hunter, who worked as a buyer and fashion director at Bergdorf Goodman, has been appointed fashion and creative director of the California-based resale company. This new role signals Poshmark’s ambition to become an authority in the fashion resale space, by bringing its curation, styling and creative direction in-house, informed by Hunter’s two-plus decades in the industry.

Other new hires include: Yoshitaka Matsuzawa as SVP of seller and community experience, leading product development across consumer experiences and AI; Kishore Kumar Mohan (formerly The RealReal) as engineering SVP; Lesley Clifford as VP of merchandising, also a new role supporting a more strategic approach to assortment and brand relationships; and Beth Newman (formerly Canada Goose) as PR and communications director.

Company comments: “We’ve been deliberate about bringing in leaders who add deep expertise in their respective fields and fresh perspectives to Poshmark. With experience spanning fashion, technology and retail, they’re strengthening our leadership team and helping us sharpen our fashion point of view,” chief revenue officer Elizabeth von der Goltz said in a statement.

Background: Stephan Sturm has decided to step down as chair and member of the supervisory board of Hugo Boss, following discussions between the brand and its now-largest shareholder Frasers Group. The Mike Ashley-owned business upped its stake in the German brand in mid-August, from 30.28%% to 47.89%; the rising share comes on the heels of Frasers’s June takeover bid of £1.72 billion, which the Hugo Boss board deemed “inadequate” and urged shareholders to reject.

Now the largest shareholder of the Hugo Boss business, Frasers Group is edging closer to expanding to its portfolio further, following the acquisition of UK department store Harvey Nichols last month. Sturm will continue to serve as chair until a successor has been elected.

Company comments: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Stephan Sturm for his leadership, commitment, and dedication to Hugo Boss. We respect his decision and will work closely with him to ensure a smooth transition,” deputy chair Sinan Piskin said in a statement.

Background: Space NK has named Emma Simpson-Scott as CEO, succeeding Andy Lightfoot, who is stepping down after a decade heading the beauty retailer. Following a period of significant growth and transformation, including its recent acquisition by Ulta Beauty, Simpson-Scott will now lead the business as it matures further. Previously, the executive spent seven and a half years as CMO and 10 years at Space NK altogether.

Company comments: “Under Andy’s leadership, Space NK achieved significant growth, strengthened its position as a market-leading beauty retailer, and successfully transitioned into the Ulta Beauty family,” Kecia Steelman, president CEO of parent company Ulta Beauty, said in a statement. “Emma is a highly respected retail leader who brings deep customer insight, retail expertise and a passion for building exceptional teams. I look forward to our continued work together as she leads Space NK into the next chapter of growth.”

Background: Southern Californian brand St. John has named former co-creative director of Kenzo Humberto Leon as creative director. Beyond Kenzo, Leon co-founded fashion concept store Opening Ceremony in 2002 and is best known for his distinctive multidisciplinary approach to design. At St. John, Leon will oversee the knitwear brand’s image, design, and overall creative direction.

Company comments: “Humberto brings a rare instinct for honoring our history while making it feel entirely new. He understands that true luxury lives in how clothing makes people feel, which is the very spirit Marie Gray built this house on. Together, we’re introducing St. John to a new generation who may not have felt it was made for them until now,” CEO Mandy West said in a statement.

Background: Richemont has appointed Anton Rupert as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board. Rupert, the son of Richemont chair Johann Rupert, has served as a non-executive director on Richemont’s board since 2017. He served as director of Watchfinder from July 2018 until December 2019. Since January 2021, he has served on the advisory board of Asia Partners Fund LP I, a regional Southeast Asia private equity fund focused on growth-stage technology-based opportunities. Following the meeting of Richemont’s board of directors on September 8, Richemont announced his appointment as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board of directors. He will serve alongside Bram Schot, who was appointed non-executive deputy chair in 2024 and who will continue in his role.

Company comments: “This appointment is an important step in the board’s long-term succession planning,” Richemont chairman Johann Rupert said in a statement. “Richemont’s strength has always rested on the continuity that comes from close family involvement, on rigorous governance, and on an unwavering commitment to creativity and craftsmanship. Having Anton and Bram serve together as non-executive co-deputy chairmen ensures that each of these foundations is given the attention it deserves: Anton will continue to safeguard the creative and product priorities that define our maisons, while Bram will ensure that our governance remains of the highest standard.”

Background: James Kelly has been named CEO of Theory, after joining the brand in 2022 as CFO and later as global co-chief operating officer. As global CEO of both Theory and Helmut Lang, Kelly will oversee both brands’ headquarters functions, commercial operations, and global growth initiatives. Before joining Theory, Kelly helped scale Uniqlo’s US expansion. He succeeds Dinesh Tandon, who will transition into the co-chief operating officer role, as well as returning to his role as CEO of Theory China.

Company comments: “James has been an instrumental leader for Theory over the past several years, bringing strategic vision, operational excellence and a deep understanding of our business,” said Kazumi Yanai, chairman of Theory. “As James assumes the role of global CEO and Dinesh focuses his leadership on one of our most important markets, we are further expanding our global organization and positioning Theory for continued success around the world.”

Background: Charlotte Fournet, the niece of Kering chair François-Henri Pinault, has been named CEO of jewelry maison Pomellato, succeeding Kering Italia president Sabina Belli. Fournet joined Saint Laurent in 2014 before moving to Gucci in 2019 and then Bottega Veneta in 2020, where she climbed the merchandising ladder to become director just over three years ago. Krizia Cucurachi, who joined Dodo in 2024 as global product and brand director, has been promoted to CEO. Prior to joining the brand, she spent more than a decade at Swarovski across several senior leadership positions. Both will report to Kering Jewelry CEO Jean-Marc Duplaix, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Jewelry is a strategic growth pillar for Kering. Pomellato and Dodo are two highly distinctive houses with strong identities and tremendous potential. Charlotte’s extensive experience across several Kering houses and Krizia’s strong track record in brand-building and transformation make them ideally positioned to lead the next phase of growth for Pomellato and Dodo,” Duplaix said in a statement.

Background: Sabina Belli, who joined Kering as CEO of Pomellato in 2015, has been named president of Kering Italia. Before joining the French luxury group, Belli held senior marketing and executive roles at WPP, L’Oréal Luxe and LVMH, spanning the likes of Christian Dior Parfums, Moët Hennessy, Veuve Clicquot, and Bvlgari. Since this April, she has also led Kering Accademia per le Eccellenze, a Kering initiative dedicated to preserving and promoting Italian craftsmanship, alongside serving on the directors board of the Kering Foundation. In her new role, Belli will report directly to CEO Luca de Meo, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Italy occupies a unique place in Kering’s history, identity, and future. Its creativity, craftsmanship, and industrial excellence are at the heart of our houses and the long-term vitality of the luxury industry,” de Meo said in a statement. “Sabina brings a deep understanding of the Italian luxury ecosystem and a strong ability to build partnerships across business, education and public institutions.”

Background: Kristin Bauer, who spent three years as chief supply chain officer for sneaker retailer Foot Locker, will join Converse as chief operating officer. As parent company Nike works to revive its Converse business, following consecutive quarters of slow sales, it is rebuilding a leadership structure to help propel growth. Bauer will report to Nike COO Venky Alagirisamy.

Company comments: “We are excited to welcome Kristin and look forward to the perspective she will bring as we continue to build momentum for the brand,” Nike said in a statement.

Background: Jane Ewing has been named chief commercial officer and executive vice president of Nike, reporting directly to CEO Elliott Hill. She joins after a 14-year tenure at Walmart, most recently serving as interim CEO for Sam’s Club China. She also previously held senior leadership roles at Diageo. In her new role, Ewing will lead Nike’s global marketplace organization, including Sales and Nike Direct.

Company’s comments: “Jane’s experience, leadership and global perspective will help us continue this work and accelerate growth across Nike Direct and wholesale. Her role is vital to creating even stronger connections between brand, product and marketplace while serving athletes* and consumers around the world,” Hill said in a statement.

Background: The British Fashion Council (BFC) has announced that David Pemsel is stepping down as chair after four years in the position and 10 years on the executive board. During his time as chair, the BFC achieved record revenue figures (£14 million in FY2024/25), raised £7.2 million through the BFC Foundation and secured a multi-million-pound investment from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. Pemsel also appointed Laura Weir as BFC CEO in early 2025. A successor will be announced in September.

Company comments: “David has been an exceptional chair and an unwavering champion of British fashion. His leadership has helped strengthen the British Fashion Council as an organization, creating the stability, governance and long-term foundations that enable us to deliver our ambitions for the industry,” Weir said in a statement.

Background: Alexandre Oulès has been named chief operating officer for the LVMH beauty division, reporting to Véronique Courtois, president and CEO of Parfums Christian Dior and of the LVMH Group’s beauty division. According to the internal announcement, his new role will “oversee manufacturing, supply chain, and purchasing across the beauty division, driving stronger convergence between maisons across all three functions”. Oulès joins from Balenciaga, where he was appointed COO in October 2023. He previously held roles at L’Oréal, Guerlain, Celine and Moët Hennessy.

Company’s comment: “I am delighted to welcome back Alexandre, whose pursuit of operational excellence is widely recognized. His knowledge of the group and the specificities of the beauty world will strongly contribute to the overall efficiency of our operations,” Courtois said.

Background: Maya Dukes, who previously worked at Macy’s as head of graphic design (2001-2007), will return to the retailer as executive creative director. Dukes has more than two decades of experience leading creative strategy for some of the world’s best-known consumer brands, including her most recent role leasing global creative at Delta Airlines. At Macy’s, Dukes will report to CMO Sharon Otterman, overseeing the company’s creative and storytelling to bring the Macy’s brand back to life and help propel its Bold New Chapter strategy.

Company comments: “I am excited to welcome Maya back to Macy’s. Her experience translating brand strategy into compelling storytelling, elevating the customer experience and modernizing the creative process will be critical as we strengthen Macy’s for the future,” Otterman said in a statement.

Background: Skims has appointed its first-ever chief design officer, Erin Magee, best known for her time at Supreme, where she spent over 20 years. Most recently she held the role of chief creative officer, under which she led the brand’s creative vision, design, product development, and product strategy across apparel, accessories, collaborations, and special projects. Skims has also promoted Kim Schraub, who has been on board since Skims’s founding, to chief brand officer from her previous role as creative director. In her new role, Schraub will balance creative and commercial. Prior to joining Skims, Schraub worked at Abercrombie, Victoria’s Secret Pink and Yeezy.

Company comments: “Erin brings an unparalleled creative vision and a proven ability to build brands that transcend fashion and become cultural touchstones,” CEO and co-founder Jens Grede said in a statement. “Her eye for design, her deep understanding of product and her instinct for what resonates make her exactly the right person to lead Skims into its next era. We’re incredibly excited to welcome her to the team.”

“Kim has been with us since before Skims existed. She helped turn an idea into a brand that people genuinely love,” Kim Kardashian, Skims chief creative officer and co-founder, said in a statement. “Her creative instincts have helped shape everything about how Skims shows up in the world, and this promotion is a reflection of the enormous impact she has had, and the trust Jens and I have in her vision. I can’t wait to see where she takes us next.”

Background: Vuori has appointed Carey Collins Krug as CMO. She joins from Abercrombie & Fitch, where she spent the last seven years, four of which she held the CMO role. Prior to Abercrombie, Collins Krug held top marketing positions at David Yurman, Ralph Lauren and Donna Karan. At Vuori, she will lead the brand’s cross-channel marketing initiatives, and focus on global expansion.

Company comments: “Carey brings the kind of brand-building, consumer engagement and cross-functional marketing leadership that will be instrumental as Vuori enters its next chapter of growth,” Joe Kudla, founder and CEO of Vuori, said in a statement. “Her experience helping global lifestyle brands sharpen their storytelling and build deeper connections with consumers aligns closely with where we’re headed as we continue to scale.”

Background: Rains has appointed Tom Bettinson as CEO, succeeding co-founder Daniel Brix Hesselager, who will transition into a business development role after leading the company for a year and a half. Since the initiatives core to Brix Hesselager’s transformation plan, in particular retail development, have been implemented, the focus will now shift to driving commercial success through these investments. Bettinson first joined Rains in 2017, helping to establish the brand’s UK business, before stepping away and rejoining as CSO, with responsibility for all company sales channels, in 2025.

Company comments: “I stepped into the CEO role to lead a fundamental transformation of our concept and organization. It was an extensive undertaking that required swift decision-making. Today, the foundation is in place, and the time is right to pass the baton,” Brix Hesselager said in a statement. “The priority now is ensuring excellence in execution and driving commercial success across all areas of the business. Tom is the right person to lead that next phase.”

Background: Pandora has appointed André Branch as president of North America, one of the Danish jewelry brand’s largest growth markets. Branch brings more than 25 years of experience across global consumer, beauty and lifestyle brands, most recently having served as CEO at Ariana Grande’s R.e.m. Beauty. At Pandora, he will lead the business’s next phase of regional growth, focusing specifically on enhancing customer relevance and brand appeal. Branch is succeeding Luciano Rodembusch, who departed the company in February.

Company comments: “André is a highly accomplished commercial leader with a strong track record of driving growth across global consumer businesses. His ability to combine strategic clarity with disciplined execution makes him exactly the right person to lead our North America business and drive the next phase of growth in the region,” chief commercial officer Massimo Basei said in a statement.

Background: Skims has hired Jasmine Sevan as vice president of communications. With nearly two decades of experience, Sevan will play a key role in advancing Skims’s global communication efforts, further strengthening its position at the intersection of fashion, culture, and innovation. She most recently served as global communications and brand partnerships director at Victoria Beckham, where she led the comms strategy during a period of significant growth, spurred by the brand’s Paris Fashion Week debut, collaborations with Mango and Gap, and the global launch of Netflix documentary, Victoria Beckham. At Skims, Sevan will report to chief communications officer Tracy Nguyen.

Company comments: “Jasmine is an exceptional communications leader with a sharp strategic mindset and a deep understanding of how brands shape culture,” Nguyen said in a statement. “Her experience building reputation for fashion’s most-respected brands, alongside her relationships across media, fashion and entertainment, makes her an incredible addition to Skims.”

Background: Birgit Kretschmer will succeed Harm Ohlmeyer as chief financial officer of Adidas. Kretschmer spent 25 years of her career at the sportswear giant, following a six-year tenure as CFO of German fast fashion company C&A. Harm, who helped with the appointment of Kretschmer as his successor, will stay close to Adidas, ensuring a smooth leadership transition.

Company comments: “I am extremely happy that we have signed Birgit to be the successor of Harm. She knows the industry, she knows Adidas, and she has added the knowledge of cost discipline working as the CFO of a vertical retailer like C&A. I really look forward to welcoming her back on our team,” CEO Bjørn Gulden said in the company’s half-year earnings release.

Background: John Schlifske has exited the Kohl’s board after nearly 15 years of service, stepping down as chair to enter retirement. In his place, Wendy Arlin, who has been a director since 2023, will take on the chair role. Arlin has more than three decades of finance and consumer brand experience.

Company comments: “With deep financial and retail expertise, Wendy provides valuable perspective to both the board and the management team. She has been a valued voice and a natural leader in the boardroom since joining, and I look forward to working with her in this new capacity,” said Michael J. Bender, Kohl’s CEO and board director, in a statement.

Background: Whoop, the wearable fitness tech brand, has named Kyle Leahy as chief commercial officer. She will oversee the company’s commercial operations as it continues to scale across international markets and new channels, specifically its healthcare go-to-market strategy. Leahy comes from Glossier, where she transformed the beauty brand from a direct-to-consumer business into a global omnichannel company, bringing it to profitability during her three-year tenure as CEO.

Company comments: “Kyle has a proven track record of leading strong brands through rapid growth. She knows how to expand premium distribution and build the right partnerships without losing what makes a brand special. That experience will be critical as we bring Whoop to more people around the world,” founder and CEO Will Ahmed said in a statement.

Background: Skims has promoted Tracy Nguyen, formerly executive VP of communications and entertainment, as chief communications officer. Nguyen, who has been at Skims since 2024, will continue to lead global communications for the intimates brand, as well as collaborations and cultural activations across entertainment, sports, and brand partnerships. Most notably, the executive was key in building the partnership between Skims and Nike last year, and was subsequently appointed co-general manager of the venture — a role she will continue in alongside.

Company comments: “From her time as a trusted advisor across my entire brand portfolio — when Skims was just an idea — to joining Skims in a formal executive capacity more than two years ago, Tracy has been an incredible partner and leader. She understands the brand at its core — how to protect it, grow it, and put it in front of the right audiences at the right moments,” said Kim Kardashian, Skims chief creative officer and co-founder, in a statement.

Background: Manolo Blahnik has appointed former Chloé executive Kimberly Mimnaugh as managing director of Americas. Beyond her most recent role as VP of North America retail at Chloé, Mimnaugh’s luxury commercial experience spans various leadership positions at the likes of Brunello Cucinelli, and Theory and Helmut Lang. At Manolo Blahnik, she will deliver the commercial strategy for the brand’s New York-based subsidiary, across retail, wholesale and e-commerce.

Company comments: “Kimberly brings an exceptional combination of luxury retail expertise and commercial leadership. Her proven ability to accelerate direct-to-consumer growth while maintaining a strong wholesale business makes her ideally placed to lead this next phase of our growth in the Americas. I look forward to working closely with her,” CEO Kristina Blahnik said in a statement.

Background: John Smedley, the British knitwear brand that’s been in operation for more than 240 years, has revamped its executive line-up. Jess McGuire-Dudley, managing director since April 2025, has been named CEO, while Bryan Jackson is returning to the company as senior independent director, after retiring last year following 11 years as chair. New recruits include COO Brian Lancaster and CFO Stuart Pannell.

Company comments: “Today, we announce the appointment of a strengthened executive leadership team that combines deep industry expertise, operational excellence, and a shared commitment to securing the long-term future of John Smedley. With ambitious plans to strengthen John Smedley’s position as one of Britain’s most-respected luxury manufacturing brands, this C-suite will take the company into its next phase of growth,” McGuire-Dudley said in a statement shared with Vogue Business.
