#6735. Men Are Outspending Women on Botox. Here’s What They’re Asking For

Guys are going to increasingly wild lengths to achieve their version of the idealized man. Looksmaxxing, as we’ve come to know it, has included surgical procedures to reshape their eyes, taking a hammer to their face to create a more chiseled jawline, and breaking their legs to gain a couple inches. But an OG in cosmetic procedures is seeing a resurgence in men, too.

Chances are you’re familiar with Botox: localized injections to smoothen wrinkles in common areas like the forehead, the eyes, or around the mouth. Long viewed as a treatment limited to the ladies, it’s increasingly becoming another form of male upkeep. Now we’re learning that men are outspending women on the popular procedure. According to an October 2026 report by Guidepoint Qsight, a medical aesthetics data and intelligence provider, men spent an average of $529 per neurotoxin visit in Q3 of 2026, compared with $455 for women. (The figures include not just Botox but also competitors like Daxxify and Xeomin.)

The potential explanation is simple: Botox is an easy way to look a little younger, more well-rested, and even less angry or severe. (As a built-in bonus, it’s virtually painless—especially compared to the barbaric looksmaxxing trends circulating as of late.) According to a 2025 survey of 2,900 aesthetic plastic surgeons, men accounted for over 15% of all Botox cases that year. It was also their top non-surgical treatment by a landslide.

The growing cohort of men opting into “Brotox” believe it’s money well spent. Nancy Samolitis, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Los Angeles and co-founder of facile, has been treating men for years but has recently seen an uptick in male clientele, aged anywhere from 35 to 70. These days, “they’re more interested in skincare and more open to procedures,” she says. Many also book their first treatment nudged by their spouse or significant other who are existing patients. Others come in simply wanting to look better but not knowing what treatment to get. In many cases, Botox fits the bill.

While the uninitiated might think the injections make guys look surprised or less masculine, good work can be undetectable. Still you, just fresher.

Kyle Waldrop, a 37-year-old product designer in Los Angeles, first started getting Botox three years ago. “I’ve always been good about keeping up with a skincare routine and taking care of myself, so Botox felt like a natural extension of what I was already doing,” he says. His goal isn’t to change his face but to slow down wrinkles before they become obvious. He gets Botox for his forehead lines and crow’s feet, and recently started treating his neck lines, too.

But it’s not always about looking younger. Men are also using Botox in less obvious places. David Kim, MD, board-certified dermatologist and the founder of Soho Dermatology in New York City, treats the chin for more projection, as well as the underarms to combat excess sweating. Bell Yoo, NP, a board-certified nurse practitioner and the founder of Mimo Aesthetics in West Hollywood, adds that she injects the masseter (and sometimes temporalis) muscles for guys who struggle with jaw clenching or teeth grinding.

Aesthetically, men usually aren’t looking for the same thing from Botox as women. For starters, many want to soften their lines without erasing them. Preserving some natural movement is key. “My female patients often love that smooth, ‘glass skin’ appearance, whereas some of my male patients think it looks too waxy or oily,” Yoo says. Men also tend to opt out of a Botox brow lift, which many women request. “Men would much rather maintain a slightly heavier, lower-set brow than end up with an overly arched or ‘Spock’ brow,” Yoo says. Per Samolitis, this requires different injection points and doses tailored for guys. Kim, meanwhile, is careful not to overdo the crow’s feet. “It looks more natural when men have lines around the eyes, and it makes their face look better overall,” he says. These techniques quell the fears that guys have about looking less masculine or overdone. For most, the ultimate goal is to look relaxed and rejuvenated—not tight and taut. “When it’s done well and with the right amount, you look like yourself, just a bit more rested,” Waldrop says. “I still have all my natural movement and expressions, which is important to me.”

All that subtlety comes at a price. Men may end up paying more than women to treat the same areas, but the higher price tag is actually expected: Men often have larger, stronger facial muscles, which require more units to achieve their desired results, Yoo says.

While more men are embracing Botox, some remain tight-lipped about it. Yoo says that most of her male Botox patients are pretty discreet. “I think there’s still some stigma around men receiving cosmetic treatments, and many would rather keep it to themselves,” she says. Waldrop, however, is an open book. “I don’t really see it as something worth hiding or feeling that weird about,” he says. “Guys are already spending money on skincare, haircuts, hair transplants, working out, and all sorts of things to look and feel better, so I don’t really see why Botox should be treated any differently.”

For Waldrop, Botox is less a dramatic intervention than another item on his grooming checklist. He doesn’t see it as something that needs to be announced or apologized for. At the end of the day, “it’s really not that deep,” he says.

#6734. For More Volume and Less Oil, Start With These Dry Shampoos

I have fine hair and an oily scalp, which means a fresh wash looks great for about a day before my roots start to fall flat and my bangs give up on me. For years, I’d wash my hair every morning, until I realized all that shampooing and blow-drying could be swapped for something much easier—dry shampoo. A little at the roots on day two buys me another day or two between washes, and it’s saved more than one blowout I wasn’t ready to let go of. These days, a can lives on my vanity, another in my bag, and one permanently in my suitcase.

The reason it works so well comes down to what’s inside. Most formulas rely on ingredients like rice starch to soak up the oil sitting at your roots, which is what makes hair look fresh again, but getting rid of that oil also takes away the weight that makes roots fall flat in the first place. That’s why a good dry shampoo gives you a little lift almost instantly, and the powder leaves behind just enough texture to help a style hold without feeling stiff. If you’ve ever noticed that second-day hair is easier to style than freshly washed hair, that’s a big part of the reason.

Below, the best dry shampoos to use this season and beyond—according to the pros and Vogue editors.

Picking the perfect formula for your hair type makes all the difference. “All textures can use dry shampoo, but it may not be necessary or as beneficial for someone with coily hair,” says celebrity hairstylist Erinn Courtney. “Straight, wavy, or loosely curled hair benefits from dry shampoo most. Some dry shampoos are made for more oily hair, so they should be picked according to what kind of help your hair needs to feel fresh again.” Brooklyn-based hairstylist Mickiela Smith—also a trichologist and founder of hair-care platform—adds that for those with allergies or sensitive skin, it may be worth having a conversation with your doctor as they can provide a medicated, waterless shampoo to ease scalp woes.

Trichologist and colorist Bridgette Hill says that depending on hair type and texture, a dry shampoo can be used up to twice a day. “The important factor is ensuring there is a healthy hair care routine that balances the use of dry shampoo,” she notes. “If someone is using a dry shampoo daily, a proper shampoo with water should be performed at least every two to three days.” Board-certified dermatology nurse practitioner Catie Boucher reminds us that if we’re using dry shampoos regularly, it’s also essential to ensure we’re properly removing product buildup from our scalps during hair wash regimens. “I’ll be honest, I only wash my hair 1-2 times a week. I used to wash my hair daily, and not only did it not help with oiliness, it was a lot of work with long hair,” Boucher tells Vogue. “If you’re a dry shampoo loyalist like myself, or you use a lot of styling products, addressing product build-up with a scalp detox is never a bad idea.”

Dry shampoo can absolutely be part of a healthy haircare routine, as long as it’s used correctly and in moderation. “I see it as a styling and refreshing product rather than a replacement for washing your hair,” says Macias. “One of its biggest advantages is that it allows you to extend the life of a blowout or hairstyle, which can sometimes mean less frequent heat styling. From my professional perspective, that’s particularly useful when working with colored, fragile or heavily styled hair.” In any circumstance, the scalp always needs proper cleansing. “Using too much product or layering it repeatedly without washing can leave the scalp feeling uncomfortable and the hair looking dull,” warns Macias, who advises to only use dry shampoo where it’s needed, avoid overapplying and maintain a regular cleansing routine that suits your hair and scalp.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue's vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry's standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to dry shampoos, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, ease of application, spray vs non-aerosol, packaging, finish (ie: whether it leaves a white cast), and the hair-care concerns they address. #6732. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6731. Area’s Toms Collaboration Is Made for the After-Party

Designer Nicholas Aburn on bringing the brand’s signature sparkle to the humble Toms Alpargata.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

“I love designing a big look,” says Nicholas Aburn, the creative director of the maximalist, party-ready brand Area. “But there’s something to be said for making special things that people can actually wear. I want to make the dress that you had the best night in, that you got laid in, that you went home with your partner for the first time in. It has to be fun and special, but also it has to be normal enough that you actually wear it.”

Aburn, who worked at Demna’s Balenciaga and is now in his second year at Area, carried that idea into the brand’s spring/summer 2027 collection. Amid the razzle-dazzle—crystal-covered looks, sculptural silhouettes, and metallic heels that announced themselves with sound—came a surprise: Toms. The humble shoe, part of a limited-edition collaboration available now, received an Area-sized makeover, with the Alpargata style reimagined through the label’s party-inflected lens.

The limited-edition collection recasts Toms’s cult silhouette in five variations. The Crystal Slit, available in white and black colorways, riffs on Area’s celebrity-favorite jeans of the same name, with crystals diagonally tracing the vamp. Balletcore gets two takes in the ballet flat: one with a statement crystal shoelace bow, the other covered in tonal rhinestones. There’s also something on offer for the minimalist: the Sculpture Alpargata, which features origami-like folds. Toms’s molded footbed and plush insoles lend themselves to all-day (and night) comfort, while the embellishments bring an intentional after-party sparkle.

Aburn is often approached by brands about collaborations, but Toms was an easy yes, even if the two might seem worlds apart. “I think even Toms was surprised that I was up for it,” the designer said. “Some of my colleagues were like, ‘That’s the one you are willing to pull the trigger on?’ But Toms is iconic, it’s American, and I like that it comes from this very casual place.”

That easygoing spirit came through on the runway. The shoes were styled with some of the collection’s more relaxed pieces: ink-splattered shorts, a draped cowl-neck top, and pooling white jeans with feather trim. It’s how Aburn envisions them being worn in real life. “At weddings, everyone takes off their heels and puts on those pass-out flip-flops,” he explains. “I like the idea that you bring the Toms in your bag and throw them on when you’re tired. You still have your dress on, your hair is kind of messy. Everything gets a little cooler at the end of the night.”

Aburn, like many, associates Toms with the “indie sleaze” era, when they were ubiquitous with skinny jeans. (He bought his first pair after seeing Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen wear them.) Now, with Area’s signature embellishments in the mix, Aburn already has a few dream wearers in mind.

“[The] Sculpture, which doesn’t actually have sparkles on it, I would be very excited to see guys in. I’d love to see Jacob Elordi in those. Taylor Swift has been a big supporter of the brand; she’d look great in the Crystal Slit ones. And I’d love to see some cool downtown girl like Ivy Wolk wearing the ballet flats.”

#6729. With the ‘New’ Yeezy, Ye Says He Wants to ‘Let the Clothes Do the Talking.’ But Who’s Listening?

“I don’t have a lot of words tonight,” Ye told me, not long after concluding his Yeezy Season 01 runway show in Los Angeles on Wednesday evening. “I’ll let the clothes do the talking.”

You might read that quote and be surprised to hear that Ye said it warmly, with an all-32-bared smile. But for those still paying attention, his relatively upbeat demeanor tracks with the tame-not-turnt persona that Ye has performed through most of 2026; the one that’s been slowly-but-surely trying to reamass the cultural capital he’s spent most of the last decade either annihilating or reclaiming. Legions of fans have proven they’re still all in; the culture at large remains justifiably dubious. The question this week is, how will Ye’s return to fashion affect the calculus?

Upon arrival, a typical Hollywood warehouse exterior turned into a Frank Herbert-esque interior as soon as you crossed the threshold. Inside, a hundred or so guests sat on two rows of unbroken benches that encircled a large white mound in the center, lit by a heavenly white glow from above. Inside was a mix of the usual cool kids: models (including the runway-favorite teen rapper Nettspend) and recurring characters in the overarching, enduring Kanye Universe. There was Fear of God founder Jerry Lorenzo, who made conversation with Don C, while 2 Chainz was patiently posted up in a hooded black leather coat like ’98 Wesley Snipes. Big Sean, rebuffing the sweltering indoor temperatures in a shearling jacket over a crewneck sweater, caught up with Hit-Boy.

Models on the Yeezy Season 01 runway, which featured a characteristically minimalist set piece.

The 19-year-old rapper Nettspend walked in the show.

Once everyone was seated, the lights dimmed as the unmistakable opening piano note of “Runaway” set the show into motion, with one lone model striding out in a killer black trench. From there, two more models, men this time, walked out in the opposite direction; what followed was a bit of organized chaos with the number of models and paths alternating at random intervals to the tune of a playlist that zipped between new Ye music (UK garage vibes, it would seem) and a gothic orchestra not unlike the scores Danny Elfman used to chef up for Tim Burton.

The fits were crisp, practical and tactical. Most of the menswear was ready-made for basic maneuvers, while the women’s looks were sleek and casual, with a few Milla Jovovich-in-Fifth-Element skimpy ensembles thrown in because Ye can only restrain himself but so much. The most notable thing, about the guys especially, were the relatively streamlined silhouettes: close-cropped coats, bombers and vests, fitted pants and sweats. Where past Ye lines championed and emblazoned the path for the baggy wave, with oversized boots and pants you could swim in, Ye seemed to be brazenly planting a flag back on the opposite end of the spectrum.

Nearly 12 years, and a dozen lifetimes, since his debut Yeezy Season 1 runway show in 2015, the notion of a “Season 01”—his first formal showing since his damning 2022 show in Paris, the one with the “White Lives Matter” shirts—is a conspicuous attempt to clear the slate. All of his previous shows had been produced in collaboration with Adidas, who severed ties with Ye four years ago, after he tweeted a tirade of antisemetic remarks. This time around, to let the clothes tell it, Ye is locked in. I don’t have an image of every single Yeezy Season line seared into my brain, but I feel comfortable saying Ye’s latest was the first time I looked at one of his collections and objectively thought, I could wear that. Most of the gear is quite solid—and familiar Ye's running the same playbook with Season 01 that he’s run with his music, and to some degree, his persona. It’s the Yeezy gear you know and love(d), refined to make it that much more palatable, similar to the way a song like “Whatever Works” puts him back over chipmunk’d soul samples. And true to the title, it does indeed; the fact that it does is maybe a testament to the brilliance that got lost in the insanity. But is playing the hits (quite literally, with “Runaway” opening the show) what we want from one of the most paradigm-shifting—and absolutely chaotic—creative minds of our time?

Historically, Ye’s designs are so focused on an idea of utilitarianism that they ultimately come off as a bit drab, if not downright dystopian. Essentials like hoodies and beefy leather jackets are still central to his vision, but as the models strode around in his usual earth-toned palette—save for a handful of black looks to start, and a bright pop of reds at the end—it became clear that Ye was putting on the same show in a different kind of stadium. The same sci-fi silhouettes, tweaked to their cleanest shape and most pleasing hue, sans screenprinted hate speech. Ideologically, the runway show wasn’t far off from the experience of hearing his 2007 hit “Good Life” all these years later, ringing off stadium speakers, carrying 80,000 people along on a wave of wistfulness— even if Ye himself only performed approximately 75% of the lyrics against a backing track.

In keeping with all of his other moves this year, Yeezy Season 01 is Ye presenting a safer, rule-abiding version of himself: Ye with just art, no antics. Much in the way that his latest album, Bully, eschewed any lyrics that say, shouted out R. Kelly or Bill Cosby (which is more than can be said about 2024’s Vultures 1), it felt like a deep sigh of relief to see him present clothes that don’t feature appalling slogans, at a fashion show with Candace Owens nowhere in sight. But the compromise for a sanitized Kanye is also one that can’t help but feel anodyne as well. The New Ye doesn’t needle, but he’s lost Old Ye’s knack for trying something new. Of course, we’re also well over a decade into the Yeezy experiment—at this point, the present has caught up to the futuristic vision Ye first dreamt up back in 2015. There’s a whole new generation of aspiring designers creating in his image, kids who fancy themselves trailblazers whose paths just loop back to Ye: streamer Kai Cenat just launched his own clothing brand, Vivet, while N3on attended Wednesday night’s show, skipping the Yeezy space gleefully documenting every interaction. It feels as though all of this has happened before, and all of it will happen again.

Mystery. Intrigue. Chaos. This is the typical life cycle for a Ye project, be it music, fashion, or otherwise. An announcement materializes, hype ensues. Then, inevitably, the seams start to show and it becomes apparent that he isn’t inviting you on a pre-planned journey so much as building the plane in real time, seconds before takeoff. And then, through sheer force of will, or maybe even genius, the result ends up so captivating that the speedbumps hardly matter. He’s still a master showman, and all it takes is a strong yearning for the Old Ye to find yourself surrendering to it. The efficacy of that last factor, though, has undeniably waned over the years. For much of the 2020s, in the midst of many a manic outburst or worse, Ye’s messes have hardly cohered into something objectively beautiful. The intrigue curdled into perverse bemusement; for every unwavering diehard fan, there was a rubbernecker tapped in to watch the circus.

The 2026 version of Ye has been an exercise in proving how many people will show up when he shuts up, and whether he can make it back from the brink if he delivers the right spectacle.

The result is the most well-oiled the Yeezy Machine has ever been. An album that more or less dropped when he said it would, for once. A smattering of live shows across the world, each in a sold-out stadium boasting record-breaking rap concert attendance where he leans on his most enduring strengths: visual spectacle and a bulletproof catalog. The only area left to renegotiate is fashion…which brings us back to Wednesday night in LA.

These are the scenes you’d expect at a Ye event, but the first sign that the overall vibe was different and more relaxed was that the man himself was at the door, tucked off into a hallway, immaculately dressed in a fitted all-black leather fit offset by a ridiculously large and ornate gold waist fixture—every bit the Dune-caliber fit as the space we were standing in required. Ahead of the show, he posed backstage flanked by his wife, Bianca Censori, and the four kids he shares with his ex, Kim Kardashian (including 13-year-old North, who was sporting her unmistakable blue-raspberry locks). At Yeezy events past, you’d expect to see harried staff scrambling, while Ye was somewhere out of sight but exuding stress and anxiety out into the atmosphere. But on Wednesday, the 49-year-old beamed as friends made their way past him to their seats. Even a three-piece-suited Kid Cudi came over to say hello.

Ye backstage with his children, from left: North, Psalm, Chicago, and Saint West.

Fifteen years ago, Yeezy Season 01 would’ve caused a massive sea change in the menswear world almost instantaneously, with the wave starting in SoHo then slowly emanating out into the beyond. In 2026, does Kanye still move that needle? The Year in Ye has been one big display of his ability to Don Draper the culture at large, and shock us all by “how much it never happened.” There’s no controversy big enough to keep him away for too long and very few fences he can’t mend.

For example, Sean and Cudi ceased their umpteenth falling out with their old label boss two months ago at a guest-packed, blockbuster homecoming show in Chicago on Ye’s tour stop; their show of support tonight only underlined how deeply the hatchet has been buried yet again. When I spoke to Big Sean after the show, he could only marvel at how much Ye has “given” to the culture across all different categories. One-time GOOD Music COO Steven Victor said the show made him feel like Ye “has his shit together,” noting that Ye admitted to him that he was still working out the model patterns hours before showtime. In past Yeezy Seasons, the cram-effect would’ve been apparent, but here, Victor said he wouldn’t have noticed because it all seemed to go off so effortlessly.

As for the man himself? I spoke to him, but again, he didn’t have much to say, at least on the record. He seemed excited that I picked up on the intentional disharmony of the model routes, and explained that the space we were standing in was a “language I’ve been working on for 10 years” called “DROAM,” which refers to the minimalist design he hopes to apply to stores, urban planning, and a home for himself.

“I got a quote for you,” Victor interjected. “The king returns!” Ye laughed. The question remains, though: Is he welcome?

#6728. How New York and L.A. Celebrated Diwali in Style

Diwali—which translates to “festival of lights”—fêted by the global South Asian diaspora is a five-day celebration that began on Friday, November 6, a date decided by the Hindu lunar calendar. Diwali marks the new year, brings the promise of prosperity, and signifies the triumph of good over evil. While customs range across religion and region, the festival often means dedicating hours to baking sweets and lighting an unfathomable number of tea light candles, as well as giving up meat, fish, and alcohol. There’s also the deep cleaning rituals—to make room for blessings.

But in the U.S., more epicurean customs have emerged, which means weeks of parties, dinners, and gatherings in the lead-up. It’s proving to be a loophole for more indulgent fanfare before the official start of Diwali. Here’s Vogue’s look inside the celebrations everyone was talking about this year.

“Look around, look out the windows: We’re in New York City,” Jessel Taank told the crowd gathered at Boom at the Standard High Line. For the ŌUSHQ founder and Real Housewives of New York star, this soirée was one she had been dreaming of for some time. “On January 1st I wrote in my little notebook, ‘Host Diwali at The Standard’ as it was something I really wanted to do,” she said. “Growing up, Diwali was more of an intimate, community thing and what it’s become is so extraordinary.”

For the second annual Diwali Noir party presented by the fashion platform in partnership with the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Taank was joined on hosting duty by Prakti Beauty founder and model Pritika Swarup and the CFDA’s Marc Karimzadeh.

The high-octane evening invited guests to embrace an “Indian-inspired” dress code. “We really wanted to crush the stereotypes, because when you think of Indian fashion it is really occasionwear-heavy, big lehenga cupcakes, and embellishments,” Taank told Vogue. “I don't think Indian fashion is like that anymore. There’s a lot of creative energy coming from the Middle East and India that doesn’t get enough credit and recognition.”

Taank wore a metallic and bejeweled chocolate gown by Prabal Gurung, while Swarup opted for a bright punch-pink floor-length Rahul Mishra dress. “Look at everyone here tonight,” Swarup chimed in. “We wanted them to have their own interpretation of what modern Indian fashion is—and everyone looks incredible.”

Jenna Lyons donned sunglasses and an all-black ensemble topped with a bow, designer Sami Miro adorned herself in jewels from luxury Indian brand Outhouse, and mother-daughter duo Rachel Roy and Ava Dash took traditional Indian garments—palazzo pants and baroque blouses—and played with silhouettes, adding plumes of crimson fur and a flash of midriff.

While Diwali was the reason for the celebration, the night itself felt like an exercise in cultural exchange and discovery. Guests included Daniel Boulud, Bibhu Mohapatra, Kate Davidson Hudson, Katya Tolstova, Madhulika Sharma, Ankur Jain, Carly Cushnie, Ronny Kobo, Michelle Ochs, Roopal Patel, Dhaval Bhanusali, Azeezah Khan, Natalie De’Banco, Priya Shukla, Jay Sean, Akbar Hamid, and Junaid Mahmood, alongside Taank’s fellow cast members Sai De Silva, Erika Hammond, and Devyn Simone.

The evening also marked the official re-launch of ŌUSHQ’s multi-brand e-commerce website and the introduction of its new editorial destination dedicated to fashion, culture, and designer discovery. Behind the bar, towers of Johnnie Walker Blue Label bottles spiraled towards the ceiling as bartenders whipped up martinis, margaritas, and poured countless glasses of Champagne. Hammond and De Silva sipped cocktails and giggled with Miro, while stylist Micaela Erlanger perched at the end of the bar with Natasha Das, founder of Danarys, who nibbled on spicy bites of lamb, and morsels like samosas and pakora. “Diwali is quickly becoming one of my favorite party seasons,” Erlanger quipped.

On the other side of the room, the dance floor heaved, as Bollywood favorites like the 1999 hit “Dilbar” blended with Afro tech, while the Egyptian hit “Ah Ya Albi” played alongside Keinemusik’s “Move.” The music paused once briefly to give way to dancers who, atop the bar, performed a routine that, much like the dress code, blended India and the West.

“Can I just say, I don’t remember the last time I was in a room with so many beautiful people and so many beautifully dressed people,” added Karimzadeh, senior director of content and communications at the CFDA. “This is amazing.”

As speeches concluded, the party loosened further, turning from a bustling soiree to an all-out “rager”—to quote Taank. EDM and hip-hop boomed through the speakers, drinks spilled, dresses were trampled on, and by 1 a.m. the Champagne eventually ran out.

“We take for granted that the journey from gas to dust to protostar to star to supernova takes more than just a miracle—it takes time,” Gold House executive chairman and CEO Bing Chen shared in his remarks at The Majestic Downtown. It was a fitting metaphor for what Gold House called its largest Gold Diwali yet.

The organization threw its celebration for the Festival of Lights in Los Angeles, marking both its expansion as an institution and Diwali’s growing relevance. “Diwali is a celebration of light, community, and connection, and we wanted to bring that spirit to our Gold Diwali while honoring how culture shapes who we are and the possibilities we create,” Chen said.

The event began with the cast and producers of Ramayana: Part 1: Rise of a Legend introducing themselves and the film, released on November 5, which has already grossed over $56 million at the box office. It is also the most expensive film to be made in the region.

Gold House met the moment and announced a new partnership with nonprofit film fund South Stack Studios to launch the Gold Stack Shorts Fund, supporting short films and micro-series focused on South Asian stories.

The crowd, which was a bustling gathering of prominent entertainers, CEOs, and creators, brought together the likes of Freida Pinto, Tan France, Hannah Simone, Avantika, Dhar Mann, Richa Moorjani, and Rhea Raj, as well as Blumhouse president Abhijay Prakash, Poshmark founder Manish Chandra, and Anita Chatterjee.

Many attendees stuck to tradition, with jewel-toned lehengas, statement jewelry, saris, and bright sherwanis, but some played around with patent corsets in place of blouses and mini skirts.

Around the room, orange and golden marigolds were arranged in big, lush clusters with tropical palm fronds and brass lanterns. Friends, old and new, came together and enjoyed Diwali customs: Some grazed on a South Asian menu by Rasoi Catering, many danced as DJ MissNINJA performed with a live tabla performance, and others congregated in a dedicated Carrom Game Lounge where they played the traditional board game.

Indian luxury designer Anita Dongre debuted a one-off carrom board, painted by hand in collaboration with Gold House, that recontextualizes the tabletop game as a contemporary design object. Also on display was the Cuyana x Gold House Marigold Charm, a limited-edition piece released earlier in October.

Indian fashion house Sabyasachi’s multi-year collaboration with The Metropolitan Museum culminated in his first New York show in almost 20 years. So hosting the first Diwali party of its kind inside the hallowed halls of the storied institution, in many ways, felt fated.

“Ever since New York started having an official Diwali calendar, I wanted to host a party—and what could be a better venue than this,” designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee told Vogue. “It’s so iconic and it’s so New York. I think people are excited about this, so I’m very honored.”

Inside the American Wing’s Charles Engelhard Court, a crowd gathered to show off their opulent garments, from sleek sherwanis and richly textured shalwar kameez to sequined dresses and sharply tailored suits. Close friends of the designer, like Anjula Acharia, Jessel Taank, and Micaela Erlanger, all wore head-to-toe Sabyasachi looks, right down to the jewelry.

Guests in attendance included Kal Penn, Amy Fine Collins, Fern Mallis, Rhea Raj, Romilly Newman, Alioune Badara Fall, Nell Rebowe, Shruti Ganguly, Marie Ecot, Merritt Beck, Linda Fargo, Isiah Magsino, Imran Amed, Yumi Shin, Jully Patel, Angelica Hicks, and Carlos Mota.

As a six-piece band rattled off sultry renditions of songs like Dean Martin’s “Sway,” attendees were greeted with silver trays of Dom Pérignon Champagne and Petrossian caviar. Though most ended up mesmerized by what stood in the center of the room: A spectacular 16-foot-long grazing table, which was more like a culinary cornucopia outfitted with a peacock and an astounding bloom of ranunculus, roses, peonies, and winterberries. On offer, towering croquembouches, meringues, decadent cakes, and overflowing displays of fine chocolates and Indian sweets were placed alongside a lavish raw bar of fresh Maine lobster and oysters, fine Iberico ham, and endless types of cheese.

As Bollywood actress Rani Mukerji and designer Waris Ahluwalia eagerly posed for photos with Sabyasachi, excited brides-to-be lined up to introduce themselves to the designer, brimming with equal parts awe and nerves. Other guests sipped on spiced margaritas—which seems to be the emerging signature cocktail of the Diwali season—and lounged by the fountains.

Once the drinks dwindled and the band packed up, guests slowly made their way outside, reluctant to end the glamorous night. As everyone spilled out onto the iconic Met steps, a few who glittered even in the darkness of the crisp fall night beckoned for one more photo. For some, this was just another swanky party in Manhattan, but for those who grew up celebrating Diwali, it was a night for the history books.

Buzzy Indian restaurant the Ambassador’s Clubhouse turned Manhattan’s NoMad into a vibrant hub of revelry, as Anjula Acharia welcomed an exclusive guest list to her glitzy annual black-tie ball. “So many of you didn’t get plus ones,” she quipped over the mic. “So it means that all of you have to talk to everybody.”

The beloved All That Glitters Diwali Ball once again celebrated South Asian excellence, presented in partnership with Lexus. Guests in attendance included Avantika Vandanapu, Jay Sean, Rhea Raj, Bela Bajaria, Jessel Taank, Aasif Mandvi, Poorna Jagannathan, Mira Nair, Amrit Kaur, Nimesh Patel, Sheena Melwani, designers Falguni and Shane Peacock, and Revolve’s Divya Mathur.

“Tonight is my love letter to New York and all the South Asians here that are rising and thriving,” Acharia said. “So many of you have been grinding for decades. This is a celebration of all the work that you do for our community and for yourselves. I’m just so proud to honor all of you and I really mean that from the bottom of my heart.”

New York’s sudden cold snap was no match for the glamour that was put on show. Outside, some braved the cold for a Rhudeva scent station that offered engraved bottles of perfumes, including Dusky Diwali with notes of saffron, salted pistachio, and sandalwood. Inside, the room was a smorgasbord of crimson, as red flowers layered every surface from floor to ceiling.

As guests cozied up, sipping on piquant negronis, lassi-flavored cocktails, and martinis, bright plates of Punjabi food were passed around. Think: Wagyu-infused naan and lamb curry to samosas and spiced bites of goat. Subtlety was not on the menu, nor was it the dress code. Feathers trailed behind glittery saris, sequins caught the candlelight, and silk pooled and swished, while jhumkas and bangles clinked as Calvin Harris, Burna Boy, Charli XCX, and Vishal Dadlani boomed through the speakers.

“This is a far cry from the Diwaliis that I used to host myself, 20 or 30 years ago on Riverside Drive,” filmmaker Mira Nair told the crowd. “We are all here to be counted for, to be seen, and to be actually celebrating ourselves and our amazing community, that finally is visible in the most powerful of ways.”

East met West, as Jagannathan opted for South Asian designer Rahul Mishra in an untraditional rendition of desi opulence. Taank took a more modern route, and revealed her back tattoo with a pearlescent Tarun Tahiliani halter gown, while actress Avantika stuck with tradition in a warm copper lehenga and clutched onto a Coach Tabby purse.

For everyone in attendance, more was, well, more. Acharia floated across the room in a gilded silver Falguni Shane Peacock train adorned with feather cuffs, and Raj also tapped the designer for a custom magenta feathered two-piece that felt fitting for the rising pop star.

As the dance floor got warmed up (and subsequently didn’t stop until after 1 a.m.), Anita Chatterjee, founder of A-Game Public Relations, recalled: “Years ago, I remember being in Anjula’s Tribeca loft, where she put together a small Diwali party. Back then, she told me: ‘One day, everyone's gonna know about Diwali. There's going to be so many parties, and that’s what I want. I want our holiday and what we do to be seen by all.’ Anjula: mission accomplished. We did it!”

Passerine co-founders Maneesh K. Goyal and Alvina Patel Buxani shut down their Flatiron restaurant and set the scene for an early Diwali celebration with their second annual A Luminous Table dinner.

The gathering, which also raised funds for the Asian American Writers’ Workshop, was co-hosted by filmmaker Mira Nair, journalist Radhika Jones, and novelist Salman Rushdie.

A crowd from across fashion, finance, politics, and art convened, including Tamron Hall, Aasif Mandvi and B.D. Wong, Bibhu Mohapatra, Waris Ahluwalia, Alok Vaid-Menon, and June Ambrose, who eschewed her signature statement hat for sparkles and silk.

In true desi style, guests wore bright splashes of color, embellished lehengas, and luxurious saris, filling the air with soft metallic pops of bangles and jhumkas. Those without traditional outfits reveled in color, sparkles, and sequins. After all, it’s one of the few times all-black is considered a faux pas in New York City.

After a cocktail reception with plenty of Moët Hennessy on offer, a family-style dinner was served by executive Chef Gaurav Bathla. Guests took their seats at tables laden with bud vases of tulips, hyacinths, and carnations and quickly made introductions. Ambrose shook hands with Zara Rahim, Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s senior advisor, Rushdie and Italian artist Francesco Clemente chatted over red wine, and art curator Racquel Chevremont and her fiancé Mel Corpus made fast friends with their seat mates.

Siblings and friends were purposefully separated, as were some couples. “I created the seating chart that way intentionally,” Buxani told Vogue. “I wanted to create new friends so I separated some old ones. I think I have a good idea of who would get along.”

The food forged connections too. Starters like Goan chicken cafreal, Tamil shrimp Chettinad, and a samosa in Levantine katafi were quickly devoured, followed by baskets of naan and rice and a short rib pot pie filled with Old Delhi nihari, plumes of steam escaping from under its laminated pastry when theatrically cracked into.

Community was the guiding principle of the night, as co-hosts shared their stories of how Diwali offered respite as they navigated identity, immigration, and religion.

“When I was growing up in Bombay, the festivals were for all of us. It didn’t matter if we were Hindu, Muslim, Parsi—Diwali was ours,” Rushdie shared. “We all celebrated everything. And I think that this spirit is alive in this gathering.”

The celebrated novelist also noted that this energy is no longer part of the India he once knew.“There is something going on in India right now. India is boiling. And I would feel wrong not to say, maybe it’s not the thing to say in a restaurant, to celebrate the cockroach. But the young people of India have given us the most hopeful moment for a very long time.”

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is a propulsive Gen Z political movement in India that emerged earlier this year, using protests and demonstrations to demand government accountability, transparency, and major reforms across employment, education, and elections. Some have even referred to it as the Mamdani effect.

“I’m here as a mama cockroach,” Nair announced to the room to raucous cheers and applause, as the room swelled at the mention of her son, Zohran Mamdani. “Happy Diwali to all of us who believe in change. God knows the Cockroach Janta Party is reminding us that it is not enough to be quiet, it is not enough to celebrate, it is not enough to cease to question.” Her speech culminated in the room serenading her with a surprise birthday singalong.

As hot sticky date puddings covered in jaggery caramel filled the tables, Goyal stood for one last announcement. “In the old school tradition of people who live above their bodegas or restaurants, my husband and I, we live above this restaurant. There’s an after-hang at our apartment upstairs, and whether you come for 10 minutes or for two hours, everybody’s welcome. And let’s be honest, we’re New Yorkers. We like to see each other’s apartments!”

As the last sips of chili margaritas and tomato martinis were polished off, people slowly began heading for the door, and onwards to Goyal’s apartment for one more drink, one more story, and to make one more friend.

#6727. It Will Become Easier and Easier to Regrow Your Hair

With new technology, hair loss might be a thing of the past.

As part of the Future of Beauty Awards, the ELLE beauty team looked ahead at what will be next in beauty and wellness.

It’s been a trying decade: A pandemic, political turmoil, and everyday stressors are enough to make anyone’s hair fall out, and it has. Nearly 30 million women in the United States experience pattern hair loss, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Add on the potential of GLP-1-related hair loss, and we seem to be in an endless cycle of shedding. But could we finally be approaching a way to cure it? New in-office injectables and prescription drugs are poised to change the game for good.

Newly available at dermatologists’ offices, Xvie is a multi-signal, exosome-rich concentrate made from amniotic fluid. Exosomes are tiny vesicles released by cells; they contain proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. “Xvie takes a multi-signal approach to hair thinning by supporting cellular communication,” says Trillitye Paullin, PhD, a founding member and chief scientific officer of Xvie. Amy B. Lewis, MD, a dermatologist in New York who uses Xvie clinically, says she has seen it work its magic in real time and uses a magnifying camera to show patients where it has helped encourage new growth—which she calls a “quantitative result,” since they’re able to count new follicle growth. Xvie is currently in trials as an injectable, but right now, doctors can apply it topically on the scalp after microneedling to bolster hair growth.

One topical drug, PP405, currently in clinical trials has doctors excited for its ability to wake up dormant stem cells in hair follicles. A Phase 2 trial done with UCLA found that patients who applied the molecule to their scalps for four weeks didn’t just get peach fuzz—they experienced “terminal hair” growth, meaning full shafts that have the potential to be long and thick. “Importantly, it regrew hair even on bald scalps,” says Marc R. Avram, MD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Weill Cornell Medical College specializing in hair loss. “That’s against dogma.” While the molecule still needs to go through Phase 3 trials, Avram is hopeful that it could be available for patients within two years. Once it’s approved, it will likely be a great option for reversing female- or male-pattern baldness (otherwise known as androgenetic alopecia).

PP405 isn’t the only molecule with potential. Flourish Biologics is developing a patented technology based on the discovery that the parathyroid hormone—which binds to receptors in the body to control calcium levels in the blood—also contributes to hair growth. Its injectable targets androgenetic alopecia. Right now, it’s only being tested on animals, but David Leffell, MD, an emeritus dermatological surgeon at Yale and the chief executive officer of Flourish Biologics, thinks that a shot for humans is on the horizon. “While early animal tests have been strong, there are a number of steps before the human trials, which will probably occur in 12 to 18 months,” he says.

Doctors are also excited by a new form of minoxidil. “It works even better,” confirms Avram, based on data from ongoing clinical trials, though he notes that peer review and approval are still pending. Everyone has heard of Rogaine, a topical form of the drug. (Cue Aidan snatching his from Carrie’s hands in Sex and the City and snarling, “It’s preventative!”) The current version of oral minoxidil spikes quickly in the bloodstream, which may cause dizziness and heart palpitations—and while it does work, it isn’t the ideal concentration for sustained hair growth, according to a paper published in Dermatology Times. The new extended-release form has been shown to stay at the ideal dosage for hair growth over the course of 12 hours, with less risk of cardiac side effects. Biopharmaceutical company Veradermics finished a Phase 2 trial with encouraging results, and a long-acting oral minoxidil pill might be available as early as 2027. But for anyone worried about hair loss, it’s worth talking to a doctor now. “We’re in an era where if you seek treatment early, you can keep a good head of hair on your head,” Avram says.

A version of this story appears in the November 2026 issue of ELLE.

#6726. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6722. Mocha Brown Hair-Color Season Is Here—and It’s Universally Flattering

There’s something about this time of year that makes everybody want to go darker. From their nail polish to their wardrobe, it’s a turn toward rich, darker shades. So it’s only natural that hair color would follow suit, going deeper and darker too. This winter in particular, it’s all about mocha brown.

Also called mocha chocolate, the rich, glossy shade was first popularized by celebrity colorist Jenna Perry, whose multidimensional brunette wizardry has fans like Bella Hadid and Kaia Gerber. Since then, the smooth and chocolaty hue—which combines darker espresso tones with lighter, milkier brunette shades—has become popular with a much wider section of the A-list, with Hailey Bieber and Daisy Edgar-Jones among the latest devotees.

“It reminds me of a chocolate mousse or a rich chocolate cake,” Perry tells Vogue. “That’s where the name came from. I thought mocha chocolate resembled the decadence of this shade of brown.” In line with sweater weather, Perry has churned out individualized takes on what she calls the “universally flattering brunette hair color” for a slew of stars, including longtime client Emily Ratajkowski and Amelia Gray. “A deep, rich brunette is chic,” Perry says. “The color reflects warmly in the sun, so it doesn’t ever look drab.”

According to Stephen Buller and Anita Rice, founders of Buller and Rice salon, these cacao tones feel luxurious for winter, particularly when the color isn’t completely flat. The key? Having a varied tone. “This is important throughout the lengths and ends so it reflects light and feels expensive rather than looking like one solid block of dark color,” they say. “This also gives clients who have had years of balayage an opportunity to go darker without feeling as though they’re simply covering everything up.”

Celebrity hairstylist Lorraine Dublin says that these indulgent, chocolaty shades look especially beautiful on textured and curly hair: “Think deep espresso brown with subtle ribbons of mocha, creating a rich, multidimensional finish,” she previously told Vogue. “It works beautifully on textured hair because the tonal variations catch the light, highlighting the shape and movement of curls, coils, and kinks.” She recommends asking your colorist for a “rich espresso base” with “delicate mocha or cinnamon brown accents,” which will impart a soft, seamless color melt.

Another important part of mastering the mocha chocolate look is keeping hair strong and shiny. “What makes this hair color so incredible from the start is having healthy hair,” explains Perry, who adds that preserving pigments with a color-safe shampoo and conditioner is key. Try Matrix Total Results Brass Off Shampoo to nix brassy or red tones. You can also use an at-home gloss or color conditioner, like Glaze Supergloss Color Conditioning Hair Gloss Chocolate Gleam or John Frieda Brilliant Brunette Color Vibrancy Conditioner, to prolong your hair’s vibrancy.

If a rich shade of mocha chocolate sounds like a delectable prospect, discover even more mocha brown hair-color inspiration to take to your salon below.

#6720. Our 11 Favorite Watches Coming to the Biggest Auctions of the Year

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

This is the biggest weekend of the year for vintage watches. It’s the year-end watch auctions in Geneva, where many prestigious houses bring their very best pieces to market. And it’s never been a more enthralling time to keep a close eye on what happens in Geneva over the next few days. In the first half of the year, the number of million-dollar watches nearly eclipsed the total for the entirety of 2025. A couple of the pieces listed below, including a unique Rolex and a rare Patek Philippe in stainless steel, have estimates above a million bucks.

Writer Oren Hartov and I pored over hundreds of lots to bring you our 11 favorite watches plus one bonus selection. See them all below.

You know a banger is coming up for sale when the house behind it doesn’t even bother capping its price range. Auction estimates are routinely and famously low to encourage bidders, and this watch’s starting point is still $1.2 million. Why? Well, have you ever seen a Rolex like this before? Before Rolex defined the look of modern watches with pieces like the Submariner, it operated similarly to many other manufacturers in Switzerland, willing to make one-off pieces and experiment frequently with its design.

This square beauty from the early 1940s is “most probably unique,” as Phillips auction house writes in its essay on the piece. This exact piece last hit the auction block in 2004, and no other example has come up for public sale since. It’s crazy to see how much this watch’s case shape resembles Heuer’s similarly blocky Monaco, which wouldn’t be released for another 25-plus years. Unfortunately, as cool as this watch is, it does not come with onyx prayer beads. —Cam Wolf

There’s Patek, then there’s complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples in insane condition. This watch checks all those boxes. A reference 1436, it’s a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph, meaning it can time successive intervals of a race or event. One of just two stainless steel examples known to the market, it has an estimate of $2.4-$4.8M, a testament to its rarity and importance. —Oren Hartov

Yet another rare watch executed in stainless steel, this fabulous Lange 1 boasts a gorgeous two-tone dial in blue, with darker subdials contrasting against a cobalt-colored main dial. Dating to 1999 and first sold by the German retailer Oeding-Erdel, it’s one of approximately 30 pieces made in the most utilitarian of metals. Originally fitted with a more standard silvered dial, it received its current navy-blue dial as a replacement and is one of just two stainless steel Lange 1s known in this particular configuration. —OH

Renewed interest in Urban Jürgensen stemming from its recent relaunch under the directorship of Kari Voutilainen, who has since left the CEO position but remains on the company’s board, has seen watches such as this early-’90s ref. 2 garner more attention. A lovely perpetual calendar-moonphase, it’s housed in a classically inspired 37.7mm yellow gold case with cornes-de-vache-style lugs, a stepped bezel, and an incredible dial with the brand’s signature observatory-style hands. Someone tell Timothée Chalamet. —OH

Chopard has a hard-earned reputation for putting out some of the most finely made watches in Switzerland. It’s not just the nerds who are familiar with its work anymore, either. If we (the nerds, obviously) were sending a watch in a bottle to help share that message far and wide, this Lunar One, which looks like something out of Superman’s icy Fortress of Solitude, wouldn’t be a bad choice. This is Chopard’s first watch to combine a perpetual calendar and a moonphase, which is like shaving truffles on caviar. I love that the Roman numerals at 4 and 8 o’clock look like columns nearly buckling under the weight of the center of the dial. This watch also comes with several fun add-ons, like onyx prayer beads plus a ring and a pen set with diamonds. —Cam Wolf

While many younger collectors are obsessed with the Cosmograph Daytona, true “Crown” heads know that other pre-Daytona chronographs sometimes present an even more compelling proposition. This ref. 3525 ‘’Bariletto,’ dating to the 1940s, is not only the first Oyster-cased Rolex chronograph, but it’s also the only known stainless-steel example carrying the signature on the dial of Proud’s, a Rolex retailer based in Sydney. Manually wound, paired to a handsome beads-of-rice bracelet, and measuring a compact 36mm, it comes from the collection of important Italian collector Pucci Papaleo. —OH

While this stainless steel Patek may look like a normal ref. 2509—a beautiful hand-wound dress watch from the midcentury—it’s actually a “school watch” modified by a watchmaking student at the Geneva Watchmaking School. Dating to the 1960s, it’s housed in a 35mm stainless steel case and features a lovely dial with the ‘Ecole d’Horlogerie Geneve’ signature instead of Patek Philippe’s. Open it up, and the hand-wound movement is signed by Norbert Henry, the watchmaking student who assembled and finished it. While it may not attract the attention of more typical Patek collectors, its under-the-radar qualities make it a potential sleeper hit. —OH

It’s tough to argue with the sheer beauty of Vacheron’s mid-20th-century output, much of which is vastly underappreciated compared to comparable pieces from the likes of Patek Philippe. This splendid yellow gold ref. 4072 with a two-tone multi-scale dial dates to the late 1940s—one of my favorite eras of watch design. Powered by the hand-wound cal. V 492 movement and featuring a lovely set of long, contoured lugs, its dial is in fantastic condition, with applied dart and Roman indices, sharp printing, a crisp signature, and legible tachymeter and telemeter scales. It will surely find its way onto the wrist of a collector with excellent taste. —OH

This watch’s dial depicts Saint George, who, according to legend, slew a dragon while on horseback. This is a perfect use for the rich, deep colors you get from enamel. The flames licking at Saint George are beautiful shades of orange and red. He triumphantly lifts his spear as his steed rears its front legs. It’s very cool how much story you can get from this little 35mm timepiece. —CW

Watch collectors might pony up a few thousand for one of independent watchmaker F.P. Journe’s used tissues at this point. However, they’ll have to settle for a host of accessories coming to auction instead this weekend. The maker is so in-demand that, in addition to his timepieces, houses are selling his empty watch boxes and a set of toys that resemble him. This lot is in the middle of those two extremes: a wall clock made to resemble Journe’s Octa Réserve de Marche. Although I’m not gonna lie, flipping this over and seeing the compartment where you stuff in the batteries is a bit of a buzzkill. —CW

They used to make everything look more elegant. This original Longines design was developed in 1931 with famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. It is technically a pilot’s watch, but its elegant, icy-blue dial and Roman numerals would make it the fanciest model on many red carpets in 2026. This is a model from the ‘80s inspired by that original design, and it comes on an absolutely righteous beads-of-rice bracelet. Someone is going to get this guy for around $2,500 if the estimate is correct! —CW

In Rolex world, even the advertisements sell for thousands of dollars. It’s hard to blame people when we’re talking about a rare poster of a GMT-Master wearing a snow-dusted Rolex beanie. Awwww. (Relatedly, imagine if Rolex sold that beanie!? Oh, boy.) —CW

#6719. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6717. Inside Designer Carla Fernández’s Vibrant Mexico City Home, Full of Indigenous Textiles and Art

When the Mexico City–based writer and curator Su Wu started working on her new design book, a theme began to emerge: She kept noticing the presence of pre-Hispanic architectural and design traditions in modern Mexican interiors.

It was from this realization that Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes was born. The book features 16 homes across Mexico—those of artists, architects, designers, and more—all shot by photographer Luis Garvan.

Wrought iron doors designed by Carla Fernández.

“When I began this project, I thought that we would be documenting a history, like the aura surrounding the artifacts in a museum, the apparitions of the past,” Wu writes in the book’s introduction. “Instead, what I’ve found is the vibrant, living presence of Indigenous ideas in Mexico.”

“In the guest bedroom, pink silk curtains dyed by Fernández cast a glow in the room. The bedspread is from her personal collection of Mesoamerican textiles, made of undyed wool in Teotitlán del Valle, Oaxaca.”—Su Wu

One space that exemplifies those ideas is Casa Flora, the colorful brutalist Mérida home and studio of the Mexican fashion designer Carla Fernández. As a designer, Fernández seeks to preserve the textile traditions of Indigenous and Mestizo communities through collaborations with artisans, bringing ancient practices to a contemporary audience. Fittingly, the home is full of Mesoamerican art and textiles.

Fernández led the renovation of the house, which dates back more than a century and now hosts workshops for Taller Flora, her design lab, which focuses on traditional Indigenous clothing techniques. (You can also stay in the home; the designer lists it for stays on Airbnb.)

Fernández’s husband, the artist Pedro Reyes, created several elements of the space, including a concrete outdoor shower, as well as some of the tiles throughout the space. His sculptures—including a prototype of Mitla Sillas, chairs inspired by the pyramids of the Mitla archaeological site in Oaxaca—are found throughout the home.

The outdoor shower designed by Pedro Reyes.

Reflecting on Fernández’s home, Wu tells Vogue: “I was very moved when writing the book with the idea of the ‘void’ in Mesoamerican architecture, and how so many architects, going back to the writings of Teodoro González de León, described the patio as a central, defining feature of the Mesoamerican home, a space that is at once enclosed and open to the elements. And in Carla’s home, I think there are many moments that exemplify this idea of the boundary between interior and exterior being not a physical one, but rather a marker of movement across psychological states.”

“A latticed window, known in Mexico as a celosia, is a central part of Mesoamerican architecture, used for cross-ventilation and to create a permeable sense of separation and shadow.”—Su Wu

Prototypes of Reyes’s Mitla Sillas chairs.

For Wu, Casa Flora is also a prime example of an idea that chef Elena Reygadas wrote about in her foreword to the book, “which is that handmade things are meant to be lived with no matter how precious, or especially if precious.”

“An equipale chair made of bent wood by the Wixárika people in Nayarit sits in front of a backstrap-loom tapestry of the Torre Latinoamericana, the iconic skyscraper in Mexico City designed by architect Augusto H. Álvarez. Made by artisans from San Juan Cancuc, Chiapas, the tapestry echoes a collection of dresses from Carla Fernández that featured historic buildings in Mexico City.”—Su Wu

All images © Luis GarvanCasa Flora, Mérida, Yucatán (pages 244-263). Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes by Su Wu. Published by Phaidon Press.

#6716. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

#6714. GQ’s 13 Breakout Stars of 2026

Sometimes it’s fun to be early to the party. GQ launched the Breakouts portfolio in 2014 to celebrate the Hollywood upstarts who were poised to do big things. And not to brag, but we nailed it; that first group included Miles Teller, Shailene Woodley, Eddie Redmayne, and the late, great Chadwick Boseman. Over the ensuing years, we featured plenty more soon-to-be-superstars: Rami Malek. Brie Larson. Daniel Kaluuya. Riz Ahmed. Barry Keoghan. The kids from Stranger Things, when they were still kids. The cast of Succession before Succession became everyone’s favorite show.

In 2017, we put a baby-faced Timothée Chalamet on the list for his turn in Call Me by Your Name. (Our global entertainment director, Dana Mathews, fondly recalls him turning to her during the Man of the Year Party and saying, “This is the best party I’ve ever been to in my life.”) Since then, Chalamet has appeared on three GQ covers, earned four Oscar nominations, and become a household name (and maybe been to a few more great parties).

We took a few years off (okay, fine, seven), but 2026 feels like exactly the right time to revive GQ’s Breakouts portfolio—now through a wider lens. Yes, though we’ve got eyes on Hollywood’s next big things—like, say, Sly Stallone doppelgänger Anthony Ippolito; Gen Z class clown Owen Thiele, of Adults; Misty Green’s astounding leading woman, Rosalind Eleazar—not everyone is working the camera. We’re excited to introduce you to the West Coast’s hottest up-and-coming rapper in AZ Chike and put you on to Fcukers, whose debut album, packed with rowdy electro-pop bangers, made them first in our hearts and on our pregaming playlists. We’ve also got podcaster and journalist Pablo Torre, whose relentless reporting upended a $7.8 billion NBA franchise, and Jordan Firstman, an internet-born comedian who wrote and directed a film that commanded a lengthy standing ovation from Cannes audiences (right after they finished crying).

Point is, our Breakouts class of 2026 brings together 13 fully minted stars who did something that feels increasingly impossible: They captured our attention in a time when it feels like attention is more fleeting than ever. Welcome to their party.

#6713. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)
