#6677. 22 Best Airbnbs in Upstate New York for a Weekend Away from the City 2026

If you live in New York, pretty much anything qualifies as an excuse for a weekend Upstate. A clanging radiator blasting dry heat into your apartment when it’s still warm outside? Time to flee to greener pastures. An overwhelming work week spent mostly in the company of your inbox? You deserve to unplug. The very first hint of a reddening leaf in the park? A seasonal sign from above—get yourself to an apple orchard.

With most small towns within a few hours’ drive of the city (and several available on a train line, for those without a car), you don’t really need a reason to spend a few days in Upstate New York. And while there are plenty of boutique hotels dotting the Hudson Valley and the Catskills, for true relaxation, why not book an Airbnb?

This time of year is all about the outdoors. Spend your days hiking along mountain trails and creeks, exploring local markets to sample all the fresh produce (and the baked goods they inspire), or hitting a brewery in the evening for a glass of cider under twinkling lights. As the weather cools, the charm offensive continues: fire pits come out, farms open for pumpkin and apple harvesting, and following the foliage becomes a perfectly acceptable way to spend a lazy fall day. Some of our favorite Upstate New York Airbnbs are located in or within walking distance of quaint towns like Hudson and Woodstock; though if you prefer a truly off-the-grid experience, we found plenty of cabins and cottages surrounded only by meadows.

Ahead, the 22 best Airbnbs in Upstate New York.

Enjoy a slower pace at this newly renovated 1890s-era farmhouse in the Western Catskills. The home is set on 25 acres of rolling meadows and forest, which lead to two streams and a waterfall. While the home has been updated to feature all new appliances (including a Vitamix), details like reclaimed wood and a bread-baking wood-stove cement the snug vibes. The main area is one big room: an eight-person dining room table connects to the kitchen, where you can spend afternoons making the most of local ingredients you picked up from a nearby farmstand. And when you head upstairs, don’t miss the claw-foot tub—it’s reason enough to book this gorgeous stay.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 5

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, window AC unit, heating, indoor fireplace, backyard, outdoor dining area.

This spot is billed as a “boutique nature retreat”—but let’s call it what it really is: an adult treehouse. It sleeps two, with a king-sized bed and hot outdoor showers. With no cell service or electricity, this is your chance to go fully off the grid; since the whole house is surrounded by forest, you’ll feel completely cozy and secluded. When you want to re-join society, the town of Phoenicia (and, more importantly, the local favorite Phoenicia Diner) is just a 10-minute drive away.

Amenities: Outdoor shower, fire pit, free parking

Best For: Fulfilling childhood treehouse dreams.

“Upstate” in perhaps only the most abstract sense of the word (it borders New Jersey, just about one hour out of the city), this lakeside spot is filled with sunlight, a far cry from the heavy wooden cabins that permeate the area. Outside, there’s a private garden with a waterfall and lily pond—and, of course, those unbeatable views of Greenwood Lake. There are plenty of wineries and antique stores nearby, as well as hikes for the adventurous weekender (the home is a five-minute walk from a path that connects to the Appalachian Trail) and a massive claw-foot tub to soak in when it’s time to unwind.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: HDTV, bathtub, record player, crib, board games, wood-burning fireplace, patio, outdoor furniture

Best For: Those who crave nature, but are afraid of the whole cabin-in-the-woods idea.

Renovated for modernity but restored with heaps of vintage touches befitting the older home’s roots, this light-filled apartment right in the heart of Hudson is great if you prefer to stay in a town rather than remote wilderness. From the zellige tiles to the antique stove, the kitchen is a particular star—anyone looking for style inspiration for an upcoming remodel will find several nooks to bookmark here. The Nespresso and tea station helps you start each morning off on a caffeinated foot, while in the afternoons, you’ll want to hang out on the porch or in the bubblegum pink claw-foot tub with a book.

Amenities: TV, sound system, crib, patio.

This new listing is the epitome of stripped-back country living: There’s no television and few amenities, so if you’re looking for a spot to indulge your off-the-grid dreams, this is it. (Though, lest you change your mind, the hamlet of Livingston Manor, with its concept stores and coffee shops, is walking distance away.) The house is a freshly renovated farmhouse, done in the Scandinavian style—from the antique furnishings to the original wood floors, every corner is steeped in character. There’s a bunk room for the youngest members of your travel party, plus a spacious kitchen for whipping up hearty breakfasts at home before heading out for the day.

Amenities: Air conditioning, pet-friendly.

Best For: Anyone looking to truly disconnect for a weekend.

Picture the prototypical lake cottage. Wood, everywhere, is a given; as is an A-frame silhouette, a fire pit and deck for grilling, and perhaps a wood-burning fireplace or two. Welcome to the Airbnb embodiment of that vision, complete with all of the above plus a few modern amenities (the Nespresso machine is a welcome addition). Sleepy Hollow Lake is a quick 10-minute walk down a trail away, for summertime guests. In the colder months, Hunter mountain and its ski slopes are a 45-minute drive away; and in between, you’ll have a third of an acre worth of land to explore on the property itself.

Amenities: Bathtub, record player, high chair, travel crib, board games, fireplace, beach/lake access, fire pit, pet friendly.

Distance from NYC: 2 hours by train, 2.5 hours by car.

No car, no problem: This charming one-bedroom is right in the town of Cold Spring, easily reachable from the city via the Metro North. You’ll be able to walk everywhere (Cold Spring Coffeehouse, a must-visit for your morning cappuccino and cardamom bun, is just 15 minutes on foot) and spend your weekend like a local. The home itself is clean and minimally decorated, with just enough original touches—including a gorgeous fireplace—to keep it from feeling too sparse. Remote workers will appreciate the spacious dining table, too, which doubles as a workspace you can spread out in in a picturesque alcove.

Distance from NYC: 1.5 hours by car, 1.5 hours by train.

Inspired by a Swiss Alpine home, this modern space is compact and minimalist, with oversized windows that really let the mountainside views seep in. Take it in up close and personal on the (covered) patio, which, in warmer months, is a great spot for a breakfast or dinner. Indoors, a colorful kitchen, shower skylight, and pellet stove all make for memorable decorative touches. It’s the right size for a solo traveler or a couple looking for a short-term stay; you’ll have all the necessities you need, but you’re encouraged to make the most of your surroundings.

Amenities: Outdoor shower, pellet stove, patio, fire pit, EV charger, pet-friendly.

Distance from NYC: Around 3 hours by train.

Best For: The no-frills traveler who still appreciates a little aesthetic effort.

Built in the ’80s by a master stonemason, this is one of the more unique options available to Catskills travelers. The home is actually a tower, with vaulted ceilings and wraparound windows offering sweeping views of the valley below. (The bathtub on the second floor is an especially great spot to take them in.) Just a quick seven-minute drive to the town of Woodstock, you’ll be left alone but not fully remote. And if it’s still warm enough, be sure to factor in enough free time for some evenings spent outdoors—the views are incredible, and between the hot tub and the deck, there are plenty of spots to take them in.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Washer/dryer, bathtub, piano, record player, board games, air conditioning, fireplace, fire pit, hot tub.

Best For: Someone who read one too many fairytale books growing up.

This charming A-frame in Tannersville is full of lush plants, good energy, and nostalgic charm. The home dates back to 1971 and is right in the heart of the Catskills, just two hours north of New York City. While the interiors are supremely serene, the outdoor deck with its BBQ and twinkly lights is where you’ll probably spend most of your time—especially if you’re visiting in fall or spring, when the weather is its mildest. Prefer to stay in? The home comes stocked with a record player and board games, for cozy nights with the whole group that are probably why you booked an Airbnb Upstate in the first place.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, heating, backyard, BBQ.

Best For: Plant parents who need a getaway.

If the idea of staying in a cabin in the woods with a cedar wood-fired hot tub sounds up your alley, book a stay at this bright home just 10 minutes from Woodstock. It’s not quite your old-school cottage: Aside from the light palette and modern decor, the bedrooms feature Casper mattresses, and the Breville espresso machine will make morning coffees on the deck all the more enjoyable. Outside, a fire pit and cedar wood hot tub and sauna make the case for ditching the dinner reservation in favor of staying in; plus, the house comes with a movie projector, for DIY movie nights.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, AC, central heating, backyard, fire pit, hammock, BBQ, hot tub.

Best For: A soak in the hot tub, beneath the trees.

From the wood-paneled A-frame ceilings to the forest green paint theme to the coffee-colored zellige tiling in the bathroom, there are plenty of decor ideas to steal from this Airbnb. Design aside, it’s well-located (hop in the car for a quick drive to the Ashokan Reservoir and little towns like Kingston and Woodstock) and surprisingly spacious. Come summer, we predict you’ll want to spend all your time on the sprawling front deck overlooking the trees—ditto the fall, as long as you pack the appropriate amount of wool sweaters to stay warm.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, sound system, indoor fireplace, fire pit, outdoor furniture, patio, pet-friendly.

We can already feel our blood pressure lowering simply admiring this tranquil Airbnb located on the outskirts of Kingston. The property offers numerous nooks for experiencing the natural surroundings—a fire pit encircled by Adirondack chairs, a tranquil pond best savored from the home’s swinging hammock, and even a screened porch just off the kitchen for early morning coffee. Inside is equally as dreamy, with plenty of natural light and cozy touches like exposed brick and a small fireplace. One perk: You can bring your pups for a small fee, so no member of the family is left behind for the next weekend Upstate.

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms; sleeps 4

Amenities: Washer/dryer, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard, fire pit, hammock, BBQ.

Hide yourself away in this atmospheric cabin perched atop Bramley Mountain near Bovina Center, a great spot for cozy restaurants and country stores. The home has a spacious atmosphere thanks to the cathedral ceilings and open floor plan, but you never lose that innately cozy feel: a wood-burning stove, wood paneling, and an atmospheric porch are all there to remind you that you’re very much in the woods. Not that there’s a bad time to book a stay here, but if you have your pick, aim for the fall. The house is surrounded by trees that turn surreal shades of scarlet and persimmon come October.

Amenities: Bathtub, outdoor shower, washer/dryer, indoor fireplace, backyard.

Best For: Turning your phone on airplane mode.

There are two types of upstate getaways: the first, characterized by spending the entire weekend in one place, relaxing and recharging. The second is spent diving headfirst into the region’s many charms, exploring shops, restaurants, and markets in several small towns. This Airbnb is ideal for the latter sort of traveler, who wants friction-less access to destinations such as Woodstock, Saugerties, and Kingston.

It also happens to be impeccably designed, with highlights like an indoor fireplace, mid-century modern decor, and a backyard BBQ and fire pit you’ll have a hard time parting ways with—it even comes stocked with firewood.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, indoor fireplace, fire pit, hammock, BBQ.

Best For: Exploring several nearby towns (and an impromptu game of chess to end the night).

Leaning into Wabi-Sabi design, this ranch-style home in the Warwick Valley is close to several lakes and hiking trails (as well as trendy breweries and restaurants). Natural materials and soft lighting set a relaxed tone for the space, and a trip to The Shed (the home’s meditation room) for a yoga session will begin each day on the right foot, as will the complimentary freshly-roasted bag of ground coffee from the owner’s favorite purveyor, Voyager Espresso. When you’re living in the foreground of the dense green forest, visible from most windows in the home, it’s impossible to not feel zen.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, yoga studio, central AC and heating, lake access, fire pit, backyard, BBQ, EV charger.

Best For: Coming back from your vacation actually recharged.

This secluded sanctuary in the Catskills forest sits on a hill overlooking an abundance of beauty, from woodlands and stream-fed ponds to a sprawling wildflower meadow. The cabin is petite (just 400 square feet) but a Wabi Sabi-inspired design lends a calming effect. A few standout details—and there are several—include the open floor plan with a winding spiral staircase in the center, natural earthy textures throughout, and a peaceful outdoor area complete with a fire pit, picnic tables, and twinkly lights. Even the bedroom is impeccably designed, with its antique chair nightstand and matching bedding; twin beds have never looked chicer.

Amenities: Toiletries, washer/dryer, record player, books and board games, window AC unit, indoor pellet stove, kitchen, fire pit, charcoal BBQ.

Best For: Reading your book beneath a canopy of trees.

Think of the typical log house, then flip that idea on its head. That’s what you get with Fox Ridge Chalet, which is anything but ordinary: A lot of it is white-washed, making it feel even bigger and brighter than it is, and the assortment of furniture is so eclectic, it has the air of a cool vintage shop. Situated on seven private acres of land, the picturesque property beckons to be explored. For the days when you decide you want to stay in, the movie screening projector, pool table, hot tub, exercise bike, and game collection should more than suffice.

Amenities: Hot tub, pool table, exercise equipment, fire pit, outdoor furniture, grill

Best For: Multigenerational summer getaways with the family.

Part of the National Register of Historic Places, this residence dubbed “The Gatehouse” was last restored in 2016—updated with more modern decor and comfy furnishings. Immerse yourself in scenic views of the Catskills Mountains and Hudson River from this historic French home while relaxing in the backyard, where a separate carriage house offers covered outdoor dining for the colder months. (Or the front yard—that storybook-perfect porch demands a few mornings or afternoons spend lounging on it.) Stay occupied with limitless activities such as hiking, biking, boating, and antique shopping, all of which can be found in the historic town of Hyde Park.

Amenities: Private balcony/patio, indoor fireplace, outdoor dining area, fire pit, BBQ grill

Best For: Staying in a home on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Pond House is a property with some serious art history cachet: It’s the former studio of social realist painter Reginald Marsh. An architect lovingly restored it into a single-family home that exudes country elegance: there are exposed beam ceilings, chandeliers, and floor-to-ceiling windows that look out onto the estate’s pond. Its most unique selling point is the main bedroom: With floor-to-ceiling glass windows slotted into wood paneling, you get a front row seat to the great outdoors from the comfort of your bed. It’ll be like sleeping in the world’s most relaxing fishbowl. (The adjacent bathroom, with its spa-like tub and equally oversized windows, is a nice companion.)

Rooms: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathrooms; sleeps 5

Amenities: private balcony, bathtub, indoor fireplace, fully equipped kitchen

#6676. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

#6674. How to Avoid Sports Injuries in Your 30s, 40s, and Beyond

At 38 years old, I’ve been fortunate enough to go most of my life without being bothered by sports injuries, despite being consistently and competitively active for the better part of three decades. On the soccer field, I’ve played on and off at club level since primary school. (I’m currently holding it down as a winger on my local club’s 30+ “seniors” team.)

Meanwhile, as a health journalist and all-around enthusiastic exerciser, I’ve thrown myself at countless physical challenges—mostly for fun, sometimes to help pay the rent. Marathons, trail races, triathlons, 24-hour relays, mud runs, obstacle course races, Hyrox—you name it, I was probably obsessed with it for a time. And through it all, the only injury I ever incurred was a torn meniscus (the undignified result of attempting a wildly above-my-paygrade basketball dunk on a charitably lowered rim, at a promotional event). If only the surgeon could have extracted the memory of that day along with the frayed connective tissue he removed from my knee. I’m pretty sure I was wearing jeans, too.

All of this to say, everything was smooth sailing for a very long time, until it suddenly wasn’t. Somewhere around the age of 35, for reasons beyond my comprehension at the time, the wheels started to come off the bus. First, a stress fracture to my foot. I noticed it one night in bed and couldn’t tell you when it happened. Regardless, it put me in a boot for three months.

Next, a torn hamstring during a routine game of pick-up football, making the same run I’d made so many times before. I thought I’d just pulled it, so I kept playing, which of course only made it worse. That decision cost me six months. Then a strained calf muscle at a gentle session of run club. And, finally, shin splints. I don’t even remember how many months that one took me out for, but it felt like forever.

This barrage of sports injuries—all sustained within a roughly two-year period—was unrelenting, each overlapping pang seemingly passing the baton to the next. Needless to say, I was miserable. And the worst part was that I couldn’t understand why this was happening to me. I had been maintaining the same activity level, same diet, same supplements, and the same sleeping habits.

You always hear people talking half-jokingly about how getting older takes its toll on the body. But nothing really prepares you for that moment when you start to actually experience it for yourself. It’s existential. Brutal. Depressing, honestly. Sometimes the best way to deal with these spiral-inducing moments is to simply talk to other people dealing with the same thing. So I recently asked my, er, seasoned soccer team’s group chat: What do you do to avoid and manage sports injuries as you get older?

Kevin, 40, chimes in first: “There’s no avoiding, mate. Just managing.”

“Funnily enough, I’ve actually started doing yoga, which has been great for mobility and stretching out my lower back,” writes Chris, 35, who battles with a recurring quadratus lumborum (QL) issue. “I was always a bit hesitant to give it a go—not because I didn't think it would help, but because I couldn't get past the fact that I'd essentially be following a similar exercise plan to my mum! I think that’s been one of the bigger adjustments as I’ve gotten older: accepting that looking after your body sometimes means doing things you might have previously associated with an entirely different generation.”

“For me, I think the most important thing is to keep going in general,” adds Brian, who recently turned 42. “I remember when I was around 20 years old, my manager at the time, who was in his late 30s and retired from playing, was doing some running on his own before the team training session started. The lads were joking and teasing him about making a comeback, but I remember him saying, ‘If you stop moving at my age, you won't be able to start again.’ I think that’s good advice.”

In some way, I suppose it’s comforting to know that this is something we all have to deal with, whether you’re a Sunday league bench warmer or in contention for the Ballon d’Or. "With age, there’s just a higher incidence of soft-tissue injuries as your muscles lose strength and elasticity,” says Dr. Brian Forsythe, a sports medicine surgeon, associate professor at Rush University Medical Center, and recreational soccer player himself. According to Forsythe, who also serves as head orthopedic officer for MLS team Chicago Fire FC and president of the Professional Soccer Physicians Society, over time athletes across the skill spectrum will ultimately begin running into the same injuries.

You may not be able to halt the inevitable march of time, but there are certainly ways to minimize and slow its toll on your body. This requires some work but could ultimately be the difference between hanging up your boots and kicking on for another 10, 20, or even 30 years.

“It's up to you to take some responsibility,” Forsythe says. “Think about the lifestyle you had when you were 17 or 18—how you took care of your body and what you looked like. Then look in the mirror and ask yourself, ‘How much of my life now resembles what it was then?’ If you’re going out and having a few pints, understand that that inhibits your recovery and decreases protein synthesis. If you’re overweight, that has effects beyond just not looking great in your clothes. It’s increased joint load, increased rotational torque. You’re more likely to get injured. So you have to set realistic expectations of what your body is capable of doing. But you can definitely still do a lot.”

If you’re not ready to call time just yet, here are a couple of strategies you can start implementing today, courtesy of Forsythe and a handful of other experts.

“Number one, and it should be obvious, is just general conditioning,” says Forsythe. Being a slightly less sedentary human being during the work week means you won’t send your body into total shock when you decide to get going over the weekend.

“A lot of injuries come from that mismatch between what we do all week and the intensity we demand from our bodies on the weekend,” says sports medicine physician Dr. Alex McDonald. As Dr. James B. Chen, orthopedic surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center, puts it: “The biggest risk isn't necessarily your age, but your schedule.”

“When you think about playing in your teens and twenties, you were probably close to your ideal body weight,” says Forsythe. Ideal body weight, or IBW, refers to the weight at which your body is able to function most efficiently and without a heightened risk of injury. “All of the forces across your joints are multiplied almost exponentially with additional pounds on your frame,” says Forsythe. For example, “the force across your knee can be up to six times your body weight.”

“If you've ever been overweight and you climb up and down stairs and notice that the front of your knee hurts, that's because of those increased pressures and forces,” adds Forsythe.

Jogging a couple of miles a week may help you get through your Sunday workout our pick-up game, but it’s not doing anything to prevent in-the-moment injuries. To do that, you have to train the way you play—whatever game that is. “It's changes of direction," says Forsythe. It's rapid acceleration and deceleration. It's pivoting, twisting, turning.” Basically, bring back whatever drills you used to do on your sports team when you were younger, and adjust them for the demands of the sport you currently play.

No matter how frequently and comprehensively you train, a complete warm-up before any big athletic event is a non-negotiable. "It helps dramatically, which is why you'll always see professionals warm up for 30-45 minutes before a match,” says Forsythe. When it comes to soccer, FIFA actually has developed a warm-up program, called FIFA ll+, specifically for injury prevention. “It’s a free routine that only takes about 20 minutes, and includes running drills plus strength, balance, and landing exercises such as Nordic hamstring curls and single-leg balance work,” says McDonald. “It’s been shown to cut injuries by about a third, but it needs to be done at least twice a week—ideally three or four times a week—to really reduce the risk of injury.”

Stretching after your warm-up is important, too, but just be careful not to overdo it. “If you stretch too aggressively, you can actually predispose yourself to muscle tendon injuries,” says Forsythe. “First warm up, and then stretch out within your range of comfort. But right before a game is not the time to all of a sudden correct tight hamstrings.”

Often, being sidelined by an injury can be more painful than the injury itself, causing guys to get back out there earlier than they probably should. “A common issue that I see is when someone sustains a minor sprain or strain, and they return to sport-specific activity too early,” says Chen, “which can result in either worsening the injury or even picking up a secondary injury.” As annoying as it might be to sit out for 2 or 3 weeks with a strained hamstring, turning that into a tear will bench you for far longer. Believe me.

Playing sports in your 30s, 40s, and beyond also means coming to grips with your body’s increasing need for routine recovery between training sessions and games. "You have to recognize that your body needs more time to recover,” says Forsythe. You may have great cardiovascular fitness and feel ready to play on consecutive days, but your muscles and connective tissues need time to bounce back. “It’s important to respect fatigue, and ensure proper recovery after games or training,” says McDonald.

To be fair, this is universally sound guidance regardless of age. But it's advice that tends to take decades to sink in. “I think that one of the key advantages of playing as you get older is that you know your body better in your 30s and 40s,” Brian’s response concluded. “You understand what it's saying to you now. You might not have even listened when you were 21!”

A version of this story appeared in British GQ.

#6673. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6672. Lara Saget’s Sculptures Mine the Ancient, Alchemical, and Divine

On the way to Lara Saget’s Brooklyn studio, I see a headstone shop, where grave markers are displayed in the window. On the next block, there’s a warehouse, its open garage doors revealing floor-to-ceiling stacks of granite and marble slabs. And inside, her studio is a bit of a quarry itself.

“This is my rock room,” the 37-year-old sculptor says, gesturing to a corner of her studio that looks like a construction site. “This is where I collect all my different little things.” She points to a pile of gray stone, explaining that it is rare Tuckahoe marble, which was used to build the Washington Square arch. When Saget saw that a hotel was set to be built on a former Tuckahoe marble quarry in Westchester County, she called the owner and asked if she could come collect some.

This practice of seeing the sublime in nature is at the heart of Saget’s practice: She sees the divine in granite, the sacred in destruction that makes way for creation. These are themes she mines in her first New York City solo exhibition, “and the world came apart,” curated by Sarah Darro, which opened at Trotter&Sholer on November 7. Saget is exhibiting the work after recently receiving her master’s in divinity from the Center for Religion and Advanced Spiritual Studies and becoming an ordained minister. This spirituality deeply informs the work, which is about regeneration, the ancient, and the alchemical.

Lara Saget, The Children and the Tree That Turned to Metal, 2026. Copper alloy and petrified wood. 11 x 6 x 3 in.

The show, which variously brings to mind the celestial sculptures of Lee Bontecou and the arresting imagery of Louise Bourgeois, has two components: wall works made from copper alloy, granite, and black marble that borrow the aesthetics of early cave drawings to depict volcanic maps and tectonic plates; and glass sculptures centered on the ancient Judean date palm, a once-extinct tree scientists were able to regenerate from nearly 2,000-year-old seeds, and the Joshua Tree, which is threatened by climate change.

Saget has a broader interest in legacy and inheritance. As the daughter of the late actor Bob Saget, she inherited not just a famous last name, but also the example from an early age of what it looks like to be an artist. Now, almost five years after his death, a documentary about him is in the works. “He was a true artist,” she says. “He was like jazz, just like this constant creation. Being surrounded by that has made it seem very normal to be constantly creating.”

In 2019, she traveled to India for the first time, spending a month in a small village at Art Ichol, a residency for artists working in bronze and stone. Saget has gone back almost every year since to make her work, which involves a 6,000-year-old process called “lost-wax casting.” She works with a team to carve into stone and use wax to make a print of its surface. She then builds a mold around the wax and stone, and constructs a kind of sweat lodge out of bricks and mud to steam out the wax, leaving a cavity for molten metal to be poured in. Every step of the process is manual.

Saget has had a lifelong interest in spirituality, but it wasn’t until the last decade, when she found the Path of Soul Transcendence, that she began to pursue it more seriously. “Honestly, my whole life, I was looking for something,” she says. “The experience of the path is really surrendering to the spirit that I am, that everybody is, and the reality that everything is one.”

It’s an idea essential to her practice, which is rooted in how materials interact with each other. “I just had the sense that when heat breaks everything down, it's all ultimately one,” Saget says. “The center of the earth, or how volcanoes are also obsidian rock, and how all these materials are basically everything. It seems like it’s totally separate, but when it's heated, it reveals it's not.”

Saget’s wall works take a bird’s-eye view, using a tiled-grid modularity that evokes sites of excavation and discovery. The Last One Million Years (2026), for example, is a map of volcanoes and tectonic plates she charted using a celestial map from NASA. The raised rock parts of the maps are from heat-trapping granite in the metal, a spontaneous interaction. The effect is a kind of spiritual archaeology, wherein Saget uses the earth’s most ancient, essential materials to tap into its profundities.

Lara Saget, Joshua, 2026. Kiln-cast glass and phosphorescent powder, 15.5 × 6 × 6 in.

If the wall works are the story of the last million years, Saget’s tree sculptures are the story of the present and future. She started making glass tree sculptures in 2016, focusing on trees that have survived against all odds. She began sculpting Joshua trees during the pandemic, when she drove across the country to Yucca Valley Material Lab in Joshua Tree for a residency. While she was there, it snowed—a rare occurrence—which made her think about how the Joshua tree survived the Ice Age. Similarly, the sculpture Rebirth of an Ancient Palm is a recreation of the ancient Judean date palm, which was brought back to life from extinction. Both sculptures feature textural, kiln-cast glass using the lost-wax process. For the exhibition, she had two children narrate an audio piece, each acting as one of the trees and encouraging people to take care of them. “Nobody could imagine that these trees could survive all of this,” she says. “It’s really about the underlying life force that continues against all cognitive understanding.”

Indeed, she’s begun to think about grief in similar terms. “Working through what seemed to be finite, and allowing what seemed finite to almost reveal itself as infinite has helped a lot,” Saget says. “Because I realized that nothing is the end of anything. It’s always in the process of becoming.”

“and the world came apart,” runs through December 19 at Trotter&Sholer at 90 Elizabeth Street in New York City.

#6669. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6666. The Vogue Business AI Tracker

The Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

The news: Gentle Monster taps Joaquin Phoenix to front its Google AI Glasses.

Why it matters: Gentle Monster unveiled a campaign starring Joaquin Phoenix for its forthcoming AI-powered glasses, developed with Google and Samsung. Directed by filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, the short film will debut in mid-November, ahead of the collection’s December launch. (Pre-orders open on November 12.) The glasses, first previewed at Google I/O in May, run on Google’s Android XR platform and integrate its Gemini assistant, offering features including real-time translation, navigation and hands-free photography.

The launch marks a significant step in Google’s return to smart eyewear, adding competition to Meta’s established Ray-Ban partnership. Google has also teamed up with Warby Parker, while Kering is developing AI glasses with Google for Gucci. Gentle Monster’s decision to enlist Phoenix and Glazer is yet another sign that fashion credibility and cultural positioning are central to Big Tech rivals’ attempts to win the smart glasses race.

The news: Amazon launches SMS-based AI shopping agent after blocking Meta’s Muse.

Why it matters: Amazon has begun testing an expanded version of its AI shopping agent, Alexa for Shopping, among a small group of US customers over text. The new SMS feature lets shoppers search for and compare products, send photographs to find similar items, track prices and complete purchases without opening Amazon’s website or app.

The move reflects a broader shift toward making every consumer touchpoint shoppable, from social media and search engines to messaging. As AI agents become accessible through everyday interactions, the distinction between browsing, asking for advice and making a purchase could become increasingly blurred. For luxury brands, the challenge is not just where their products are sold, but how they appear in shopping conversations that take place beyond their own channels.

Amazon’s decision to block Meta Muse from accessing its marketplace in September also suggests that retailers want to extend their own reach without necessarily ceding control of discovery to competitors.

The news: Zalando unveils plans for AI shopping agent that can buy from other retailers.

Why it matters: Zalando has announced plans for a new AI shopping agent that will allow customers to purchase products from other retailers without leaving its app. Called Zalando Extended, the service is being piloted with homeware retailer Westwing, with AI-powered checkout scheduled to officially launch in 2027. The agent will eventually be able to complete purchases on shoppers’ behalf, expanding Zalando’s offering beyond the products it sells directly. The move builds on its existing conversational AI assistant, which has attracted more than 22 million unique users this year, according to Zalando’s Q3 earnings update.

The retailer’s plans follow a similar move by Amazon, whose Buy for Me feature allows customers to purchase products from external retailers through its shopping app. Both point to a potentially significant change in the marketplace model: rather than requiring brands and retailers to list their products on a platform, AI agents could facilitate purchases directly from their own websites.

For brands, this could open up new routes to customers without the usual marketplace integrations, while raising questions about who controls product discovery and the customer relationship. For Zalando, it offers a way to expand its assortment without holding additional stock, while keeping shoppers within its own ecosystem.

Why it matters: Prada has launched a ChatGPT plugin allowing users in the US, the UK and Italy to discover products, explore collections and find stores using information sourced directly from the brand. As AI assistants become a gateway to product discovery, the move gives Prada a more authoritative presence in conversations it might otherwise struggle to influence. “Conversational experiences represent a natural evolution of traditional e-commerce,” said Prada Group digital director Laura Campanella. “Through this pilot initiative, we are exploring a new territory for customer engagement.”

The news coincides with the launch of Prada’s Christmas campaign this week, featuring hand-drawn animation by Disney veteran John Pomeroy. These two contrasting moves reflect a broader distinction emerging in luxury: AI for product discovery, and human craftsmanship for consumer-facing brand storytelling.

The news: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals the huge costs and risks of the AI boom.

Why it matters: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO filing offers a rare look inside the economics — and extraordinary risks — of the AI industry. As the Claude AI maker prepares for a potential $2 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reports that its revenues exceeded $33 billion in the first nine months of 2026, while its computing costs have fallen dramatically relative to sales, all suggesting a path to profitability. Yet Anthropic has also committed more than $800 billion to computing infrastructure through 2045, much of it supplied by technology giants including Amazon and Google, who are also major investors.

Crucially, the prospectus devotes 92 pages to risks, warning that future AI models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or cause harm too large for insurers to cover. For businesses embedding AI into everything from creative production to customer service, the filing exposes a central contradiction: the technology is becoming commercially indispensable even as its developers acknowledge profound uncertainty over its long-term risks.

The news: Anthropic plans European AI consultancy.

Why it matters: Anthropic is reportedly partnering with private equity firm Hg to launch a European consultancy that’ll place AI engineers and advisers in external businesses to help them integrate Anthropic’s technology, according to the Financial Times. Expected to launch by the end of 2026, hubs are currently planned in London and Berlin, with the Claude developer likely using the venture to accelerate corporate AI adoption — and even capture some of the work traditionally handled by consultancies such as Accenture and the Big Four.

Fashion and luxury businesses, many of which are still grappling with how to deploy AI, could be fertile ground for these services. But the model raises an obvious tension: while companies may welcome direct access to AI expertise, how independent can the advice be when the consultancy is backed by a company with a commercial interest in driving adoption of its own technology?

The news: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta.

Why it matters: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, an AI agent rivaling Meta’s consumer-focused Muse and OpenAI’s more enterprise-oriented Dots; the Duet has both brand and consumer use cases for fashion. It can purchase products on consumers’ behalf using Shopify’s Shop Pay and Stripe Link, while merchants can instruct the agent to set up, design and manage their Shopify stores, including inventory and orders, Anthropic announced in a blog post. Meanwhile, a “richer visual editor” — which allows brands to design and preview their storefronts within the agent’s interface before anything goes live — is “coming soon”.

It was only a matter of time until Anthropic followed Meta and OpenAI in launching a personal AI assistant. Now, the battle is on between these tech companies to capture both consumer and brands’ trust, so that the integration these agents depend on across stores and payment providers is realized. The growing competition here signals a shift towards AI-mediated purchases, potentially reducing direct customer interactions for brands and making product visibility and seamless checkout across AI platforms increasingly important.

The news: Major banks and retailers block AI shopping agents like Meta Muse.

Why it matters: A growing list of US banks and retailers are blocking AI agents like Meta Muse and Instinct from acting on their websites. Amazon and Ebay have both prohibited these models from browsing or purchasing items on their respective marketplaces, while Citigroup, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have each moved to prevent outside agents from logging into customer accounts and transacting on their behalf.

“We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right way [and] we’re building tools to do that,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week. “In the meantime, we’re not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company, because that’s too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”

While much of the fashion industry runs its direct-to-consumer sites via platform providers like Shopify — which has opened its network to AI agents unless a brand explicitly opts out — the growing calls from prominent banking officials to introduce legislation point to a bigger unresolved question: when an AI agent makes a purchase that a consumer later disputes, who is responsible for putting it right? For now, experts say much of that burden may still land with the retailer.

The news: OpenAI UK employees received £2.3 million on average in pay and shares in 2025.

Why it matters: OpenAI employees in the UK received an average of £2.3 million in pay and shares last year, according to newly filed UK accounts. The ChatGPT developer distributed £255 million in salary and equity compensation among 110 staff — more than double the previous year’s average package. The figures reflect fierce competition for specialist AI talent, although remuneration varies significantly between employees, with leading researchers commanding the largest pay.

It’s another sign that the AI bubble is far from bursting, with these salaries incentivizing employees for longer and reflecting the budgets of the venture capitalists funding the company. (OpenAI’s most recent funding round reached $122 billion in March 2026, at an $852 billion post-money valuation.)

OpenAI’s UK revenue more than tripled to £293 million in 2025, as London becomes an increasingly key international AI research and commercial hub.

The news: Pinterest launches AI-powered beauty guides.

Why it matters: Pinterest has launched Beauty Guides, an AI-powered feature that analyzes hair and nail Pins to generate personalized salon instructions, at-home tutorials and product recommendations. Available first to US iOS users, Pinterest says the tool aims to close the gap between discovering a beauty look and recreating it.

While competitors like Google Lens already use AI-powered visual search to identify and shop products, Pinterest is extending the concept to practical beauty advice. The move reflects a broader shift from AI-powered discovery to AI-assisted decision-making, while helping Pinterest turn its vast repository of visual inspiration into greater shopping intent and potential commercial opportunities for beauty brands. It also builds on the platform’s recent push into visual search advertising, giving it more ways to connect inspiration with purchases.

The news: OpenAI releases virtual try-on in ChatGPT.

Why it matters: OpenAI is introducing AI-powered virtual try-on and product-saving features to ChatGPT, deepening its push into fashion e-commerce. Users can upload photos of themselves to visualize how clothing and accessories might look on, while a new Favorites feature lets them save products and try-on images for later.

Powered by ChatGPT Images 2.5 (OpenAI’s latest image generator, released in September) the tools will roll out globally across consumer plans, with purchases still completed on merchants’ websites. The launch puts ChatGPT in more direct competition with visual shopping platforms such as Google and Pinterest, as AI assistants evolve from product discovery tools into personalized shopping destinations.

For fashion brands, it raises the prospect of ChatGPT becoming an increasingly influential touchpoint in the customer journey. Luxury brands have been hesitant to adopt virtual try-on on their own channels, largely because the tech hasn’t met their visual standards — but the latest advances in AI are rapidly improving the realism of these digital models.

The news: TikTok launches AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout.

Why it matters: TikTok has launched an AI-powered shopping assistant that provides personalized product guidance, answering questions about sizing, availability and delivery directly within the app. Alongside this, a new one-click checkout feature allows users to purchase directly from brands on their FYP, without leaving TikTok.

Developed in partnership with commerce and payment providers including Shopify, Salesforce and Stripe, the features mark an expansion beyond TikTok Shop’s existing marketplace model, more deeply embedding AI-assisted shopping and direct brand purchases into the social platform. Its aim is to create a more seamless journey from inspiration through discovery, to purchase.

The launch comes against a wider shift towards AI-powered, end-to-end shopping experiences, alongside Meta’s Muse AI agent, Pinterest’s growing shopping investment, and ChatGPT’s new virtual try-on capabilities. For brands, the challenge becomes how to surface in these AI products, where checkout is handled outside their own channels.

The news: Trump orders the US government to stop calling AI “AI”.

Why it matters: President Donald Trump has signed an executive order instructing the US government to replace “artificial intelligence” and “AI” with “super intelligence” and “SI” across all official communications and policy documents, arguing that the new terminology better reflects the tech’s rapidly advancing capabilities and economic potential. The language notably echoes Mark Zuckerberg’s vision of “personal super intelligence”, which he made central to Meta’s AI strategy last year.

The rebrand comes amid a much bigger debate over who should be responsible for keeping increasingly powerful AI systems in check. Ahead of signing the executive order, Trump convened some of the industry’s most powerful figures — including Meta’s Zuckerberg, xAI’s Elon Musk, Google’s Sundar Pichai, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei — to sign a voluntary AI safety accord.

The accord puts the onus on companies to develop internal safeguards, subject their systems to independent audits and provide board-level oversight, in line with the Trump administration’s preferred “self-policing” versus a coordinated slowdown. Amodei has been among the most vocal advocates for slowing down, while OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI have backed calls for greater restraint.

The bosses at Anthropic, Google, xAI, Meta, OpenAI, and Nvidia all signed Trump’s voluntary accord.

The news: Oura delays IPO, citing market uncertainty.

Why it matters: Smart ring maker Oura has postponed its hotly anticipated IPO, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market” despite strong demand for its wearables offering. The company had been targeting a valuation of as much as $14 billion, and expected to raise as much as $2.2 billion in the public listing.

The timing points to a broader AI-driven shake-up in public markets. Investors are increasingly scrutinizing the vast cash being poured into AI infrastructure and lofty tech valuations, even as prospective mega-listings from AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI threaten to command an outsized share of investor attention and capital. Oura’s delay offers an early glimpse of the potential divide between the tech companies attracting extraordinary sums and those competing for what’s left.

Plus, as of last week, OpenAI announced that it won’t be joining the IPO rush this year. CEO Sam Altman has said going public now would be ill-advised given the safety work still ahead.

The news: Meta unveils kawaii-coded wearable pendant to house its Muse AI assistant.

Why it matters: Just when we thought Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had finished announcing his slew of smart glasses and AI updates during the annual connect conference, there was “just one more thing”: another wearable device designed to house its new Muse AI agent, the Muse Charm. It’s a tamagotchi-esque, palm-sized totem on a looped cord designed to attach to keychains or fit into the wearer’s pocket.

The Muse Charm has a small screen to display the user’s selected Muse AI avatar. It’s unlocked via fingerprint and can be spoken into for instructing their agent to carry out tasks. Zuckerberg is still “finalizing” the components, but promised that the device will be ready to ship before the holidays.

The Muse Charm is Meta’s latest attempt at a new form factor designed to get its AI agent into the hands of as many consumers as possible. “We packed the whole muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a key chain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said. “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and show [it] what’s going on around you.”

It feeds into Zuckerberg’s promise of “personal superintelligence”, and may offer itself as a successor to the smartphone.

The news: OpenAI pauses training of new AI models, following further AI agent hacks.

Why it matters: ChatGPT maker OpenAI has paused training of its new AI models, just hours after disclosing that its AI agents had gone “rogue”. Over the summer, there were reportedly dozens of incidents where OpenAI models unexpectedly breached their system guardrails and compromised organizations’ security controls, including the US government’s.

In July, OpenAI revealed its autonomous AI agents, developed during safety trials, escaped their testing sandbox, accessed the internet, and independently hacked the startup Hugging Face back in July — the first example of an major AI-driven attack that moved faster than the humans trying to contain it.

“We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes [1 million gigabytes] of agent activity logs [digital diaries of what the agents do], and working with impacted organizations,” CEO Sam Altman said in a post on X. “Hugging Face is still the most severe event we’ve seen.” He added that OpenAI will “be as transparent as can be”, while hinting that OpenAI’s agents had also discovered vulnerabilities in “other companies” like rivals, which he said would “be their call to disclose or not”.

OpenAI said it will resume training of its most capable AI models only when “confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place, which we are working on now,” a spokesperson told Vogue Business. “People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do. This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as capabilities continue to advance.”

The news: OpenAI and Anthropic staff question how to put AI slowdown pledges into practice.

Why it matters: Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are questioning how their leaders’ recent calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models will work in practice. According to the Financial Times, staff were blindsided by the proposals, which include bringing independent evaluators inside the AI labs to scrutinize models and safety practices, leaving them to grapple with questions around how much access outsiders will receive and IP protection.

The uncertainty highlights the gap between the growing consensus that safety measures need to keep pace with rapidly advancing AI models, as well as the practicalities of implementing those commitments. It also raises questions over whether last week’s unusual show of agreement between AI leaders will translate into meaningful change around model development and release.

The news: AI’s biggest rivals unite behind calls to slow development.

Why it matters: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling on the AI industry to slow the rate at which its most powerful models become more capable, warning that safety measures are struggling to keep pace. His proposals include embedding independent evaluators inside AI labs, greater coordination on safety standards, and international cooperation. Anthropic has committed to bringing independent evaluators inside the company, giving them employee-like access to scrutinize the safety of its models.

What’s more, some of Amodei’s biggest rivals are backing him. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the tech company would also introduce independent evaluators, while xAI’s Elon Musk endorsed Amodei’s call and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis said the proposal was “heading in the right direction”. The rare consensus comes after a series of AI safety incidents and high-profile researcher resignations intensified concerns over increasingly autonomous systems.

What’s yet unclear is whether the industry’s newfound agreement will translate into a meaningful slowdown, or how the biggest AI companies reconcile it with the fierce commercial race to build more powerful models.

The news: Estée Lauder Companies partners with AI startup to boost brands in search.

Why it matters: Estée Lauder Companies (ELC) is partnering with AI marketing platform Profound to track and improve how its portfolio of beauty brands appears across generative AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini. It comes as more fashion and beauty groups invest in recalibrating their marketing strategies to prioritize generative engine optimization (GEO); ELC said the strategic partnership marks a move to “operationalize GEO and AI marketing at scale”.

Profound’s software will show ELC when — and how — its brands surface or become recommended by AI assistants, and identify opportunities to improve their visibility and accuracy. The beauty conglomerate will then use Profound’s agentic tools to optimize product pages, blogs, social media, and other components so that information is easier for LLMs to comprehend and pick up.

“The way people discover beauty is being rewritten, and we intend to shape that shift rather than react to it,” said ELC global chief digital and marketing officer Aude Gandon, adding that the sector is undergoing an “industry-wide transition”, as consumers increasingly use AI for product discovery and recommendations.

The news: Daydream adds Siri and camera roll search via Apple’s new iOS 27.

Why it matters: AI shopping platform Daydream is integrating deeper into the iPhone with the launch of two features built on Apple’s new iOS 27 tools. Users can now find shoppable matches for clothing in photos saved to their camera rolls, or ask Siri to search Daydream’s catalog using conversational prompts without opening the app. Daydream is one of the early co-developers of tools built with Apple’s latest on-device AI foundation models, using its new image-context capabilities.

Daydream says the launch gives it access to shopping intent at the point of inspiration, rather than requiring consumers to begin their search on a retailer or marketplace. The company now has more than 1.5 million shoppers, as well as 3 million products spanning 10,000 brands and 325 retailers.

The news: US court rules Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic as unlawful.

Why it matters: Anthropic has won a significant legal battle against the US government, after a federal judge ruled that the Pentagon acted unlawfully when referring to the Claude maker as a national security supply chain risk. The dispute came after Anthropic refused to remove safeguards preventing its AI from being used for autonomous weapons and domestic mass surveillance, leading to federal agencies and military contractors boycotting any business with the company.

In her ruling, US District Judge Rita Lin found the government’s measures to be “illegal and baseless”, and amounted to unlawful retaliation. The Pentagon could appeal the decision.

The case reinforces growing tensions emerging around who decides what an AI system can and can’t be used for — a risk for businesses using enterprise AI. As fashion and beauty companies increasingly build workflows and consumer tools on models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, they are also inheriting the safeguards, use policies and geopolitical exposure of those providers.

The news: Amazon faces lawsuit over training AI models on video content from Twitch.

Why it matters: The class action lawsuit against Amazon has been brought on behalf of millions of Twitch streamers who allege the platform’s parent company, Amazon, used their content to train AI without permission or compensation. According to the BBC, reportedly 215 million hours of content was generated via the platform in the first few months of 2026 alone. While the use of these videos was only announced in August, allowing people to then opt-out of having their data used this way, it is unclear how long Amazon was harnessing this content.

The legal proceedings tie into concerns around the ownership of content that’s hosted on Big Tech-owned platforms, as well as its illicit commercial usage that leaves creators without compensation or rights. Twitch and Amazon are yet to comment on the proceedings.

The news: Alibaba raises £7.5 billion to invest in AI.

Why it matters: Chinese retail and tech giant Alibaba is issuing 710 million shares in Hong Kong at around £10.54 each, with expectations of raising roughly £7.5 billion. The plan for the proceeds is to develop its “full stack” AI capabilities, including new models, chips, and computing infrastructure.

The move comes days after Alibaba’s quarterly profits reportedly plunged 75% off of rising AI infrastructure spend, as the business aims to capitalize on the strong sentiment for tech companies in China’s stock market, offset its slowing e-commerce business, and power proprietary tech such as its Qwen AI models.

Alibaba has ramped up its AI investment since being blacklisted by the Pentagon in June, alongside other Chinese companies deemed as a national security risk to the US. The company is potentially looking to compete with Silicon Valley’s suite of AI makers, while shifting gears to tech to be able to maximize and support its fashion operations in-house.

Why it matters: On August 18, the trial commenced for a lawsuit filed in 2023, in which 29 US states claim Meta violated multiple federal and state laws protecting children. Beyond the potential billions of dollars Meta may have to pay out if found liable, the states are demanding the tech leader make changes to its Instagram and Facebook models, such as removing like counts and the “infinite scroll”.

If Meta loses, the way young people experience social media may be forced to change. Through features designed to keep consumers using the platforms as long and as often as possible, the states believes Meta “chose to exploit” young people to grow its user base and ultimately its business. The trial poses questions for brands who utilize these social platforms for monetization and brand-building purposes — in terms of both accountability, as well as having to recalibrate their partnerships with social media and their methods for reaching younger audiences.

The news: Phia faces fresh scrutiny over affiliate attribution.

Phia is rapidly becoming a case study in the governance risks surrounding AI-powered shopping agents and browser extensions. As luxury brands increasingly experiment with AI commerce assistants and affiliate-driven discovery, the controversy highlights the need for rigorous oversight of attribution, consent and partner incentives. It also raises broader questions about how AI shopping tools should earn commissions and the level of transparency brands should expect from technology partners across AI and affiliate marketing.

The news: Anthropic investors eye a record $2 trillion IPO.

Why it matters: Anthropic investors are modelling an IPO worth more than $2 trillion, which would make it the largest public listing in history if achieved. According to the Financial Times, expectations are being fueled by the Claude maker’s rapid enterprise revenue growth and confidence that demand for frontier AI models will continue to accelerate. Anthropic has not confirmed a target valuation and remains in its quiet period ahead of a potential October listing, meaning the figure reflects investor expectations rather than company guidance.

A $2 trillion listing would reinforce the dominance of a handful of AI infrastructure companies that increasingly underpin the tools luxury brands rely on. It also adds fresh momentum to the AI bubble, characterized by the sector’s frothy valuations, underscoring that investor appetite for the biggest commercial AI models remains strong, despite growing questions over sustainability and returns.

The news: Mark Zuckerberg releases AI manifesto, unveiling “open source” Meta AI model, Muse Glimmer.

Why it matters: Alongside the release of Muse Glimmer, a new lightweight version of Meta’s most powerful AI model, which is “open source” (freely available to outside developers), CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote a 6,500-word consumer-facing manifesto titled The Future Is for Everyone: The Path to a Positive AI Future.

As well as pitching the company’s plan to release free AI models to “billions of people”, Zuckerberg’s essay positions the tech as a tool for creativity, entrepreneurship and self-expression rather than replacement. By outlining an optimistic vision of consumer AI alongside its open model strategy, the company is attempting to differentiate itself from rival companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, who have warned that AI is dangerous and should be tightly controlled.

In a direct comment on rivals’ AI strategies, Zuckerberg wrote: “Meta is the company primarily focused on building personal superintelligence for everyone. Most other labs are focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions, so if those labs lead, then the balance of power will favor larger institutions over individuals.”

It’s a move that speaks to broader consumer fears of AI’s impact on livelihoods — both from an economic standpoint and in terms of creativity. Rather than framing AI around productivity or cost savings, Meta is increasingly positioning it as a creative collaborator.

The news: Daydream launches B2B arm for AI fashion search.

Why it matters: AI shopping startup Daydream is expanding beyond its consumer app with Powered by Daydream, a white-label platform allowing fashion brands to embed its conversational and visual AI search directly into their e-commerce sites. Launch partners include Staud, Alice + Olivia and Cult Mia, with more than 25 additional brands signed on, according to the startup.

It joins a growing cottage industry of startups promising to “AI-proof” brand websites, betting that retailers would rather rent AI capabilities than surrender customer relationships to a new generation of shopping apps. At the same time, as the market for consumer-facing AI shopping apps becomes increasingly crowded, with many still struggling to prove shoppers want a new place to begin their purchasing journeys, it’s a notable pivot.

The news: Salesforce invests in Brunello Cucinelli’s AI platform, Callimacus.

Why it matters: Solomei AI, the Brunello Cucinelli-owned tech company behind Callimacus, has entered into an investment agreement with CRM giant Salesforce. The AI-powered platform, which launched in January 2026 via the Brunello Cucinelli e-commerce site, aims to position itself as the next generation of pageless websites and applications — rather than guiding customers through a standardized site experience, Callimacus’s AI agents are designed to recognize each visitor’s intent and generate a personalized shopping navigation in real time.

The Salesforce funding will support the push for Callimacus to be adopted by businesses across Europe and North America, and, if the transaction goes through, pending authorization by the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, the CRM firm will join seed shareholders such as the Cucinelli family holding company, Foro delle Arti.

The Callimacus system aims to offer businesses a new way to engage customers in the agentic age, beyond static e-commerce sites. Its majority ownership by Italian luxury label Brunello is also significant, considering its founder’s long-term interest in AI, as well as its popularity among the Silicon Valley tech set — the growing relationship between tech and fashion is now well-documented.

The news: Prime Minister Andy Burnham appoints the UK’s first AI minister.

Why it matters: Andy Burnham, who was officially named Prime Minister on July 20, appointed Kanishka Narayan MP as the UK’s first AI minister in one of his initial moves. The decision represents the acknowledgement of AI as a vital policy challenge for the government, considering the risk to British jobs, health and safety concerns, as well as the uncertainty surrounding the impact the tech might have on economic structures. It also comes off the back of Burnham’s belief that nations have a limited window to take control of AI and shape its impact on the country. However, some say the move reflects Britain’s efforts to join the global AI race, attempting to catch up with the likes of the US and China.

The news: OpenAI’s new merch line draws less-than-enthusiastic response.

Why it matters: OpenAI has opened its Supply Co. merchandise line to the public, selling branded T-shirts, hoodies, caps and accessories that it describes as “physical expressions of research energy”. Previously reserved for employees, the collection borrows from the language of limited-edition fashion drops, complete with archival pieces and collectible ephemera.

The internet, however, is largely unconvinced. Across social media, many are questioning who the products are for and likening the launch to Silicon Valley’s latest attempt to become a lifestyle brand, with critics taking aim at everything from the pricing to the aesthetic.

It’s the latest in a string of attempts by Big Tech and AI companies to borrow cues from fashion — whether that be merch, Palantir’s workwear jackets, or Meta’s AI smart glasses — in an effort to transform themselves from software providers into cultural brands.

The news: Apple escalates dispute with OpenAI over ex-employees.

Why it matters: Apple has intensified its dispute with OpenAI by contacting dozens of former employees now working at the ChatGPT parent company, asking them to retain documents that could become evidence in an ongoing trade secrets case. The move follows the lawsuit Apple filed last week, which alleges confidential information relating to its future hardware projects may have been taken by former staff who later joined OpenAI’s expanding devices business. OpenAI has rejected the allegations, saying it neither sought nor benefited from Apple’s proprietary information.

The fierce competition for experienced hardware talent reflects a broader shift, as AI companies look beyond chatbots towards consumer devices. Both Apple and OpenAI are reportedly developing AI-powered smart glasses, a category that could take wearable AI mainstream.

Apple enters that race with decades of experience building consumer hardware and one of the world’s most recognizable design identities. Meanwhile, OpenAI is trying to establish those credentials more rapidly through its partnership with Jony Ive and the acquisition of his AI firm, io.

The news: Meta discontinues controversial Instagram AI feature for new AI image generator.

Meta’s wider Muse Image text-to-image model, developed by its Meta Superintelligence Labs division and integrated across Meta AI, is still in place. The model enables users to generate images from text prompts, edit existing photos, apply visual effects, create custom graphics and produce creative assets within Meta's apps ecosystem, including Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook. It’s part of Meta’s broader strategy to embed generative AI directly into its consumer products, rather than offering it as a standalone creative tool.

The news: Meta tests always-on “super sensing” smart glasses, FT reports.

Why it matters: Meta is testing a new line of smart glasses that would continuously record audio while taking photos every few seconds, according to the Financial Times, which cited multiple people familiar with the matter. The idea behind the new glasses, according to the reports, is that wearers could then ask the Meta AI model that’s built into the glasses what they have seen or heard, or to recall part of their day.

The news: Phia shopping app accused of claiming unearned affiliate sales.

Why it matters: AI shopping app Phia is facing criticism after an investigation by Bloomberg found that it improperly collected affiliate commissions on online purchases. The claims center on the app’s browser extension, which is alleged to have replaced existing rival affiliate tracking links with its own during checkout, allowing it to receive credit for sales it may not have originated. Phia has said the behavior resulted from a technical issue that has since been resolved. Given that Phia’s business centers on affiliate revenue, the allegations throw the startup’s credibility into question. They’ve also prompted renewed scrutiny of affiliate tracking practices across AI-powered shopping tools.

Fashion brands increasingly rely on affiliates — including publishers, creators and shopping platforms — to influence purchasing decisions, with commissions tied to accurate attribution. If AI shopping assistants increasingly become another layer between consumers and retailers, questions around who deserves credit for a sale, and how that credit is assigned, will likely become more significant.

The news: Film studio Neon acquires rights for Sam Altman biopic Artificial.

Why it matters: Indie film studio Neon has closed a deal to acquire the rights to produce Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s forthcoming $40 million drama about Sam Altman’s leadership of OpenAI, after Amazon unexpectedly abandoned the project despite nearing completion. It comes after Netflix, A24, Mubi, and Focus all chose not to back the film after viewing it at pre-sale screenings, per reports by Variety.

Variety also reported that, according to those who have seen the film — which is set during a tumultuous time at the AI company, when Altman was fired and then reinstated as CEO in late 2023 — Guadagnino’s portrayal of the executive is less than favorable.

The move reignites questions about Big Tech’s growing influence over culture: Amazon’s decision followed its multi-billion-dollar OpenAI partnership, prompting speculation over whether commercial relationships are beginning to shape creative output. The news follows Google’s $75 million investment in indie film studio A24, which experts say was a bet on its creative influence and cultural legitimacy.

The news: “Exuberant” AI spending could threaten the global economy, the Bank for International Settlements warns.

Why it matters: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), often referred to as the central bank for central banks, has warned that Big Tech’s trillion-dollar AI spending spree risks ending in a prolonged investment bust, if the promised returns fail to materialize.
